Cavity magnomechanics provides a setting in which microscopic materials can drive significant mechanical movements, resulting in previously unattainable scaling of magnomechanical effects. Utilizing two-dimensional magnetic materials with inherent spin-1/2 properties, we have developed a model describing the interaction between an optical cavity, mechanical cavity membranes, and these materials, taking into account pure spin exchange coupling. Our findings include the analysis of steady-state scenarios characterized by non-trivial spin, orbital, and electromagnetic states. Additionally, we have explored the influence of imperfect single particle conditions on these states, as well as the feasibility of creating Bell-like states through both one- and two-photon inputs. Our proposed design sets a foundation for integrating cavity magnomechanics into novel 2DM-based devices, opening doors to novel applications in magnomechanics and quantum information handling. Furthermore, our study lays out a roadmap for achieving the quantum MacKay effect, which could serve as a landmark in the field. It discusses the means to accomplish this phenomenon using magnetic materials missing this element. Our proposed design also provides a basic framework for integrating cavity magnomechanics into novel 2DM-based devices, opening up new avenues for magnomechanics and quantum information handling. Lastly, it outlines a plan of action to achieve the quantum MacKay effect, a notable milestone in the field, and suggests that two-dimensional magnetic materials could be used to accomplish it. \\

This study introduces the Evolutionary Pathway Creator (EPC), a novel approach to learning control policies for quadrupedal robots using reinforcement learning. In contrast to traditional methods, EPC trains a policy that generates suitable body poses in addition to movement commands. In doing so, EPC obviates the need for complex state observation mechanisms, thereby simplifying training and reducing the likelihood of control instability. In experimental validation, EPC demonstrated the ability to create an adaptable control policy capable of executing diverse movements on a soft-bodied robot without prior knowledge of dynamics, resulting in improved performance over a basic reinforcement learning method. Furthermore, EPC demonstrated robustness on a hard-bodied robot with minimal additional training. In comparison to a leading reinforcement learning method, EPC achieved faster training times and produced more consistent results. The study highlights EPC's potential for widespread application in learning control policies for a broad range of robots. This research proposes an approach for reducing the computational expense of nonlinear optimal controllers through self-modifying hardware implementations, but due to online learning limitations, this method is only suitable for a limited number of rewirings. Consequently, we introduce an unsupervised reinforcement learning algorithm capable of extending the efficacy of nonlinear optimal controllers beyond the limitations of learning-based methods. Building upon a model-free linear quadratic Gaussian (LQG) controller, we have developed two-phase training methodology, comprising an initial unsupervised reinforcement learning period, during which a linear controller optimizes a linear approximation of the nonlinear system's dynamics, and a subsequent model predictive control (MPC) step, which refines the linearization and increases the robustness of the linear controller. This two-phase approach enhances the performance of LQG over both standalone linearization and MPC methods. Additionally, we have demonstrated that our reinforcement learning-based linearization can serve as a transferable solution for similar nonlinear systems with modified inputs, achieving an average 30% reduction in the required number of training steps when applying the learned controller to novel systems. This two-phase training methodology, combining reinforcement learning and MPC, expands the applicability of model-free nonlinear optimal controllers, making them more practical for systems with limited data availability, where traditional model-based approaches may not be feasible. Moreover, our approach has the potential to complement existing hardware redesigns to reduce implementation costs and improve system affordability. This research has been enabled by a novel tool, the Python AGent for Nonlinear Control (PAGC), which allows for the simultaneous online and offline exploration of the nonlinear system's dynamics in real-time and is an essential component of the presented two-phase training algorithm. A new study used data from SOAR/MOSAIC and VISTA to expand our understanding of this relationship for a subset of galaxies within the CDFS field, focusing on how galaxy morphology affects their masses. By analyzing an initial cohort of galaxies with provenaceous metal content between 0.01 to 0.25, researchers found that elliptical galaxies have a greater mass ratio compared to spiral galaxies. This difference suggests an average variation in mass ratio ($\log M_{\rm halo}/M_{\rm star}$) of nearly 0.5 for all galaxies within the given mass range ($M_{\rm star}$ = 10$^{9}$ $M_{\odot}$) and that mass ratio increases with stellar mass. Furthermore, an analysis of the masses of galaxies with provenance metal content between 0.01 $< Z < $ 0.25 revealed a decline in the difference between elliptical and spiral galaxies, suggesting that the difference in mass ratio arises due to star formation differences early in a galaxy's life. This discovery could imply that mass-dependent suppression of star formation leads to more massive halos attached to galaxies with reduced metal content. This finding is consistent with theories of gas heating and their subsequent impact on a galaxy's mass. Continuing observations with VISTA and PFS are essential to further explore this relationship, particularly among galaxies with earlier star formation. While aerosols play a crucial role in Earth's energy balance, there is a lack of comprehensive information about their optical properties. Our team developed innovative methods using stellar photometry to measure aerosol optical depth (AOD) and cloud effective transmittance. Employing wide-field telescopes allows for simultaneous observation of hundreds of thousands of stars, enabling highly spatially-resolved AOD mappings. Our approach generates precise AOD maps at a scale of ~10 km. We validated these observations by comparing them with ground-based measurements, and found good agreement with regional AOD averages. We demonstrated that our technique produces reliable results under varying aerosol conditions. This aerosol retrieval algorithm was tested using data from the SKYMAPK network and the UKMO reanalysis dataset. Incorporating stellar photometry into operational aerosol remote-sensing systems allows for an expansion of spatial scale from ~10 km to ~100 km at a cost of reduced temporal resolution. This novel technique may become a vital tool for monitoring global aerosol patterns if widely applied in operational systems. Utilizing temporal integration over multiple nights enables precise aerosol depth measurements. To better understand this process, we developed two theoretical models one involving magnetic forces and the other photoevaporation, both of which were validated by comparing their predictions with actual radio observations of the TW Hydrae disk. However, unlike the magnetic model which failed to account for the observed emission lines when it exceeded a certain threshold, the photoevaporation model produced results that closely matched the observed emission lines without exceeding a certain threshold. Furthermore, we discovered that the photoevaporation model emits a bright plasma with properties similar to that observed in other protoplanetary disks. Despite this, both models struggled to account for the observed emission lines at very close proximity to the star. We introduce a new method, dynamically weighted inertial forward-backward (DWIFOB), to tackle broad monotone inclusion problems. By combining the forward-reverse algorithm with a dynamically adjusted step size and weighted acceleration techniques, we ensure convergence to solution sets to any monotone inclusion problem. Furthermore, we prove that DWIFOB operates within a specific region and, under certain conditions, yields convergence rates for $\ell_1$-monotone inclusion problems. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we apply DWIFOB to optimization problems and reveal its advantages over other acceleration techniques, such as Tikhonov regularization, the Chambolle-Pock algorithm, and the accelerated forward-reverse algorithm. Our empirical testing also validates its superior performance across various scenarios. A relevant MATLAB code for DWIFOB can be accessed via https://github.com/tiepeng/DWIFOB. This study broadens the applicability of the forward-reverse algorithm to include optimization problems involving non-differentiable $l_1$-norms, representing a key contribution that outperforms prior acceleration methods, particularly when data availability is limited. Additionally, we propose a new version of the forward-reverse algorithm, the weighted inertial forward-reverse (WIFR) method, which exhibits convergence to solution sets for any monotone inclusion problem. Although it demonstrates a more restricted convergence zone compared to DWIFOB, WIFR exhibits superior performance in numerical testing, especially when data availability is limited, and shows potential for further improvement by incorporating a weighted acceleration technique. We also examine the differences between linearly constrained and unconstrained optimization, revealing new insights and highlighting potential areas for future research. Finally, we investigate the relationship between the step size and weighted techniques in the forward-reverse algorithm, which poses an open research question for future exploration. In terms of its practical applications, this study has far-reaching implications for using non-differentiable $l_1$-norms in optimization problems, which are extensive in various fields, such as image denoising, compress sensing, and genomics. These areas often involve working with sparse data, which can be effectively regularized using the $l_1$-norm to encourage solution feasibility. Given the simplicity and broad applications of DWIFOB, along with its enhanced performance as demonstrated in our analysis, we firmly believe in its potential as a leading algorithm in solving monotone inclusion problems and optimizing tasks involving the $l_1$-norm. A key area for future research will be its extension to handle multiple variables in optimization

In the framework of the quark-meson model, we have investigated how quarks interact with mesons in a specific phase of matter where chiral symmetry is broken. Utilizing a theoretical description with meson fields that deviate from symmetry, we have simulated this interaction at varying temperatures and quark densities. Our simulation reveals the existence of two types of phase transitions, one of a solid-like and one-phase liquid state, which arises from the collective behavior of mesons. Furthermore, at lower temperatures, we have observed a second-order phase transition that differs from a similar transition in a symmetry-preserving model, as well as an abnormal phase transition that causes the quark condensate to decrease with increasing quark density. Additionally, we have assessed the relationship between this phase transition and the disruption of chiral symmetry by fitting a parameter that represents a characteristic energy scale. Finally, we have estimated that, at approximately $T \approx 18$ MeV, the quark-meson system undergoes a phase transition similar to that which occurs in matter at the end of time following the Big Bang, known as the quark-nugget phase transition, which arises from the spontaneous formation and decay of quark nuggets, a hypothetical form of matter thought to have a role in the cooling of the early universe following the Big-Bang. Our simulation shows that this type of phase transition does not occur at zero temperature, contrary to expectations. However, at approximately $T \approx 18$ MeV, we have observed a first-order phase transition, which indicates that, in the quark-meson model, the quark-meson interaction results in a cauldron-like state of matter, while, at higher temperatures, it transitions into a solid-like and one-phase liquid state. Moreover, we have discovered that, in matter where chiral symmetry is broken but not completely broken, it transitions into a cauldron-like state, whereas, in matter where chiral symmetry is broken, it transitions into a solid-like and one-phase liquid state. Moreover, we have determined that, at approximately $T \approx 18$ MeV, it transitions into a cauldron-like state, which is not accompanied by a decrease in quark condensate, while, at higher temperatures, it transitions into a solid-like and one-phase liquid state, which is accompanied by a decrease in quark condensate. Our study has therefore established that, in matter composed of quarks and mesons, it transitions into a cauldron-like state

Investigations into mercury-based semiconductors and topological insulators are gaining significant momentum due to the potential to improve device performance, as they possess naturally existing low-energy states near the Fermi level. Our computational studies have discovered a newly identified class of topological insulators, comprising mercury telluride compounds, which exhibit large band gaps and are stabilized by an internal tetrel bond. Phyiscal examinations are recommended to verify that these materials display non-metallic, semiconducting properties. Notably, mercury telluride topological insulators have the capacity to undergo dynamic stability, whereas their tin counterparts are dynamically unstable, exhibiting phonon soft modes. Our research also predicts that these materials can be successfully crystallized using chemical pressure, leading to a transition from semiconducting to topological insulator phases within CdMn$_4$Te$_3$ and CdHg$_3$Te$_2$. Additionally, mercury telluride insulators exhibit exceptional robustness against external distortion, including high external pressure, where the band structures and topological properties remain preserved. Overall, these findings suggest that mercury telluride compounds represent an exciting and versatile family of semiconductor and topological insulator materials.

Reinforcement learning agents can be vulnerable in certain situations, particularly when their behavior is outside of a controlled environment. Exploiting these weaknesses, an attacker can influence the learning process of these agents for personal gain, often without directly affecting the reward structure. A novel form of attack examined in this research involves manipulating the attack speed of a bandit agent, revealing a significant gap in current defense mechanisms. This research investigates the application of a distinctive class of aggregate functions that can efficiently support distributed machine learning operations on complex networks. Next, we develop a machine learning algorithm utilizing these functions and prove its effectiveness. Finally, we conduct network simulations to illustrate the algorithm's capabilities and evaluate its performance. Notably, our results demonstrate that using this aggregate function type, the computational overhead is predominantly concentrated at a single node, while other nodes incur minimal or no overhead. A key goal in modern atomic physics is developing an ultra-sensitive device capable of not only trapping a single atom but also accurately identifying its microscopic state. To achieve this goal, we propose an innovative optical micro-trap system which not only provides a robust tool for physics experiments but also serves as a fundamental component for quantum communication and computation. Our design utilizes the principles of phase difference and interference to channel atomic waves into a confined space. By integrating an additional laser into the system, we can adjust the trap's frequency to match an acceptable range, thus capturing atoms through a process of recollision. Our calculations show that this system is capable of holding a single atom at an incredibly low energy level, and we predict a successful capture rate of around 88 percent at a temperature of micro-Kelvin. Furthermore, we outline a strategy for measuring the single atom's magnetic or electric dipole moment. Our concept has potential applications in fields such as ultracold physics, quantum information, and atomic spectroscopy, and could be implemented using existing technology to build an integrated trap system capable of single-atom manipulation and measurement.

The creation of nitrogen can significantly impact the final composition of new cores, affecting both its size and structure - a larger amount of nitrogen means a core will be smaller and more dense. The occurrence of extremely massive stars, typically spanning a narrow mass range, offers a unique test of our understanding of nitrogen synthesis. These stars are hot throughout their entire existence, meaning they do not experience the significant cooling and contraction that would limit the amount of non-hydrogen and helium matter they contain. As a result, they should possess a substantial amount of nitrogen. Predicting the effects of social phenomena on online platforms is crucial for anticipating and mitigating severe online events such as misinformation campaigns. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have been successful in this social impact forecasting task, but previous work has only evaluated its performance on a single dataset, leaving the performance on other datasets unknown. A new approach involves adapting GNNs for forecasting by refining their architecture through additional layers or connection methods. Despite a lack of empirical evidence, some modifications are more than others and it is not known how they would perform on other datasets. To address these limitations, a novel GNN architecture, referred to as the Social Impact Forecaster (SIF), is proposed. SIF's connection method mimics the propagation of information online by only connecting nodes with similar characteristics, thus preserving the important spatial relationships in the data. SIF's performance is compared to alternative modifications and a comprehensive evaluation is conducted using six real-world datasets. SIF achieves the highest overall accuracy and fastest training time, demonstrating its versatility and making it a suitable candidate for adaptation on other datasets. To further empower the adaptation of GNN architectures, a set of simple and effective improvements, referred to as Train and Evaluate Time Expansion (TETE), is proposed. TETE involves refining GNN architectures through additional layers or connection methods based on their performance during training and evaluation. TETE is empirically shown to improve the performance of GNN architectures by up to 5.5% accuracy and reduce their training time by up to 2.3x, making it a useful approach for adapting and improving GNN architectures. To facilitate the reproduction of these results, the source code and datasets used in this study are made available for public use. Additionally, a set of GNN challenges, referred to as the Social Impact Forecasting Benchmark (SIFB), is established to standardize the evaluation of social impact forecasting methods. SIFB comprises of ten tasks that target various social phenomena, such as misinformation propagation and event forecasting, across different datasets and evaluation metrics. SIFB is made available for public use, enabling the community to standardize the evaluation and comparison of social impact forecasting methods. Our proposal is an optimization method for extracting object orientation from observed features. We begin with a straightforward observation that for an ideal pose estimation outcome, image features provide perfect, undistorted projections of geometric shapes. This leads us to develop a full least squares error function to account for all distortions. We incorporate this criterion into a classic least squares procedure commonly used for extracting object poses from observed features. We present theoretical evidence that this modified approach will yield a unique solution under specific conditions. We also conduct experiments to demonstrate its performance. Specifically, CLS outperforms existing methods in accurately localizing a 3D cube when its projections on the image plane are manually altered. Additionally, CLS has been an integral part of computer vision systems for a long time, making it a reliable and established technique. We also examine its performance alongside other established methods, such as PNP and ICP, using a large-scale dataset and achieve better results. Lastly, CLS has been independently validated in other studies as a highly effective method for 3D pose estimation. Ultimately, our approach provides a fundamental contribution towards achieving robust 6 DoF object localization. We publically release the code for our approach at: https://github.com/isl-incubator/complete-least-squares. Also, the corrupted pose estimation dataset can be found at: https://github.com/isl-incubator/cluttered-3D-objects-dataset. This study investigates the challenge of colorizing grayscale videos captured by multiple cameras without using any image labels. Different cameras can capture varying color information due to misalignments, differing exposures, and other factors. Our proposed method, 'Cross- Camera Profound Colorization', utilizes a keyframe-based strategy to develop a cohesive color framework for videos captured by multiple cameras. It involves aligning cameras initially and then adjusting the colors captured by each camera to match a standardized keyframe. This method was tested using the Real-World Profound Challenge dataset and evaluated using two metrics: the gradient of the luminance zone and a multi-scale structural similarity index. Our results show that our method outperforms other baselines in generating video colorizations that are consistent across cameras. Our method can be found at: https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~vgg/research/video-colorization/. Experimental data and code are available at: https://github.com/tomjhelbing/video_colorization. Supplementary material is available online. This study was funded by the EPSRC and a studentship from Sony Europe Limited. It was carried out at the Visual Geometry Group, University of Oxford. \textit{Published at the British Machine Vision Conference 2022.}

GitHub's large repository of code involves significant maintenance operations, such as updating software versions, formatting file contents, and compressing files. These tasks could be automated but instead often require manual intervention, with developers repeatedly processing same files with different modifications. Leveraging this repetitive maintenance potential, this study proposes a novel technique called meta-maintenance. It involves analyzing execution data of maintenance tasks to identify opportunities for automation by grouping similar files based on their content and predicting the required modifications. Using a dataset of 1.13 million GitHub repository clones, the research demonstrates that a significant proportion of maintenance activities can be automated and these tasks are concentrated in a limited number of repositories. These findings showcase the feasibility of the meta-maintenance technique and its potential to streamline GitHub's maintenance processes. Furthermore, exploring the technique's applicability to Compose, a popular GitHub-powered service for updating software versions, yields encouraging results and opens doors for its application on other maintenance services as well as to Compose's development team. The study also introduces MANTK, a meta-maintenance toolkit, to facilitate the analysis and the application of this technique to maintenance services, and provides initial evidence of its effectiveness using a sample of 15,581 GitHub repositories. The research and its tools can be further extended by investigating the following questions: How to train models to predict file modifications? How to address concerns related to file confidentiality when applying meta-maintenance? How to handle maintenance activities not amenable to meta-maintenance. Difficult control issues in power systems pose a challenge due to non-linear characteristics, unpredictable events, and the interdependence of system parameters, making it essential to develop robust controllers with minimal computational effort. Although the multi-layer perceptron and Proportional-Integral controllers have been successful in addressing specific challenges, they fall short in tackling the broader difficulties. Meanwhile, deep reinforcement learning has shown promise in solving complex control problems, but its high computational requirements and lack of general applicability to various systems limit its feasibility. This research introduces a two-tiered deep reinforcement learning framework, addressing both the difficulty of non-linear parameters and the unpredictability of events, while also ensuring efficient computational demands. Moreover, the framework's structure allows for easy adaptation and the deployment of a control strategy for an interconnected multi-machine power system using a single GPU. The results indicate that the proposed framework outperforms existing methods in predicting system dynamics and suggests a significant improvement in overall power system efficiency. The study's findings showcase the capability of the two-tiered deep reinforcement learning framework in solving critical power system control issues effectively and efficiently. The development of this framework has the potential to pave the way for the deployment of a deep reinforcement learning-based control method in real-time, thereby improving the performance of power systems worldwide. The proposed framework's structure can serve as a versatile framework for solving various control challenges in power systems and similar complex systems. Finally, the study confirms that the adoption of a two-tiered deep reinforcement learning framework can significantly mitigate the difficulty of control issues arising in power systems due to their non-linear characteristics and the unpredictability of events, while ensuring efficient computational demands. The details are available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/AymanMekhita/Two-tiered-Deep-RL-framework.git. The initial findings from the first part of this research indicated that black holes of a certain mass range originate from a process other than stellar evolution.  This second part delves into alternative methods of black hole creation, focusing on how (super)massive dark holes emerge through these methods.  It shows that when active galactic nuclei, powered by dark matter accretion, are observed over broad wavelengths, they can exhibit broadband spectra resembling those of radio-loud active galaxies.  Two mechanisms are identified as distributing dark matter: a process involving the collision of colliding shells and a second mechanism involving fractal fragmentation.  It is found that the latter mechanism is more likely to give rise to (super)massive dark holes.  A model based on the second mechanism predicts an overall mass distribution of dark holes at $z<6$ that is in line with observations.  It is proposed that the growth of massive dark holes, following their creation through fractal fragmentation, is largely the result of the accretion of dark matter prior to the formation of light.  This would mean that massive dark holes, at least those above a certain mass, are primarily found in regions with higher than average dark matter densities.  It is suggested that subsequent mergers, involving dark matter clouds surrounding early galaxies, are responsible for seeding (super)massive dark holes.  A theoretical mass distribution of (super)massive dark holes, resulting from this process, is found to be in good agreement with independent observations of massive dark holes.  It is predicted that this process will lead to an overall abundance of (super)massive dark holes that greatly exceeds that of regular black holes.  It is proposed that massive dark holes, at least those above a certain mass, are primarily found in regions with higher than average dark matter densities and that a related feedback mechanism could help to resolve long-standing discrepancies in the modelling of galaxy evolution, particularly as they pertain to their growth rates and overall shapes.  It is suggested that further work will be needed to fully establish the role of fractal fragmentation in seeding (super)massive dark holes.  It is proposed that a key test of this theory will involve comparing the distribution of (super)massive dark holes, across a given mass range, with that of regular stars at $z<6$. To gain deeper insight into complex materials, researchers utilize inelastic neutron scattering as a powerful tool. Despite its effectiveness, analyzing the data often proves challenging due to its complex and multi-dimensional nature. Recent advancements in neural networks have presented an opportunity to apply supervised learning to this analysis. However, trusting the results relies on the network's transparency. This study introduces an adjustable, interpretable neural network to interpret inelastic neutron scattering data. Inspired by the success of similar applications with image classification, we adapted a convolutional neural network to process spectral data and developed an interpretable, adjustable version based on a multi-layer perceptron. By comparing the performance of these and other conventional approaches, we demonstrated that the adjustable networks offer a viable option for data interpretation. Furthermore, examining the decision trees generated within these networks provided valuable insights into the underlying connections between the material's properties and its spectral. This finding showcases the potential for these networks to serve as tools for discovering these connections, thereby broadening their utility in scientific applications. Ultimately, this work establishes a foundation for utilizing adjustable neural networks to interpret inelastic neutron scattering data and highlights their promise in simplifying data analysis and shedding new light on the underlying physics within complex materials. This study's findings also contribute to the ongoing discussion on the transparency and trustworthiness of neural networks in scientific applications. The code and datasets used in this study are publicly available via GitHub <https://github.com/andersonmoraes/Quasi-2D-NN> and PID <https://doi.org/10.17632/6z7a9b47909>. Over the past thirty years, preprint databases have undergone significant development and growth, transforming the way researchers share their research findings and citation habits. This change will be analyzed and discussed in detail. Initially, preprints served as an unofficial channel for researchers to disseminate their work quickly, as print journals had limited capacity and long publication cycles. However, with the emergence of the World Wide Web, preprint databases gained more significance, allowing researchers to rapidly make their work available to a broader audience before it was officially peer-reviewed. This facilitated an accelerated research workflow, enabled researchers to build upon each other's ideas more efficiently, and led to an increased dependence on preprints within the scientific community. Consequently, concerns about preprints potentially undermining traditional publishing models arose; yet, it is evident that both approaches will coexist in the future. Instead, the preprint system has become an integral part of the scientific ecosystem, and its continued evolution will likely be driven by technological advancements and changing researcher attitudes towards openness and collaboration. Ultimately, the preprint system has proven to be a dynamic and dynamic adaptation of the scientific ecosystem, and its continued evolution will be driven by the interplay between technological progress and shifting researcher values. This article presents a retrospective exploration of the preprint system's development, presenting a vision for its future growth and the preprint system's future role in the scientific community. Specifically, a search was conducted across major preprint platforms using specific keywords, resulting in the collection of 944 distinct preprint metadata records from arXiv, DOAJ, PubMed, and Zenodo dating back to the early 1990s up to the COVID-19 pandemic outbreak in 2020. The analysis encompasses preprint characteristics, including preprint types, research fields, and preprint dissemination methods, as well as the preprint cycle duration, including preprint versions and citation counts. The preprint system's development and growth are presented through interactive visualizations and statistical aggregates, revealing insights into preprint databases and their potential to accelerate research processes. The preprint data also includes references to the preprint authors' profiles, facilitating an examination of preprint publishing as a professional activity. The investigation looks into the links between preprint databases and the preprint publishing process, as well as the preprint system's role in the biomedical and computational scientific communities. Interestingly, a distinct pattern of collaboration and research sharing emerged within both communities, driven by distinct technical characteristics of the preprint platforms. Recent advancements in machine learning have driven the development of improved latent factor models through the use of representational learning methods like Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). However, the success of these models is largely based on empirical evidence and their theoretical properties remain poorly understood. In this study, we provide a differential equation and chance motivated GNN framework for latent factor models that offers insights into their design and evaluation. The proposed framework is grounded in the analysis of a stochastic gradient descent (SGD) process applied to a latent variable model represented by a graph. The resulting differential equation and probability measure provide insight into the algorithm's dynamics and basins of attraction. The findings motivate the development of GNNs for latent factor models in two settings: when the graph is known and fixed, and when the graph is unknown and must be estimated. The proposed graph neural network estimators outperform existing methods on synthetic and real-world data, according to multiple criteria for model fit and prediction accuracy. The source code for these methods is publicly available. The study offers a new perspective on latent factor models through the lens of differential equations and probability, and the proposed GNNs offer design principles for improving the fit and performance of such models. The analysis and algorithms presented in this paper may be of interest to researchers working on representational learning, graph neural networks, and latent variable models. The results may also be of interest to researchers working on differential equations, probability, and optimization, as the algorithms developed in this paper could offer insights for these fields. The proposed GNNs could be of interest to practitioners working on companies, markets, industries, domains, datasets; the source code for these methods is publicly available. The study offers a new perspective on latent variable models, and the proposed GNNs offer design principles for improving their fit and performance, particularly in contexts such as retail, sales, finance, economics, marketing, consumer behavior, and patient outcomes. The algorithms and measures developed in this paper could offer insights for understanding and modeling these domains. The differential equation and probability, as well as the design principles for graph neural networks, offer insights for understanding and modeling the dynamics and basins of attraction in these domains. The proposed graph neural network estimators outperform existing methods for predicting company similarity, market direction, industry trends, domain behavior, and patient outcomes. The source code for these methods is publicly available. We also design a family of vectorial Boolean mappings with exceptionally low nonlinearity, boasting a linear characteristic with prime characteristic field size $\char'40$. Moreover, we develop an algorithm to compute slim Sidon sequences within a specific range and demonstrate the efficacy of these mappings in cryptographic applications, specifically in side-channel attacks. Furthermore, we prove the $\theta$-uniformity of a particular mapping with exceptionally low nonlinearity, which we show generates slim Sidon sequences of significantly larger ranges with a simplified computation process. We also propose an iterative formula for generating slim Sidon sequences of the form $\langle v_{i-1}, v_i \rangle$, where $i \in \mathbb{Z}$, which significantly facilitates their computation. This research introduces an innovative sampling technique for binary arrays with a fixed margin, utilizing a modified measure that takes into account the distribution's margin enforcement, thereby resulting in uniformly spaced samples across the array's parameter space. A revised formula allows for efficient computation by mapping the array's parameters to a reduced dimensionality space, where the sampling measure can be easily calculated. While this method's performance is most evident in high-dimensional systems, it also demonstrates utility in lower-dimensional scenarios. A numerical examination highlights the algorithm's speed and accuracy in comparing the distribution of binary array outputs with and without noise. Additionally, this study showcases the application of the sampling technique in exploring the basins of attraction in a system featuring a saddle-node biforce point. The approach presented can be adapted for use in both continuous and discrete systems. The findings of this research may contribute to advancements in studying the behavior of binary arrays, an area with potential applications in coding theory and neural network analysis. The implemented algorithm has been made publicly available on GitHub under the name 'nuSAM'. The accompanying documentation includes a detailed guide to using the code. The deposited code can be utilized to generate the figures shown in this study and is further enabled by the inclusion of a Jupyter notebook file. Introducing a theory-based model to adjust parton distribution functions when evaluated at different energy scales and various perturbation theory orders. It incorporates a novel approach to deal with higher-order terms beyond perturbation theory's conventional limitations. The model utilizes a residual low-energy density matrix to represent non-perturbative interactions and incorporates concepts from instanton theory to calculate this density matrix. The resulting parton distribution functions are fitted to large-scale experimental data, producing phonological parameters that reflect the inherent characteristics of the QCD vacuum. Furthermore, this fitting process allows the model to determine a low virtuality scattering amplitude up to the fourth order in α_s. The adjustement procedure is shown to significantly improve the quality of parton distribution function fits, particularly for structure function data. The model is specifically tested with data from deep inelastic scattering, but it has the potential to be extended to adjust other non-perturbative quantities, such as gluon distribution functions and fragmentation functions. The article also explores implications of parton distribution function adjustments on the calculation of nucleon structure functions in the context of interacting quark and gluon scanning. The latter is a novel approach to understanding low-energy QCD phenomena in terms of instanton-induced non-perturbative effects. Finally, the article examines the validity of diffractive adjustment, revealing discrepancies between theory and diffraction data. The latter is likely due to the presence of diffraction-like backgrounds in experimental data. The model is available in public form at github.com/AndreySinyukov/PDF_ADJUSTMENT. The associated dataset is available at 10.6084/m1.fwine.1000.22. The complete derivation is available at arXiv.2209.14091. This study introduces a new method to create a parametric oscillation-based optical frequency comb using a microresonator. Through experimentation, it's demonstrated that initiating parametric oscillation in a microresonator through an integrated pump laser driver can produce multiple spectral holes within the device. These holes serve as optical memory units capable of storing and queuing phases as they rotate. As more pump power is added, the frequency spacing between these holes can be accurately controlled and made to match a desired comb pattern. This technique provides a means for generating frequency combs with specified characteristics, thereby paving the way for the development of innovative optical frequency comb sources and photonic integrated circuits. Furthermore, it's theorized that this approach can be adapted for use in other platforms, including Kerr microcavities and superconducting qubit arrays. This mechanism of parametric oscillation may also be employed in quantum computing systems to build complex entangled states. This research therefore holds potential for advancing both classical and quantum photonic applications. This capability could provide a new pathway for the metrological application of microcombs. Quantization has gained significant interest due to its capacity to reduce storage and processing requirements during inference. There's an underlying assumption that quantization also improves model generalizability, however this isn't thoroughly understood. This study investigates the connection between quantization and generalizability by analyzing the non-linear kernel of binary-weight neural networks (BWN) based on the spectral properties of their convolution operator. We demonstrate that the generalizability of BWN is heavily influenced by its kernel's low-rank structure, which is affected by the quantization error. We further show that the quasi-hierarchical nature of binary weights contributes to better generalizability when compared to equally performing full-weight models. To promote generalizability, we propose two novel optimization techniques focused on reducing the upper bound of the quantization error. These methods are versatile and can be utilized in various quantization methods across different domains. We evaluate our approach by achieving state-of-the-art results on ImageNet using binary-weight quantization techniques. Additionally, our method excels in fashion dataset NuevaYork by outperforming top-1 accuracy metrics by a substantial 5.46 %. We also successfully apply our findings to full-weight CNN models, resulting in a 7.53 % improvement in top-1 accuracy on ImageNet using a well-known quantization method. Code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/jbmanu/bwn_qb. extension/hq-bwn. extension/.html. Spectral analysis reveals that optimizing binary weights generates low-eigenvalue pairs that enhance generalizability, resulting in a low-rank structure from the convolution operator. This analysis confirms that the effectiveness of binary weights originates from their unique low-eigenvalue pairs. It is interesting to explore the generalizability of binary weights in the phase of network training, which differs from the commonly applied quantization methods in the post-training phase. While both approaches share some common aspects, the low-eigenvalue pairs in the training phase contribute more significantly to the generalizability. Therefore, we propose two novel optimization techniques focused on reducing the upper bound of the quantization error, which is applicable to both binary-weight and full-weight CNNs during both phases. Two commonly used spatial depictions, the grid-cell map and the topological map, are examined in the context of new lessons learned from reinforcement learning. Grid-cell maps, effective for covering a search area through the incorporation of extrinsic reward signals, may appear more capable of describing spatial learning induced by intrinsic motivations. On the other hand, topological maps, facilitating efficient navigation by emphasizing structural relationships over metric distances, can be seen as an outcome of selecting relevant features in the face of varying extrinsic rewards. Ultimately, these findings suggest a more significant role for the learner in shaping the spatial representation, with the environment playing a lesser part, and prompt a reevaluation of the established theories. It is also discovered that the induction of topological maps can be attributed to a combination of local optima presented by the extrinsic reward structure, as well as novel views of the search area resulting from rotational maneuvers, which break the symmetry in the topological structure and enable efficient navigation. This study represents the first instance where a biological spatial representation is reexamined in light of computational learning experiments, with the outcome potentially contributing to a deeper comprehension of the underlying neural mechanisms. At the same time, this research remains a preliminary attempt at incorporating insights from computational learning to illuminate the mysteries underlying spatial cognition in animals. As such, it primarily aims at inspiring new theoretical developments, rather than providing a thorough evaluation of the existing frameworks. It is also worth noting that the incorporation of intrinsic motivations, a salient aspect of this study, may not be applicable to all scenarios of spatial learning, where the extrinsic reward structure remains the primary driver of the topological map depictions. Future works will build upon this foundation, particularly with regards to incorporating multiple views through mobility, as well as the integration of intrinsic motivations in scenarios of spatial learning. It is anticipated that these developments will lead to a more precise evaluation of the induced topological maps depictions. To further confirm this expectation, a related contribution has been made in a companion paper, where the topological map depictions induced through the extrinsic reward structure are reexamined in scenarios of search-based reinforcement learning, where the learner navigates through a search area under the influence of extrinsic reward signals. This research has been awarded an best-paper award at the 2020 Conference of the American Association for Artificial Intelligence. This journal extension draws upon some of the key outcomes from this research, particularly involving intrinsic motivations in scenarios of spatial learning. Determining precise planetary orbits presents an enduring challenge in astrodynamics, a complex problem that even Isaac Newton struggled with when asking Albert Einstein about it. This critical issue has not been fully resolved, as evident from the numerous approaches described in N-body dynamics literature. One such approach, outlined in a 1927 paper by Louis de Fornel, involves creating a randomized force framework to facilitate the convergence of chaotic N-body systems to stable orbits. Although theoretical support for this method exists, no implementation of it has been documented in scientific literature. This report executes an N-body code using the REBOUND simulation tool to evaluate the effectiveness of a randomized force in finding periodic orbits for 3-6 body systems. Notably, our findings show that the randomized force can facilitate the convergence to stable orbits in all tested configurations within a relatively low number of steps. Additionally, we observed that the randomized force exerts a non-uniform influence on quaternions used to represent Euler angles in REBOUND's implementation, potentially improving its convergence rate. To enhance the reliability of our results, we performed both probabilistic analysis and quasi-Monte Carlo sampling to arrive at our conclusions. Finally, we discovered that the effectiveness of the randomized force depends on the cutoff radius used to eliminate short-range interactions, a parameter that requires further optimization in its current form. As a potential improvement, we suggest incorporating variance reduction techniques to increase the effectiveness of the randomized force, an enhancement we plan to explore in future work. It's worth noting that our analysis suggests utilizing an evolution time of $\tau$ in the range of several thousands to achieve satisfactory results. Future iterations of this approach should focus on addressing a potential issue of path dependence, which may arise from using REBOUND's fixed-step integrator, and documenting its convergence rate in relation to N-body indices $\nu$ and $\tau$. The implicit observation model, a key location tracking privacy framework, relies on calculating implicit variables to maintain user anonymity. However, this model has a significant flaw in environments with little location variability. To address this issue, we've developed a new framework that assesses the implicit model's effectiveness in environments with varying location patterns. Our analysis shows that while the implicit model offers more accuracy than the explicit model, its gains are largely seen in environments with consistent location patterns, a setting in which the implicit model is most often unnecessary. Data collected through resting-state fMRI via an ensemble of scanners at
multi-site locations presents a challenging task. Combining data from various
sites necessitates careful consideration of factors including instrumentation,
scanning protocols, and subject demographics, as well as coordinate transforms
to account for physical locations and magnetic field variations. Our study employs
a rigorous statistical approach to assess the influence of site-specific and
general factors on accuracy in predicting brain connectivity patterns. We utilize
an ensemble learning technique to develop a predictive model for multisite fMRI
data, demonstrating that incorporating subject-specific information enhances our
ability to predict connectivity patterns accurately. Furthermore, our analysis
estimates how accurately our predictive model replicates true connectivity in the
general population, as evidenced by cross-validation and data manipulation. Our
findings highlight that deep learning-based predictions for multisite fMRI data
are both reliable and generalizable. We calculate a lower bound for population
accuracy our predictive model achieves, specifically greater than 94%, and reveal
that cross-validation yields highly accurate predictions at four distinct sites. 
Notably, our analysis shows that cross-validation performs similarly to testing
using data from only one site, indicating that our model is resilient to changes
in data origins. We quantify the influence of site-specific and shared factors
on prediction precision, and examine the extent to which our model's predictions
reflect true multisite population dynamics. Our study establishes a statistical
baseline for a deep learning-based model's performance on a complex, multisite
dataset, and provides a usable template for evaluating other classification
models particularly suited to multisite and resting-state fMRI data. Additionally,
we make available a full implementation of our model, known as MultiSite-CFCN, on
GitHub for the benefit of the neuroimaging community. This publicly accessible
resource can be utilized to evaluate the model further on other datasets and
evaluate alternative approaches to multisite fMRI data. It may also prove
helpful for researchers working with multisite datasets who wish to validate their
data using our model. We make available the model implementations and our full
dataset of 32 subjects via the link below. \par

Zhang and Zhou proposed a theory relating entropy with the Ricci curvature of complex networks. Building on their work, our research extends the definition of Ricci curvature to directed graphs with a lower bound on this curvature, except in a single node. Under these conditions, we demonstrate the existence of a unique stationary Gaussian Markov random field with specific characteristics, such as a constant mean and uncorrelated components, thereby allowing for the normalization of a Gaussian field in the graph. Furthermore, we analyze thermal transfer and density of measures on these graphs, revealing unique asymptotes for both cases. Our findings are supported by numerical simulations on various networks, including an Erdos-Renyi model, a small-world model, and a network based on human communication. These experiments verify our theoretical conclusions and highlight the connection between the lower Ricci curvature bound and heat diffusion in the networks. Additionally, our work introduces a new method for characterizing the density of measures using Gaussian free fields, which may be useful in analyzing other types of random fields. Ultimately, our study sheds light on how entropy and thermal transfer are affected by the Ricci curvature of complex networks. To address these limitations, we have developed a new transition state representation called Transition state with word ends (TSE), which only utilizes word-end information along with its position. This novel approach eliminates the need for expensive fully connected layers, making linear computations possible again. Building on TSE, we have created several advanced transition state representations (TSR) based on relative positions. One of these variants, Relative End-Transition state with 4th order (RET4), has achieved notable success. A computational model reveals that pressure not only modifies the density of states at the Fermi level but also introduces significant changes in the interatomic distance, which conforms to experimental results. Furthermore, pressure-induced variations in the isotope effect and critical temperature are closely linked to changes in the density of states at the Fermi level. Notably, analyses under 127 and 155 GPa pressures show that the density of states at the Fermi level presents a saddle-point structure, a characteristic that diminishes with increasing pressure. While the critical temperature under 127 GPa experiences an isotope effect of 0.8K, the critical temperature under 155 GPa shows an isotope effect of 0.4K. By incorporating phonon corrections using a self-consistent RPA approach, we have estimated that the critical temperature under 200 GPa still surpasses 35K. Our study also demonstrates that the H$_{3}$S hydride superconductor adheres to an exponential isotope effect. Additionally, pressure has an amplifying effect on the van Hove singularity and the superconducting critical temperature. Although the H$_{3}$S hydride superconductor's stability under pressure is uncertain due to uncertainties surrounding a positive superconducting trend beyond 155 GPa, our analysis provides a theoretical foundation for exploring high-pressure superconductivity in doped molecular crystals. This study may also inform research on magnetic and transport properties in doped molecular crystals under pressure. When evaluating the effectiveness of a test in identifying causal relationships, Fisher's mean effect size is often utilized to compare the magnitude of causal and non-causal associations. However, the significance of Fisher's mean effect size in establishing causal relationships remains unclear. We previously demonstrated that LaRue's mean effect size is a precise indicator of the strength of associations contributing to a signal, but its relationship to non-causal contributions is more complex. Here, we reveal that LaRue's mean effect size can be expressed as a product of Fisher's mean effect size and a measure of causal confidence. Consequently, the confidence interval of LaRue's mean effect size is influenced by both the confidence interval of Fisher's mean effect size and the variability in causal confidence. We then establish a method for assessing the reliability of causal inferences by integrating the confidence intervals of both LaRue's and Fisher's mean effect sizes. Moreover, this integrated approach allows for a comprehensive evaluation of consistency between signals generated by common underlying causal mechanisms, as well as signals that may be non-causally related. Finally, we utilize this integrated framework to reassess the credibility of past research on the HAP, demonstrating that while a narrow range of data supports this theory, the existing research is susceptible to non-causal influences. In summary, the significance of Fisher's mean effect size in establishing causal relationships is best understood within the context of our integrated approach, which treats it as a critical, though not sole, indicator of credibility. We argue that this integrated ethological framework should be employed to assess the causal relationships underlying behavioral phenomena. Ultimately, this research highlights the necessity for a more nuanced evaluation of evidence in behavioral neuroscience, emphasizing the significance of integrating multiple effect sizes to evaluate signals and assess the reliability of causal inferences. Numerical investigations into the merger of a black hole and a neutron star have been conducted through simulations incorporating various factors such as electromagnetic fields, neutrino emission, and fluid dynamics.  By analyzing the outcomes under diverse initial conditions including magnetic field arrangements and strengths, as well as differing equations of state for neutron stars, researchers have gained insight into the significant influence of these variables on the gravitational wave signals and mass ejection events following the merger.  Computations using an advanced general-relativistic simulation model have revealed notable effects of electromagnetic force, neutrino feedback, and fluid non-linearity, resulting in the creation of extremely long-wavelength inhomogeneities and extremely short-lived, high-energy neutrino emissions.  Furthermore, differences in equations of state for neutron stars have been found to significantly affect the final mass of the black hole created in the merger, leading the research team to suggest that neutron star collisions could serve as precise indicators of how matter behaves under extreme gravitational forces.  Importantly, these findings emerge during the initial seconds following the merger, preceding the emergence of distinct mass ejection events, and could thus be directly compared to observations of gravitational waves for greater understanding of neutron star physics.  Additionally, research implies that electromagnetic force plays a crucial role during the initial minutes of neutron star collisions, ultimately shaping the outcome and resulting configuration following the merger.  As grational waves from neutron star collisions can potentially be detected by upcoming instruments like LISA, research into these phenomena using realistic models becomes essential for accurately interpreting future observations.  As demonstrated by the studies presented here, even basic simulations involving electromagnetic force, neutrino emissions, and fluid non-linearity yield significant outcomes, indicating the necessity of future simulations to surpass present computational limits and simulate merger times spanning up to one hundred seconds.  In doing so, researchers predict that future observations could reveal an "emission decked" double binary system comprising a black hole and neutron star, potentially illuminating fundamental astrophysical and theoretical hurdles.  In particular, research indicates that neutron star collisions could offer a unique window into the final seconds of these objects as they merge with a black hole, potentially yielding valuable insights into the physics of neutron stars.  In contrast, research into the collisions of neutron stars and black holes suggests that these events may fail to illuminate the dense matter at play, instead yielding data more closely aligned with stellar collapse models.  In general, research into neutron star collisions using realistic models has shed light on previously unexplored aspects of these mergers, and indicates that future observations could yield substantial outcomes

The online crowdfunding scene is becoming increasingly popular, allowing anyone to secure funding by garnering public support. Our cross-cultural study encompassing over 10 million crowdfunding campaigns from Wikipedia and CrowdSource, spanning countries such as China, United States, Brazil, and India, revealed key factors that influence campaign success. We analyzed these indicators across four diverse populations and found that they share three common ones: (1) crowd engagement through social media, (2) public feedback from donors, and (3) high initial fundraising success. We explored the impact of these factors on campaign success, discovered patterns specific to population preferences, and proposed general strategies applicable to a broad audience. Our findings also shed light on the evolution of crowdfunding over time. Ultimately, our study's insights can guide users on how to effectively organize and promote their crowdfunding campaigns. The Kalman filter-based method for ordering tasks for multi-point robotic manipulators has a fast calculation speed but lacks adaptability to changing task orders. In contrast, machine learning algorithms can learn task sequences over time, but they are slow to adjust to unexpected modifications in task ordering. Despite some advancements, these algorithms often overlook the inherent structure of task ordering and often fail to utilize the spatiotemporal relationships between tasks. This study presents a new technique to learn task sequences using a variational autoencoder-based model, which accounts for the inherent structure and spatiotemporal relationships between tasks. This method also leverages clustering analysis to identify underlying patterns in task sequencing and reduces dimensionality of the task data, making it more efficient. Additionally, this study integrates the new approach with a real-time control mechanism for multi-point robotic manipulators, demonstrating its effectiveness through simulation-based testing. Compared to other state-of-the-art methods, this new approach demonstrates improved speed, adaptability, and data efficiency for a variety of task settings. Further information about this research is available online. The source code for replicating the study's results, along with the implemented software, can be found on the repository at https://github.com/fatemehkarimy/APRML_Tasks. A video demonstrating the study's results can be found at https://youtu.be/6RQ6m2M2gK8. This research has been funded through an NSF grant number 1921705. This study involves human subjects and has been approved through IRB number 2022TIMP2012A.

This study investigates how source variability affects video search outcomes and our engagement. To examine this, we employed virtual agents to simulate human search query behavior, analyzing the impact of source variability on search results and our viewing preferences. Additionally, we attempted to mitigate source variability by incorporating a watchability prediction model. This approach successfully reduced source variability and improved video recommendations, making them less prone to system-generated biases. Notably, our strategy also boosted user satisfaction with the recommended content. This research presents a novel source variability assessment method, utilizing virtual agents, that can be applied across various platforms to enhance user experiences and video recommendations. Furthermore, this study offers a model-based solution to minimize source variability and improve content retrieval quality. Specifically, we applied this approach to the video search domain but assert its applicability and adaptability to other datasets, enabling seamless integration into existing pipelines. Ultimately, this method can be dubbed "Source variability regularization" and could potentially be known by a different name if a specific dataset is employed. Crucially, our model-based approach can be replicated using deep learning models, facilitating its deployment in commercial services such as YouTube and Vimeo. Interfering with other transmissions, a common occurrence in wireless networks, complicates channel allocation decisions due to varying degrees of interference sensitivity. Existing research primarily considers non-interfering cases or assumes shared channels, excluding scenarios where multiple connections share the same band and are susceptible to interference. To address this, we've introduced a probabilistic medium access control method, accounting for interference relationships in a realistic and general-purpose wireless model. Our approach incorporates probabilistic transmission powers, aiming to optimize system performance through fair resource allocation, as demonstrated in a simulation involving wireless connections with reduced signal strength attenuation. Our results show the benefits of considering interference relationships, exemplified by reduced data transfer delays and increased network fairness compared to models ignoring such relationships. Furthermore, we've verified the effectiveness of our model through a comparison with similar non-interfering and shared-channel models, revealing a considerable gap in performance, particularly in scenarios involving a single connection interfering with others (edge cases) and shared channels. These findings underscore the importance of considering interference relationships for optimal wireless communication. Our research directly contributes to non-interfering models, offering up to 30% improved data transfer speeds, as well as a broader understanding of wireless communication principles, as demonstrated in a comprehensive simulation driven by real-world data. Lastly, we've freely released the source code of our research, allowing for replication of our results and future exploration of related topics. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) excel at semi-supervised node classification, but their effectiveness heavily relies on adequate label information for training. Acquiring numerous labels can be impractical due to the expense of human annotation or model complexity. Conversely, pseudo-labeling can increase data utilization by generating artificial labels from high-confidence predictions, which in this study, is taken to its limit. By examining pseudo-labeling's fundamentals, we propose a more effective strategy that leverages insight from pseudo-tagging. This method entails training two models simultaneously: a high-confidence model to create pseudo-labels and a secondary model to utilize these artificial labels efficiently. Notably, the proposed method offers an improvement over standard pseudo-labeling techniques, particularly when dealing with limited annotated data. Moreover, a comprehensive empirical study demonstrates the method's robustness across diverse scenarios involving various models, a range of hidden layer configurations, multiple pseudo-labeling techniques, and both citation network and European Transportation Situations dataset. Notably, the method achieved an impressive 25.8% classification accuracy when evaluated on the European Transportation Situations dataset with limited labels, surpassing baseline approaches by 10.8%. The proposed method will be made accessible through an open-source repository. Additionally, the results, including source code and datasets, can be found on an online repository for reproducibility. This work represents the first investigation into training GNNs using artificial labels generated from high-confidence predictions, which serves as a foundation for further exploration into training GNNs using artificial edges and nodes in the future. It has potential applications in tasks such as misbehavior detection in social networks and product description classification for commercial market analysis. The method was found to be particularly useful when dealing with large graphs containing numerous nodes and a limited number of annotated nodes. The theoretical justification for the method involves the convergence of pseudo-labels and their similarity to genuine labels, which is supported by empirical results showing the progression of pseudo-label accuracy over training iterations. A notable discovery from the study is the polarization of node predictions during training, which can be mitigated by utilizing artificial labels efficiently through the proposed approach. The work also compares the method to established baselines, including standard pseudo-labeling techniques, as well as approaches employing ensemble learning, decoupled autoencoders, and transfer learning. In computer vision, sequences like videos demand efficient and scalable processing to differentiate from isolated images. We address this challenge by designing a neural network, called PatchNet, which builds on the idea of mapping local features between two input images to create a short-path model. By doing so, PatchNet enables the translation of input images into pre-trained backbone features at a fraction of the cost compared to traditional networks, all while maintaining their original resolution. As a result, PatchNet proves to be a versatile model, suitable for a range of tasks such as video denoising, deblurring, and compression. Notably, it demonstrates the ability to improve high-quality denoiser and deblurer models in a supervised setting, while exhibiting unsupervised learning capabilities with self-supervision. Furthermore, PatchNet exhibits adaptability on various datasets through a single training procedure. With significant memory and computational efficiency, PatchNet presents an appealing solution for working with long video sequences. The functional Gaussian graphical framework is a widely applied method for modeling dependencies in functional data, including graphical representations, differential equations, and distance-based models. Graphical models offer advantages in estimation efficiency and flexibility. This study specifically explores the functional X-distance model and the graphical Gaussian process, focusing on their equivalence and underlying assumptions. We demonstrate that the functional X-distance model reduces to a multivariate Gaussian process under certain conditions, particularly when dealing with independent and identically distributed functional observations. However, this model does not generally capture dependencies in functional data without making specific assumptions about the process generating the data. In contrast, the graphical Gaussian process provides a more general framework for representing dependencies in functions without precluding diverse stochastic processes, including those with dependent functional data. We establish that the functional X-distance model and the graphical Gaussian process are equivalent under specific scenarios, including when working with Markov Gaussian processes, as well as in cases where the trajectories are linearly related. We illustrate our findings with a real-world dataset from the study of neurodevelopmental trajectories. This research contributes to the ongoing development within the functional Gaussian graphical framework and its variants, with implications for modeling dependencies in functional data and using distance-based methods to inform statistical inference. At the same time, this work highlights the potential of the graphical Gaussian process to inform and complement existing approaches to modeling dependencies in functional data, offering insights into its capabilities and limitations. Assembling the human genome from next-generation sequencing data is a computationally intensive task that's becoming increasingly feasible with higher-throughput machines.
However, existing parallel approaches using compressed data formats and shared memory often limit themselves to a fixed number of processors and ignore memory availability, hindering full utilization of distributed-memory architectures like GPUs and clusters.
We introduce PARC, a new algorithmic strategy enabling efficient assembly of long-read data in distributed-memory environments by evenly distributing assembly tasks and ensuring contiguous memory access.
Utilizing LIBRA, a genome assembly tool, we demonstrate the versatility of our method and compare it to other approaches under different memory conditions. 
Our results show that PARC consistently outperforms other methods, including shared-memory techniques, in assembling chromosomes from human-like model organisms, while making optimal use of multiple GPUs. 
Given its versatility and performance, PARC can become a reliable tool for parallel genome assembly tasks. 
The code for PARC is openly available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/edgerec/parc. 
It is especially designed to facilitate the development of new compressed formats and can be used with other assembly tools with minimal modifications of the code. 
Furthermore, PARC's compatibility with basepair-level tools makes it an excellent candidate for enabling genome assembly using basepair-level data, a field that's only starting to emerge but holds great promise. 
In conclusion, PARC's innovative approach enables efficient assembly of long-read data in distributed-memory environments, demonstrating its potential to revolutionize the field of genome assembly. 
The experiments demonstrated that PARC can successfully assemble multiple human-sized chromosomes using 64 A100 GPUs, while also outperforming other methods, such as SCAI and MUMmer4, under different memory conditions. 
Notably, PARC's performance is most impressive when working with multiple GPUs, but it also exhibits excellent results with single-node, single-core configurations, thereby making it a versatile tool for genome assembly. 
The experiments with PARC used the LIBRA tool but the algorithm's independence means it can be easily adapted to other programs with similar results, as demonstrated by our testing. 
We therefore anticipate that PARC will become a valuable tool in the field of genome assembly for assembling long-read data, and its open-source code will contribute to the development of more efficient assembly methods.

This research focuses on improving the accuracy of structured text classification by leveraging patterns and inconsistencies within formatted text. A key challenge lies in enhancing models capable of extracting meaningful information from varied text layouts, particularly when human-generated content is involved. To address this issue, our proposed solution incorporates regular expressions as an additional input to structured text classification models. This involves learning the most relevant patterns that can aid in predicting labels, while also using these expressions to filter out irrelevant text sections, thus reducing noise and improving prediction accuracy. Additionally, our approach simplifies the process of creating training datasets with annotated regular expressions, thus lowering the barrier for organizations to implement this method. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this solution, we tested our approach against leading structured text classification models, using a dataset comprised of 36,000 articles from the New York Times, and achieved an average 25% increase in accuracy. Furthermore, integrating regular expressions as an input proved to be a distinct and valuable element, offering a comprehensive perspective on structured text content. While there may be a slight decrease in accuracy when including regular expressions, the benefits far outweigh the drawbacks, rendering this method a viable option for enhancing structured text classification. To facilitate wider adoption, our code, along with the developed model and methods, have been made available on GitHub. Furthermore, this research introduces a new evaluation metric for assessing formatted text models, specifically designed to distinguish between content generated by humans versus machines. This enables developers to tailor their models and layouts according to their specific requirements, including content types and formats. To showcase the efficacy of this metric, we contrasted the performance of various models and layouts on both human- and machine-generated content, revealing notable discrepancies and highlighting the significance of considering content origins in structured text classification. This research culminates in several key takeaways, including the potential of using regular expressions as an input to improve structured text classification, the importance of distinguishing between content types, and the possibility of using formatted text models to detect and mitigate noise. To expand upon these findings, we conducted an in-depth analysis of formatted text, specifically examining how text layouts and patterns influence structured text classification. This investigation reveals various trends, correlations, and inconsistencies, ultimately underscoring the complexity and variability of formatted text, thus emphasizing the need for further exploration in this field.
