A pioneering approach, known as Ensemble Model Output Statistics (ENOMOS), combines neural network forecasts with statistical post-processing techniques to produce precise model output predictions. One such method, the Simplified Extended Inverse Likelihood Weighting (SEILW) technique, is a widely adopted ENOMOS method that produces highly accurate results; however, its effectiveness significantly deteriorates when dealing with models that exhibit low forecast accuracy. In an effort to address this issue, we have developed an improved SEILW (ISEILW) method that builds upon the original SEILW procedure. ISEILW employs a risk metric to identify and mitigate unreliable model forecasts, thereby preventing inaccurate predictions from contaminating the final forecast outcomes. Through rigorous testing on a tropical cyclone case study, we have successfully validated the enhanced ISEILW method and demonstrated its ability to produce more accurate forecast outcomes compared to the standard SEILW procedure. Furthermore, the ISEILW method has widespread applications and can be adapted for use in a variety of ENOMOS methods and statistical post-processing techniques to produce highly accurate model output predictions. which has seen significant progress in recent years. However, there's still a gap 
between current theoretical predictions and data, especially when it comes to 
decays involving neutrinos, posing a persistent challenge to theorists. To close 
this gap, experts are employing various strategies such as incorporating final state 
correlations and using data-driven approaches to incorporate hadronic matrix elements, 
all within the context of accuracy-based physics demands. This review will outline 
the ongoing efforts to bridge the theory-experiments gap in tau physics. 

  Please note that I considered only published works up to December 2022 for this 
review. I didn't cover tau physics applications in Particle Identification or for the 
tau collider in this analysis. Also, since the topic is vast and rapidly evolving, 
this review likely lacks completeness but aims to provide a representative 
overview.

masses, and the increasingly important concept of final state radiation corrections. 
Additionally, this review touches on the underlying theoretical issues, strategies 
for incorporating new data, and potential future directions. It highlights both 
the successes and shortcomings of current theoretical predictions in order to understand 
the underlying physics better.

precision in order to fulfill the growing demands of experimental colleagues. It 
also underscores the essential role that theoretical predictions with high precision play 
in facilitating ongoing and future precision physics programs.

To evaluate and compare these solers, we analyze their energy decay in the context of Calabro's stability theory, utilizing a logarithmic boundary energy level. Additionally, we demonstrate the optimal stability properties of these solers in the case of constant boundary conditions via a Fourier Galerkin spectral method. To validate our findings, we execute and present numerical experiments in Gauss-Lobatto points. The L1 method shows a stronger optimal stability property than the CP method, but this result is contingent on the type of boundary conditions implemented. The opposite occurs when using Calabro's definition. A surprising outcome indicates that the CP method exhibits better decay rates than the L1 method in certain situations. Moreover, the maximum error bounds for both methods are nearly identical. Therefore, the Fourier Galerkin L1 scheme holds an advantage, especially when dealing with smooth boundary conditions, despite performing poorly under Calabro's stability definition. On the other hand, the Collocation scheme demonstrates robust stability and efficiency in both practical and theoretical contexts. Consequently, this method can effectively tackle unstable problems, including the von Karman plate equation, with a robust stability guarantee. Moreover, we extend our analysis to the impulsive variant of the Fourier Galerkin L1 method, demonstrating the optimal stability property and impressive performance, even for severe boundary condition cases. A theoretical justification matches the results obtained from the impulsive variant, specifically when employing Collocation as the spatial solver. Furthermore, the schemes' maximum error bounds are comparable, validating the use of the impulsive variant as a method. Moreover, the analysis extends Calabro's nonlocal stability definition, demonstrating the equivalence to a local stability criterion under specific conditions. The analysis is also applicable to various other problems, including the von Karman plate equation, with the sGS scheme exhibiting excellent performance, especially in both theoretical and practical scenarios. Building upon this understanding, a novel detection method using a self-supervised approach was developed, demonstrating improved performance compared to current methods when testing for four specific categories of OoD data. Introducing an epidemic model inspired by past studies, we refine it to account for factors like crowding, seating arrangements, and the protection offered by face masks. Utilizing data-driven approaches, we incorporate real-world data into our model. Notably, we applied a Bayesian estimation technique to a key model parameter governing the efficacy of face masks, yielding a well-fitting model outcome. Employing a forecasting strategy similar to that proposed in prior research, our results demonstrate the capability of the model to accurately predict disease transmission on urban buses, thus validating a previous proposed framework. Furthermore, our research explores the theoretical foundations of our model and provides a deeper understanding of the relationship between system variables, ultimately facilitating novel forecasting methods. Building upon prior research, our work expands upon existing studies while providing a solid theoretical basis for future work in urban bus dynamics. The combination of our epidemiological model and data-driven approaches could contribute to the development of effective strategies to mitigate disease transmission on urban buses, informing decision-making policies and guiding research into non-pharmaceutical interventions. The success of chess engines has prompted research into how humans select moves in this strategy game. By leveraging data from 8 million chess players on the Lichess platform, this study employs network analysis to examine the relationships between chess openings. By incorporating additional metrics, such as player behavior, it distinguishes between different approaches to analyzing these relationships, namely, similarity based on player preferences versus the connections between openings. Notably, this study reveals that experienced players tend to prefer more complex openings, while less experienced players show a higher preference for easier ones. Furthermore, this study also investigates how players adapt to novice opponents by "softening up" their play style when facing them. Ultimately, this study aims to provide a deeper understanding of how humans experience and interact with the intricate world of chess.

We propose a theory that certain supernovae known as pale dwarfs are the result of the consumption of a neutron star by a white dwarf following an exchange of particles. This theory is based on the radioactive heating caused by the decay of elements produced by the neutron star's rapid rotation. By matching observed characteristics of pale dwarfs with predicted ones, we establish a systematic method for identifying key features of millisecond pulsars, including their magnetic fields, spin rates, and the characteristics of the surrounding planetary systems. Our research provides a foundation for future development of more advanced and efficient shape retrieval techniques using immersive technologies. In an ideal fluid with an isentropic transformation, determining whether a initial configuration can achieve a more densely compact state is the focus.
We utilize an equation of state based on a linear relationship between pressure and density to examine this issue.
Despite having no bounded solutions, this model allows for an infinite sequence of successive states with increasing density.
We explore under what conditions these successive states can occur and whether they can asymptotically converge. 
We also consider a related optimization problem, with our analysis having implications for black hole formation in hydrodynamic simulations.

A useful tool for educating and researching on chip-level neuromorphic architectures is a simulation environment that models the hardware's behavior at a higher level of abstraction. However, creating such a environment from scratch is complicated due to the complexity of the hardware and the diversity of platforms it's designed for, making it difficult to implement and port across different platforms. Therefore, there's a need for an existing open-source framework that can be adapted to simulate various types of neuromorphic architectures. The TFlipper framework, based on SystemC, provides a suitable solution as it's compatible with IEEE 1666 standard and features a modular architecture that allows the simulation of different processor architectures. However, certain functionality required for neuromorphic architecture simulation, such as synapses and dendrites, is outside the scope of SystemC's specification. Therefore, our research modified the TFlipper framework to include the necessary functionality for simulating neuromorphic architectures. The resulting framework, although based on SystemC 2.2, is not limited to it and can be upgraded to SystemC 3.x. The adapted framework was successfully tested and validated through a transaction-level simulation of a full system scan, as well as a functional test that mimicked spike-driven neural behavior. As a result, the generated test cases effectively triggered the expected behavior in the simulated neuromorphic architectures. In conclusion, the adapted TFlipper framework provides a versatile platform for simulating various types of neuromorphic architectures using high-level programming languages, thereby facilitating research into the hardware's behavior and its transaction-level design. Furthermore, the simulated architectures can be employed for application-level simulations, providing a useful groundwork for future works. Additionally, the openness of the adapted framework means its source code can be utilized for future research and development. Lastly, we explored different options for increasing the simulation speed, albeit briefly, which presents potential avenues for future research and development. Ultimately, the transaction-level simulation of the simulated architectures holds great potential for facilitating future hardware and application development. This study aimed to expand on previous findings by exploring if conceptual feedback outperforms conventional detailed feedback in software testing education. An experimental design was employed with 80 students divided into two groups, one receiving conceptual feedback and the other, detailed feedback. Both groups showed significant improvement, but data analysis revealed no substantial cons to offering conceptual feedback with lower extra effort needed. The results also indicated no notable differences in learning outcomes based on the type of feedback provided. The study indicated that conceptual feedback is a viable option with reduced extra burdens and can lead to comparable learning outcomes compared to conventional methods. Understanding why a deep neural network (DNN) made a specific prediction is very challenging. Even by finely tuning the input data or identifying global model behaviors, we cannot determine the underlying reason for the predicted output. In this paper, we suggest an answer to this problem by introducing a new explanation method. Firstly, we divide the DNN into a feature extraction section and a decision-making section. We use concept analysis to represent the decision-making section with a set of key features and their interconnections, which are then broken down into more detailed components using integer programming (ILP). The resulting explanations are merged with the DNN's training data and model structure, making them the primary reason for the prediction. In our experiments, this explanation method performed well in domains such as text, biology, and literature, while also being significantly faster and less prone to errors than existing methods. Additionally, the resulting explanations are easily interpretable and highlight the limitations of the DNN. While these limitations apply to our method as well, the benefits outweigh them, making this approach suitable for data labeling and auditing in areas such as law, medicine, and content moderation. Ultimately, this explanation method has outperformed all other comparison methods in these domains. Interestingly, it also surpasses human explanations in these domains in terms of accuracy. In particular, this approach has achieved unprecedented levels of semantic similarity to human explanations, while simultaneously ensuring the reliability of these explanations. The implementation of this method, along with the generated explanations, can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/jjasso9/Concepts. Additionally, the related data and models can be found at https://jjasso9.github.io/Concepts. Furthermore, a demo of this approach can be found at https://conceptclarifications.github.io/. Lastly, Zhi has published a blog post on this work at https://medium.com/semantify/explainning-models-5f4b7b7b8e0c. In conclusion, this method represents a groundbreaking achievement in the field of explanation, particularly in domains with inherent conceptual connections. It has surpassed human explanations in numerous evaluation criteria and has achieved unprecedented levels of semantic similarity to these human explanations. This involves a specific function that is sensitive to the twist-3 diquark term and can serve as a distinct indicator of its presence. It has the potential to be measured experimentally, and calculating its value would allow for a quantitative determination of the diquark term. This process would help resolve an ongoing uncertainty associated with single-spin asymmetry and potentially reveal the distinct influence of the twist-3 diquark term in parton distribution functions. Implications of the twist-3 diquark term on cross section calculations and potentially novel effects in azimuthal angular momentum are also discussed. This could have far-reaching consequences for our understanding of hadronic interactions and the quark and diquark constituents of protons. This could lead to significant advancements in our understanding of parton distribution functions and potentially open up new areas of research. It is proposed that future experiments be conducted using the J-PARK 50 GeV proton beam to explore these novel effects associated with the twist-3 diquark term. This could involve examining specific correlation functions that are sensitive to the diquark term and potentially observing novel asymmetries that arise from its influence. It is expected that these efforts will help reveal more about the novel characteristics of parton distribution functions discussed here. We delve into the structure of nilpotent Hessenberg varieties in a comprehensive manner, utilizing a geometric vertex partition that enables a detailed analysis of their components. Through this framework, we derive new explicit sets of Gr\"obner bases for each Hessenberg variety based on a specific semistandard tableau order. Furthermore, our approach allows us, depending on the regularity of the Hessenberg shape, to obtain directly a complete set of Gr\"obner basis or an ideal with a minimal reduction set, specifically one resulting from a Frobenius separation, thus circumventing certain computational problems associated with ideal generation and verification of certain symmetry properties. Additionally, our analysis extends existing demonstration of the equivariance of the Gr\"obner basis under the action of the Weyl group to any Hessenberg function to a similar but more general scenario applying to nilpotent Hessenberg varieties. Ultimately, our method also facilitates a proof of the regularity of certain nonregular Hessenberg varieties. Examples are provided to illustrate our findings along with computational data for specific simple Lie types. We present supporting documentation for key software functions in Annex. Neural art generation has made significant progress in producing realistic images, but its artistic value remains to be determined. As a crucial step in evaluating the artistic merit of neural art, this study explores how images created by neural networks are perceived by human observers. Through an online study involving hundreds of people, we examined what features contribute to the artistic value of neural art and how it compares to human-created art. Our investigation used a combination of rating scales, including the Decoding Artistic Merit and the Global Aesthetic Scale, along with an analysis of the effects of stylistic factors, such as color palettes and brush styles, on the perceived artistic value of neural art. Additionally, we employed model-based inference to identify the underlying factors driving the artistic merit of neural art, and conducted a follow-up study to validate our findings. Crucially, our research found that the artistic value of neural art is influenced by different factors than its technical performance, as measured by metrics such as the Frechet Inception Distance. Furthermore, our study revealed that the artistic merit of neural art can be increased through a variety of techniques, including the incorporation of styles found in human art. Moreover, we observed consistent opinions among participants regarding the quality of neural art, indicating a convergence of opinions among observers. Our research provides a foundation for future investigations of the artistic value of neural art and its relation to human creativity. Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a widely diagnosed mental disorder, and ADHD-like behaviors are often linked to altered brain activity patterns in resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI). However, drawing conclusions about ADHD-like behaviors based solely on rs-fMRI data is complicated by the large amount of information involved. Recent research has shown that using Deep Learning (DL) algorithms can successfully diagnose ADHD-like behaviors using rs-fMRI data. This study aimed to explore how selecting crucial brain regions for rs-fMRI data affects the performance of DL models in diagnosing ADHD-like behaviors. Our research employed a widely used dataset containing ADHD-like behaviors and corresponding rs-fMRI data, and used three distinct datasets to map ADHD-related brain regions. We compared the diagnostic capabilities of DL models trained on complete rs-fMRI data to those trained on data containing only the identified crucial regions. Our results demonstrate that excluding non-essential information can significantly enhance the diagnostic capabilities of DL models, and that using data from key brain regions can reach comparable diagnostic performance to using the entire rs-fMRI data set. Notably, the efficiency gains from omitting unnecessary information were more pronounced for simpler DL models than for more complex ones. Ultimately, this research offers a groundwork for developing more streamlined and efficient DL models capable of diagnosing mental disorders using rs-fMRI data. In everyday communication, acronyms are widely used, but when readers or listeners are unfamiliar with the expanded form, they can become confusing, especially when used alone. This problem is particularly challenging on online platforms where users rapidly exchange comments, often containing acronyms and/or outdated or local references that may be unknown to newcomers or those outside the context. To address this issue, we've created MadDog, a pioneering clarification system targeting acronym ambiguities. MadDog is an end-to-end solution comprising two interconnected modules: Detection and Clarification. While other studies have focused on acronym detection or unrelated issues, MadDog innovates by tackling both detection and clarification tasks. For effectiveness, we've crafted an efficient, detail-oriented approach for each module. First, we've developed a robust acronym detection algorithm leveraging Domain-adaptive, Resource-constrained, BERT (DC-BERT) and F1-score based oversampling for enhanced precision and recall. Additionally, the Clarification module is designed with multiple pre-trained models, including T5, RoBERTa, and BART, for optimal performance, and by integrating rich context from Wikipedia and Wiktionary to provide clear definitions for ambiguous acronyms. Experimental results reveal MadDog's superiority over existing competition in terms of F1-score. Furthermore, user studies demonstrate users prefer MadDog's clarifications over competing systems. Considering its potential, we've released MadDog as an open-source platform for the community to utilize. We hope it will continually improve and evolve with growing community involvement. You can access MadDog at: https://madog.ai/clarify. We welcome contributions and corrections to enhance the dataset, especially in categories like Finance, Military, and Politics where the dataset is relatively limited. We intend for MadDog not only to facilitate communication but also to promote literacy by addressing acronym ambiguities across various domains. As online platforms expand, MadDog is poised to play a vital role in addressing this persistent issue. Our study introduces a novel concept in DNA storage, enabling the efficient organization of data through a hierarchical structure. This method utilizes the natural organization of DNA libraries in a tree-like format with multiple levels of differentiation. As DNA libraries frequently incorporate information about the sequence origin to facilitate data retrieval, our approach automatically determines the required level of detail for sequence identification. Unlike existing storage systems, which often require and update sequence tags for all reads, our hierarchical DNA storage model needs to know the sequence's starting point only once during the cDNA production process. This leads to a substantial reduction in the amount of information needed to identify a sequence, thus lowering the overhead of handling sequence identification and allowing more efficient use of DNA library space. Furthermore, as DNA storage systems may require changes to stored data over time, our model also enables support for sequence updates, merging existing sequences with updated versions. This is accomplished by combining parent and child nodes in a tree format, effectively moving sequence information to lower-level nodes and overwriting previous information with updated content. This capability not only enhances flexibility but also prevents sequence information degradation over time. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our hierarchical DNA storage model in managing sequence identification overhead, up to 41.8% improved the DNA storage efficiency when handling 100 sequences of 100 nucleotides in length using the Cambridge Genomics Centre's current sequencing technology. Additionally, our model shows a linear relationship with other storage systems, achieving equivalent performance at a similar scale. At a larger scale, our model shows a power-law relationship with other storage systems, achieving equivalent performance at significantly larger scales. This work presents a novel approach to DNA storage, enabling the efficient organization and updating of data through a hierarchical structure, a crucial advancement towards developing practical DNA storage solutions. This work sets a new standard for DNA storage systems, providing a template for future work and improving our understanding of the underlying storage medium. Furthermore, our study serves as a model, applying a novel DNA storage solution to a real-world problem. This work provides a practical demonstration, showing the efficiency of hierarchical DNA storage in real-world scenarios. Finally, our study serves as an example, utilizing hierarchical DNA storage to address a broader issue and highlighting its general applicability to real-world problems. This work can be replicated with similar results using widely available software tools, providing a clear demonstration and showcasing its efficiency. Additionally, our inputs and outputs can be shared with others, allowing the research to be built upon. This study presents a novel concept for hierarchical DNA storage, enhancing our understanding and providing a practical solution for DNA storage

Momentum-space nodal surfaces exhibit unique topological properties, characterized by quantized topological invariants and isolated zero-energy modes along related lines. This feature has been observed and harnessed in momentum-texture protected topological states, and recent implementations in photonic systems, superconductors with Rashba spin-orbit interactions, and twisted bilayer graphene have also been explored. This review focuses on the topological properties of momentum-space nodal surfaces and recent realizations in diverse systems, with a goal of advancing the understanding and application of momentum-space topology. It also examines the challenges and opportunities inherent in photonic realizations, where achieving the required nodal surfaces can be complicated by lattice discretization and surface states may be distorted due to scattering off the lattice. Nonetheless, momentum-space topology holds great promise for developing novel photonic devices, including twisted photonics. Furthermore, this area is seen to be a promising area of research at the intersection of quantum materials, quantum computing, and photonic technology.

We introduce optimized variational principles and quantum algorithmic methods for approximating the von Neumann entropy (VNE) of both unitary and Liouville dynamics. These techniques can be implemented using resources proportional to $\log^3(\varepsilon^{-1})$ for variational principles and $\log^2(\varepsilon^{-1})$ for quantum algorithms, independent of the system size. We also present experiments demonstrating the effectiveness of these methods in practice, particularly for approximating VNE in larger systems where traditional approaches based on density matrix decomposition become computationally infeasible due to the exponential growth of resources required. These experiments validate the theoretical bounds and highlight the value of the proposed methods for accurately estimating VNE in middle-scale quantum systems. Additionally, the developed techniques can be adapted to approximate other thermodynamic properties, such as the multiplicative uncertainty principle for quantum state uncertainty. This adaptation could be accomplished using resources proportional to $\log^2(\varepsilon^{-1})$. These findings enable the integration of the proposed methods into existing variational quantum eigensolver approaches, thereby enabling the simultaneous approximation of multiple properties like eigenvalues, VNE, and entanglement width within the same resource limits. This breakthrough could potentially enable the development of more robust and accurate quantum simulation methods for approximating thermodynamic properties. Furthermore, the underlying algorithms can be utilized to approximate VNE in classical circuits, and we present theoretical arguments indicating that this approximation likely requires resources proportional to $\log^2(\varepsilon^{-1})$. However, we also present evidence from extensive experiments suggesting that for a significant class of circuits characterized by slow-growth dynamics in both quantum and classical states, the proposed variational principles require significantly fewer resources than the predicted lower bound. These experiments demonstrate that the underlying principles can effectively generate nearly energy-preserving quantum states in circuit architectures and that the associated entropies can be accurately estimated using substantially fewer resources than the predicted minimum required. This finding presents an intriguing hypothesis that these dynamic systems may possess a hidden underlying structure that could potentially be characterized by a "dynamical phase transition," an concept that warrants further exploration in follow-up studies. Moreover, the proposed techniques can be adapted for approximating VNE in both quantum and classical circuits with resources that are only linearly dependent on $\varepsilon^{-1}$. This adaptation enables integration with existing unitary quantum eigensolver approaches and could potentially enable the creation of more robust and accurate quantum simulation methods for approximating thermodynamic properties, particularly when applied to dynamically stable quantum states

For effective clinical research and communication, standardized medical terminology, such as the International Classification of Diseases (ICD), is crucial. Current coding methods involving human clinicians and coding specialists are labor-intensive, expensive, and often reliant on anecdotal experience. Recent studies primarily focus on the clinical aspects of disease coding but fail to utilize the computational efficiency of machine learning. Our study combines clinical and computational knowledge to develop a multi-step, semi-supervised machine learning approach for automated ICD coding. Leveraging electronic health record (EHR) data and clinical guidelines, our model can predict primary ICD codes with up to 80% accuracy using limited labeled data. Our novel method integrates medical professionals' expertise with machine learning for a more efficient and scalable coding process. Additionally, we make our data available to support reproducibility. Our model showcases a versatile approach for combining clinical and computational knowledge, ultimately improving the understanding and analysis of disease data through machine learning. At the same time, we acknowledge the limitations of our model and encourage further research on deep learning methods for ICD coding, particularly using large datasets, long-term EHR data, and clinical modeling. To fully leverage quantum computers for machine learning, it's crucial to understand the mechanisms behind learning processes, whether or not they're being monitored. This work delves deep into the fundamentals of both quantum supervised and reinforcement learning on a superconducting quantum processor. Employing quantum monitoring to learn patterns in random data is explored, as well as the use of quantum measurement as a learning tool. Our findings indicate that, in contrast to traditional methods, quantum algorithms exhibit increased errors as the problem size grows. Interestingly, a certain level of monitoring can actually improve performance, likely due to the role of common eigenstates in the learning process. This suggests that, at least for the learning algorithms used here, quantum monitoring can provide an advantage. While the benefits of quantum learning outweigh the costs, the current techniques struggle to outperform their classical counterparts. Future advancements in quantum technology are anticipated to yield substantial gains over classical methods, making the development of reliable quantum algorithms a promising area of exploration. Additionally, the researchers utilized the quantum processor to create specialized states, known as Grover states, utilizing a previously untested learning protocol. These Grover states hold potential applications in searching databases and searching within massive datasets to find a specific item quickly. The researchers also discovered a way to use quantum errors to enhance learning outcomes, a phenomenon they term "quantum noise learning." This method could provide an extra layer of security for quantum computers, as the errors that previously hindered the learning process are now being harnessed to learn patterns in random data. The researchers speculate that this could provide an exclusive advantage over classical computers, potentially leading to the development of more resilient machine learning models. This work lays the foundation for understanding the underlying mechanics of quantum learning and monitors the learning process to improve it. The researchers employed a range of techniques, including variational learning and reinforcement learning, to explore the limits and potential of quantum learning. The study also identified areas for future improvement, pointing to the potential for quantum algorithms to overcome long-standing challenges in machine learning, particularly when working with noisy data. The researchers utilized a combination of analytical methods and numerical simulations to investigate the behavior of learning algorithms on a superconducting quantum processor. The utilization of error correction, a crucial element in scalable quantum computing, was found to substantially impact the learning process. The researchers also devised a novel approach to quantify the efficiency of error correction in quantum learning. The study explores the interface between quantum error correction and machine learning, revealing under what circumstances error correction might be necessary for efficient learning to occur. Real-world shading contains covert shadow details that convey crucial information about scene geometry. This hidden data can be leveraged to enhance photo-realism in computer graphics, metric accuracy in computer vision, and object detection accuracy in deep learning. However, existing methods often fail to accurately capture shadow information due to their simplistic assumptions about shading models, limiting their applicability in inverse problems that rely on real-world shading cues. This study introduces an effective and differentiable shadow calculation technique that models real-world shading cues and integrates seamlessly into deep learning training environments. This novel approach, known as SMMN, employs spherical harmonics to accurately predict shading cues, including shadow inception, Transverse ratio, and Anisotropic scattering. This technique has been validated through extensive testing on synthetic datasets and real-world images, demonstrating its superiority over state-of-the-art methods. Dr. Bar-Nyk is a leading researcher in computer graphics and computer vision, specializing in shading cues, verisimile rendering, and 3D reconstruction. This work is an extension of the researchers' previous findings on approximate shading cues and general machine learning methods. The influence of transverse intensity nonlinearity on dark solitons in Bose-Einstein condensates and optical solitons is analyzed. A fundamental change occurs when nonlinearity affects the dispersion, resulting in exponential instability in one-dimensional systems and a different oscillatory behavior in two-dimensional systems. Numerical simulations reveal that in two dimensions, solitons exhibit stable oscillations over a limited period. However, they eventually collapse due to the unique characteristics of the system's dispersion. The distinction between collapsing and oscillating behaviors in two-dimensional scenarios heavily depend on the relative values of the nonlinear dispersion and the linear dispersion. The oscillatory phenomena in one-dimensional systems are found to persist in a limited number of spatial dimensions, specifically three-dimensional systems. The oscillatory behavior in this scenario arises due to the absence of spatial dimension integration, leading to a non-exponential decay. The instability in one-dimensional systems is shown to persist in a particular scenario involving a (2+1)-dimensional system linked via fiber, where solitons exhibit an exponential decay. The distinction between oscillatory and decaying behaviors is observed to occur depending on whether the system is localized in a confined environment or exhibits a non-localized behavior. The decaying phenomenon in this scenario arises due to the combination of the intensity nonlinearity and wave propagation and is distinguishable from other dissipation mechanisms. The decay rate in this scenario is shown to be dependent on the soliton's initial speed. The dark solitons' instability is attributed to an energy exchange occurring between the soliton and the surrounding radiation, leading to a non-conservative behavior. The possibility of achieving a parametric soliton behavior, characterized by frequency-independent oscillations, is explored, with simulations showing that adjusting the nonlinearity parameter allows for converting oscillatory behavior into a parametric soliton. The achieved solitons persist for a limited time, with their longevity dependent on the system's linear dispersion. A method for increasing a soliton's longevity by adjusting the nonlinearity parameter is proposed, with potential applications including beam amplification and parametric devices. The study offers a fundamental understanding of oscillatory and decaying soliton behaviors, opening up new avenues for both fundamental research and technological developments in the field of nonlinear optics. Furthermore, the study provides a theoretical foundation for investigating dark solitons and optical solitons, with potential applications including Bose-Einstein condensates and linear wave propagation in optics. The underlying principles of this research can be extended to other areas, such as investigating dark solitons

Using data from the HelioSW3 workshop, which incorporated multiple imaging and magnetic observatory datasets, our research analyzed various types of disturbances associated with several major eruptions involving NOAA AR 11429. Despite initial expectations that these events would not significantly impact the lower solar atmosphere, multiple small-scale sunspot revolutions were observed, and large-scale disturbances were seen in the form of wave trains and lobes, causing widespread changes in the environment in and around the rotating sunspots. These disturbances were later joined by a high-speed jet, which reached speeds of up to 570 km per second and led to a further increase in disturbance strength, ultimately resulting in the disappearance of the rotating sunspots from the horizon. NOAA AR 11429 produced three more large-scale disturbances before decaying, each featuring a rotating sunspot characterised by high-speed jets and increased disturbance strength in the environment. Previous studies on social tagging systems focused on information generation and resource sharing, but overlooked other key aspects: how tags are used over time and shared within specific groups. This paper investigates these topics through a theoretical framework and empirical analysis of two tagging systems. Our findings explain user behavior and content evolution, revealing the significance of time and previous interactions within social groups. In addition, we discovered that users are motivated to tag content by a desire to collaborate and exchange information, rather than simply to contribute to the collective task. This understanding sheds light on the inherent value of social tagging systems and their potential applications. Based on these results, we propose strategies for encouraging engagement within existing tagging platforms and a new model for content-based collaboration. The theoretical framework developed in this study can be applied to other information systems, such as microblogging and photo-sharing platforms, to elucidate user behavior and improve the design of these services. This result upholds Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture for sums of four integers. Our approach builds upon an earlier proof by Tao, utilizing a combination of algebraic manipulations, Fourier analysis, and the inverse theorem. Additionally, this method enables a broader generalization of the conjecture for sums of arbitrary integer values. While the upper limit of the exponent in $A$'s size to $k$ hasn't been resolved, our findings improve upon the previous known lower bounds for Freiman's 4k-5 conjecture. Furthermore, this work sheds light on the structure of sets that satisfy the condition of having sums of at most four elements that are multiples of $k$. We've established that such a set $A$, if it has a size less than $3\frac{7}{8}k$, must consist of elements whose maximum gap is at most $O(k^{1/4})$. We've known the upper limit to the gap for Freiman's 4k-4 conjecture since 2009, but the new finding provides an updated insight into the Freiman 3k-4 conjecture. This study focuses on intent classification, a fundamental task in conversational AI, where a text input is classified into one or more intended purposes. Current models, however, struggle to adapt to changing intent patterns or unexpected inputs lacking semantic labels. To address these limitations, we developed a multi-task learning architecture combining classification and unsupervised intent discovery, leveraging pre-trained language models to capture task-driven representations. This method employs two learning strategies: (1) a standard supervised approach using marked data and (2) an unsupervised method involving contrastive learning to map similar intents to a single point in a high-dimensional space, regardless of their wording. To efficiently train this model, we applied a gradual training technique, initially focusing unsupervised training on unlabelled data to establish a generalised representation, then incorporating semantic labels to refine the representations and boost performance. Experimental results show that our proposed method surpasses existing baselines on the widely-used Splits 1-5 of the Restaurant Booking dataset. Moreover, it effectively handles out-ofdistribution inputs and adapts to new intents without requiring explicit semantic labels for those intents. This paper re-examines the application of the H2 formula in the Abrams-Buckingham-Snyder context within the scope of lattice statistical mechanics and related theories. Although the H2 formula has been successfully used to predict critical properties of numerous substances, its underlying mathematical concept remains unclear. Even the reviewers themselves admit to not comprehending its basis. Despite its mysterious nature, the formula appears to be linked to the solution of a specific differential equation associated with the Gibbs thermodynamic potential. However, this connection remains speculative and further study is required to verify this hypothesis. One potential approach to validating this speculation involves using numerical methods to compare the coefficients of the differential equation with those derived from the Gibbs thermodynamic potential. If our hypothesis is correct, it may be possible to derive the H2 formula through standard mathematical procedures, thereby shedding light on its origins. As a demonstration of the review's findings, we have successfully applied an alternative method to reproduce the H2 formula, providing a straightforward and understandable proof. Nevertheless, our proposed method is not limited to two-dimensional lattices and can be generalized for higher-dimensional cases. Moreover, we have extended the H2 formula to incorporate a wide range of interactions, including those beyond nearest-neighbor proximity on any lattice type. Finally, we have explored the theoretical implications of our findings and noted their compatibility with third-order terms in the free energy expansion, as well as the presence of a singular point in the Gibbs free energy. Our review concludes by highlighting the need for future research to further develop the conceptual framework underlying the H2 formula. Notably, our analysis reveals that non-interfering measurements have a associated cost of zero, thereby establishing a crucial distinction between two distinct categories of measurements, a distinction manifested in the associated cost property. Our research assesses whether quantum fluctuations occurring during an inflationary period could give rise to primordial black holes (PBHs) that subsequently decay into high-energy particles when they evaporate. It's hypothesized that these particles could be responsible for the origin of ultra-high energy cosmic rays. To investigate this possibility, we first identify the fraction of matter that could give rise to PBHs, and find that this fraction must not exceed $10^{-8}$ if we want to generate enough high-energy particles to explain the observed spectrum. Furthermore, we calculate that the predicted number of extremely high-energy events should be comparable to the observed rate, but that this rate might be contaminated by events caused by fragmentation of dark matter particles, and that a significant portion of events might be missed by observatories due to being obscured by intergalactic dust. Finally, we consider that a large number of more radioactive events might be trapped in ice caps and salt lakes, and that these could be released in response to climate change, and that this might affect the observed spectrum of high-energy particles. However, these events could not be the result of a single burst of black hole creation, but rather from continuous, intermittent black hole creation that occurred soon after the inflationary period. On the other hand, the idea that PBHs could decay into high-energy particles also provides a natural explanation for the observed density of dark matter and its relationship to bacterial growth, as well as for the observed patterns of radioactive decay that have been observed on the Earth's surface. Furthermore, this research predicts that we might soon be hit by an extremely high-energy event that could be caused by PBH decay, and that could be the largest ever recorded. Additionally, another potential source of extremely high-energy events that could be caused by PBH decay might be coming from nearby dark stars, and that these events might be masked by events caused by fragmentation of dark matter particles. Finally, the idea that PBHs could decay into high-energy particles also provides a natural explanation for the observed spectrum of extremely high-energy events and that a proposed method for observing these events might be compromised by and dependent on variables such as ice mass, time, and the shape of ice caps. Due to MAX CUT's importance in learning theory and bipartite matching's practical uses, solving sparse instances efficiently becomes a crucial goal. Although approximate algorithms exist for these problems, the performance guarantees and tractability in sparse instances were unclear. Our research provides the first PTAS for a broad class of objective functions, confirming the hypothesis that sparse real-world instances can typically be solved efficiently. We achieve this result by exploiting problem-specific structures, using a framework that allows for robust solutions within the sparsity limits. This approach also yields fully polynomial-time approximation schemes with a linear number of stages. Furthermore, we propose a new method for designing stage schemes, reducing the required number of stages and opening the door for applying similar techniques to other problems. For example, in knowledge graph verification, AI models can check the accuracy of human-generated knowledge by analyzing related text without requiring extensive labeling. High-definition hyperspectral imagery holds significant promise in urban area mapping due to its capacity to capture dimensions beyond traditional RGB colors and spatial resolution exceeding that of standard RGB imagery. This study showcases the potential of hyperspectral imagery in creating detailed, map-compatible semantic partitions, surpassing traditional RGB imagery performance. Using a dataset with hyperspectral tiles as its sole annotation source, we develop a training pipeline that produces competitive results on the Cityscape dataset, closely matching the accuracy achieved with comprehensive semantic segmentation training. This pipeline's effectiveness is contingent on utilizing hyperspectral bands as a single, high-resolution image. While incorporating additional RGB imagery channels fails to improve results, integrating hyperspectral bands reveals a 10.44% improvement in pixel-wise accuracy over RGB imagery. This research lays the groundwork for the efficient creation of detailed urban area maps using hyperspectral imagery. As the field continues to evolve, we anticipate hyperspectral imagery to become an increasingly vital data type for geospatial information systems. The proposed pipeline's maps will be made publicly available, including a generated version of the Cityscape dataset. This emission appears to originate from the surface, rather than the atmosphere, considering the energies involved. Since X-rays can penetrate through the atmosphere, it's plausible that the source of these X-rays is linked to liquid methane lakes on the facade. However, this emission displays the same longitude variation as the facade's brightness, indicating that the X-ray source is closely tied to the facade itself. This variation isn't seen in Titan's polar regions, nor in the Saturnian equatorial zone. Notably, the energy spectrum of these X-rays can be modeled using a single-component thermal plasma model, indicating a 35 keV collisional ionization equilibrium temperature. However, certain problems can be solved using a constant number of basic operations within a specific context. This paper explores more complex computations that can be solved using a constant number of operations within the RAM model, focusing on scenarios where basic operations can be executed in a constant time. It builds upon earlier findings by investigating previously unexamined types of operations. This study establishes the computational efficiency of these operations while identifying potential applications and future research areas. Most importantly, the findings demonstrate that several operations can be performed efficiently using a constant number of rotations, which are a form of shift operation that can be executed quickly. Key among these operations are polynomial evaluation, logarithmic division, and computing the most significant bit. The study also reveals that certain other operations can be performed using a constant number of operations, specifically, exponentiation, prime checking, and finding the next prime. The prime checking operation is particularly notable as it can be performed using only two comparisons. The findings indicate that these operations can be executed quickly within the RAM model. Session-based recommendation is a popular technique for generating suggestions when users don't express complete preferences. It involves predicting items users are likely to choose given the items they've selected in previous sessions. Most modern session-based recommendation models focus on learning from user behavior within individual sessions, ignoring valuable information across multiple sessions. To address this limitation, we developed a new session-based recommendation model called LGST that uses user preferences to guide session-based recommendation. This model exploits intra-session and inter-session relationships to enhance recommendation quality. Specifically, it combines session-specific and session-free user interest from a graph-based model, with each session representing a node in the graph. We found that LGST consistently outperforms existing session-based recommendation models on public datasets. However, our experiments indicate that enhancing the model with multi-head self-attention leads to a performance drop. This counterintuitive result suggests that the model over-relies on long-term user preferences, overlooking nearby selected items. To address this issue, we proposed a co-training approach to leverage user preferences within and across sessions. The model is initially trained on user behavior within individual sessions and later refined using user preferences gathered from adjacent sessions. This method further improves recommendation quality, outperforming existing session-based recommendation models, including those with multi-head self-attention. Notably, our approach increases the diversity of recommended items while maintaining comparable accuracy. The proposed model pushes the boundary of session-based recommendation, achieving superior performance on public datasets. It's particularly effective at boosting existing session-based recommendation models, even those without multi-head self-attention. This model directly addresses the session-based recommendation task, providing clear model implementations and additional details required for replication. In this paper, we present a novel algorithm to determine the non-degenerate components of a polynomial system based on its solution set and invariant sets associated with algebraic torus actions. Calculating the non-degenerate region is a critical aspect in numerous applications, yet its complexity often renders it unfeasible through conventional methods. Building on Millan's signature formula, our approach incorporates action invariants to estimate the dimension of non-degenerate components within a specified algebraic set. This algorithm demonstrates significant efficiency, enabling the computation of non-degenerate regions for multi-degree polynomial systems of dimension eight or higher, as well as extensive hypersurfaces and invariant sets of dimension seven or higher, in both rational and real contexts. Furthermore, we have released an open-source implementation of this algorithm as part of the Singular package. This work is firmly grounded in the mathematical framework of toric methods, offering a new direction in the development of this field. As a significant contribution, we have discovered that the majority of non-degenerate components in algebraic sets exhibit toric non-degeneracy, which in turn leads to an estimation of the number of such components. This research also sheds light on ongoing inquiries regarding the distribution of non-degenerate components and the nature of their intersections. Ultimately, this study aims to build on the foundational aspects of non-degenerate components, leveraging the efficacy of toric methods. Additionally, we have incorporated a new technique to determine the dimensions of mixed codimension one components, which has been made available in the Singular package as well. This research is anticipated to enhance comprehension of solution sets associated with polynomial systems of arbitrary degree through a combination of numerical and symbolic calculations. As a consequence, it is expected to offer new insights in fields such as geometry, algebra, and physics, expanding beyond the scope of toric methods alone. Lastly, we have demonstrated that our algorithm can successfully identify previously unknown components in solution sets. This research is expected to be a valuable resource for researchers in fields such as algebraic geometry, physics, and mathematics, expanding beyond the scope of toric methods alone. Moreover, it is anticipated to lead to novel applications and research directions. Finally, we have released an open-source implementation of the presented algorithms as well as additional novel algorithms in the public library Singular. This research is anticipated to extend the foundational aspects of toric methods, leveraging its efficacy to analyze solution sets associated with multi-degree polynomial systems of dimension eight or higher, as well as extensive hypersurfaces and invariant sets of dimension seven or higher, in both rational and real contexts.

A longstanding problem posed by Turan in 1941 concerns determining the minimum number of vertices for a graph $G$ with the property that no subset of its vertices induces a tetrahedron (a three-dimensional triangle, consisting of four points connected by five edges). Turan noted that any such graph with fewer than nine vertices must have at least 34 edges, whereas a cube (with 9 vertices) requires exactly 24 edges.

We addressed a variant of this challenge in the context of the $\ell_2$-metric by demonstrating an upper bound of $n \approx 7.16 \cdot 10^3$. Furthermore, our result implies an upper bound of $n \approx 9.21 \cdot 10^3$ for the standard graph metric. Both of these estimates were previously the lower bounds for the problem, with the latter due to Foreshrink et al.'s work in 2021. Our approach, with its roots in combinatorial geometry, enabled the discovery of new objects - "Slim-Cubes' with distinctive properties, facilitating an innovative construction of graphs $G$, with the number of vertices of $n$, exhibiting the desired tetrahedron-free property.

In the course of our research, new computational challenges arose, with their solutions aiding the field of graph theory. Specifically, we tackled the #SAT problem (counting the number of satisfying assignments for a given Boolean formula), with our estimate of its complexity being within $O \left( 2^{n(1 - \frac{4}{5\omega(\log n + 1)})} \right)$, where $\omega$ denotes the exponent of the matrix multiplication problem. Achieving high-quality maps involves an ongoing quest for visual enhancements. Map suppliers strive to eliminate flaws in their vector maps, with a particular focus on eliminating "buglines," the artifacts resulting from the rendering of poorly spaced polylines. To address this issue, a map renderer must incorporate a supplementary step to mitigate these flaws, with various methods proposed over the years. We have developed an innovative approach to line rendering, utilizing a fragment buffer to store bivariate coefficients that enable a more effective suppression of buglines. By analyzing the frequency characteristics of maps, we have derived an optimal threshold for the fragment buffer's clip value, which significantly improves the outcome. Furthermore, we have investigated alternative methods for determining this threshold, including a heuristic based on the standard deviation of map pixel values. We compared our proposed technique with established methods, demonstrating its superiority in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency, with a notable advantage over previous methods that also aimed to improve line rendering quality. We have successfully implemented this technique in the Globin rendering engine, which is used by several leading digital map providers, with further evidence of its effectiveness provided in the study. Additionally, we have made the source code of this engine available for public access. We hope that this contribution will facilitate the development of high-quality vector map renderers by open source communities, as well as inspire new ideas in the field of computer graphics. We have also explored other possible applications of our proposed technique, including canvas rendering, Phoenix, and Glovis. We found that, in general, the performance benefits could be significant, with up to 50% improvements in CPU usage and memory allocation, as demonstrated through a set of benchmark tests. We also analyzed the fragility of maps, discovering that frequency characteristics can be a reliable indicator of their quality. We have therefore proposed a map evaluation metric, based on the standard deviation of pixel values, which can effectively assess the renderability of vector maps, with a level of accuracy comparable to human judgment. We tested and validated this metric, demonstrating its ability to predict the outcome of line rendering using a machine learning-based approach. We also investigated the relationship between map attributes and their impact on rendering quality, uncovering a pattern that can be utilized to further refine our metric and improve the overall quality of vector maps. We have shared the results of our research, including a dataset of human assessments and algorithmic evaluations, as well as the source code of our engine, for public access. As a pulsar travels through space, it leaves behind a trail of gamma-ray-emitting particles, primarily electrons and positrons, which are trapped in a growing shell. This process is relatively brief, lasting only a few hundred thousand years, after which the shell dissipates as the pulsar accelerates more particles more rapidly. Researchers have identified a number of pulsar wind nebulae in the Milky Way, as well as several candidate sources, by analyzing data from the Lambda, Maxima Cherenkov Telescope and Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. These observed wind nebulae significantly outshine the underlying pulsar in X-rays and gamma-rays, primarily due to the acceleration of electrons and positrons by magnetic fields. By analyzing the luminosity and spectral patterns of these wind nebulae, researchers have gained valuable insights into extremely high-energy astrophysical processes, as well as the physical conditions within these nebulae and the electron-positron collision rate. Furthermore, the data suggest a close correlation between the size of the wind nebula and the speed at which the pulsar spins. Also, also a comparison between the predicted and observed gamma-ray emission from known pulsar wind nebulae revealed a discrepancy of at least an order of magnitude for some sources, indicating either a much slower expansion or a significant off-center expansion angle or the presence of an unresolved companion pulsar wind nebula. Researchers have further studied the population of these gamma-ray-emitting wind nebulae, as well as pulsar wind nebulae that emit only in X-rays, using a statistical analysis. The data suggested a close link between the population of these wind nebulae and the star formation history of the Milky Way, as well as a correlation between the speed at which these pulsars spin and the speed at which stars in the galaxy move. Also, the study revealed that a substantial proportion of these wind nebulae are hidden from observation due to dust blocking X-rays and gamma-rays from these nebulae. Using a study of a single wind nebula, researchers derived the mass of gas and dust within the Milky Way, as well as a measure of how easily gamma-rays can pass through the galaxy's dust layers. This causes climate change research to suffer from two major issues - funding limitations and a lack of relevance to practical policy-making processes. To address these problems, this study examines how different groups within the climate change community hold varying views on the topic and how these views impact each other. A network analysis is applied to standardise the language and identify connections among different groups within the climate change community, revealing distinct sub-groups within the community. This analysis also uncovers patterns in citation behaviour and finds that views within the community do affect each other over time, rather than existing independently. Ultimately, this study suggests policies for mitigating the fragmentation of the climate change community and promoting meaningful interactions within the community to address the societal implications of global change. These policies involve standardising language and promoting collaborative research, particularly in the social sciences, to address the practical concerns surrounding climate change. This could be achieved by providing funding and incentives for such research and developing decision-support tools to make the results of this research more applicable to practical policy-making processes. Soft grippers offer unique advantages in handling delicate objects, and simulations can aid in fabricating these grippers and testing their performance before physical production. However, accurately predicting the soft gripper's deformation and interaction with objects through simulation requires precise input and deformation modeling. Despite these requirements, the absence of effective sensors and accurate deformation modeling poses significant challenges, especially in regulating the gripper's movement to engage with objects. To address these issues, researchers proposed a virtual modeling and regulation protocol using the Koopman operator method, which utilizes virtual models and input signals to estimate and regulate the gripper's movement. Tested on a multi-fingered soft gripper, the results demonstrate the feasibility of the protocol in teaching the gripper to pick up objects through simulation and translating this information to real-world applications without the need for additional sensors. With further development, this protocol can be applied to various other soft robots and aid in automating the fabrication and interaction testing of soft robots. One common approach to solving non-convex optimization problems, such as training deep neural networks, involves using an iterative gradient-based method like the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm. However, standard SGD methods can get stuck in local minima and have slow convergence rates, leading to underperforming models. In response, researchers have developed a variety of modifications to SGD, but many of these improvements rely on specific assumptions about problem structures, such as smoothness properties or Lipschiz continuity. In contrast, our proposed Generalized Stochastic Gradient Descent (GSGD) method provides a more versatile solution, yielding a significantly improved performance benchmark for non-convex optimization tasks. By building on a fundamental estimate for non-convex functions, such as the sublinear expectation, our GSGD method achieves a faster convergence rate, averaging at least a 0.5h^2 iteration budget, where h represents the problem's smoothness parameter. In comparison, our best-known previous algorithms average a 0.25h^2 iteration budget. Our theoretical analysis, backed by extensive experimental results, demonstrates the effectiveness of our GSGD method in achieving faster convergence rates, along with improved generalization performance, particularly in the context of deep neural network training. Additionally, our proposed algorithm offers enhanced flexibility and applicability, empowering researchers to achieve superior outcomes in various optimization challenges. Furthermore, our experiments highlight the practical benefits of our GSGD method, demonstrating its ability to outperform existing algorithms, even when testing on real-world datasets, such as the CIFAR-10 data set. In summary, our study establishes the Generalized Stochastic Gradient Descent (GSGD) method as a superior choice for solving non-convex optimization problems, ultimately leading to improved model accuracy and faster algorithm convergence. Crucially, our theoretical and practical results underscore the significance of considering the problem's smoothness properties in the context of non-convex optimization, advising researchers to prioritize generalization methods, such as our proposed GSGD algorithm. Additionally, our study opens up new avenues for exploration, suggesting future research could investigate the applicability of our GSGD method to the well-studied twin machine learning paradigm. Furthermore, our work raises intriguing questions about the potential extension of our GSGD algorithm to the distributed learning scenario, potentially leading to novel and important research contributions in the area of decentralized optimization. Our approach mimics the methods used for finite-band approximations in the Laplacian and phase-shift perturbation theory. A key benefit is that it allows for efficiently calculating energies with relatively low computational requirements. This technique is adaptable to a variety of scenarios, including impurity models and Anderson models, which we've demonstrated through examples. Our findings also include the existence of unique ground states in these models. Additionally, we've analyzed the properties of finite-band approximations, including their accuracy and the behavior of approximation errors. The extensive collection of articles on Wikipedia serves as a significant source of information for training various natural language processing models. However, relying on the entire wiki would be ineffective due to the varying quality of its content. Identifying and isolating individual paragraphs or sections based on editor behavior could provide a potential solution. By examining the actions of different editors, including their ratings of article quality and corresponding revisions, it is possible to pinpoint sections that require improvement. This study proposes a method that uses machine learning to identify sections of poor quality on Wikipedia by reviewing patterns in editor behavior. Editors' assessments of article quality act as labels for a supervised learning model, while revisions and comments function as supplementary data. Furthermore, the research presents a pattern-based technique for categorizing articles according to their language-independent quality. An analysis of the performance using a dataset of manually labeled articles demonstrated that the proposed method accurately predicts sections of low quality with a high level of confidence. With an overall accuracy rate of 90 percent, the model outperformed a control group consisting of randomly selected articles. An experiment involving hidden-Markov models revealed that incorporating information about editing habits and comments significantly enhances the prediction of quality sections. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the proposed method can isolate sections of mediocre or high quality with a moderate level of accuracy. Although the overall accuracy rates for these scenarios are lower compared to the low-quality scenario, they still exceed the baseline defined by a group of randomly selected articles. The research presents a novel approach for qualifying wiki content using patterns in editing habits and provides a useful tool for further development in natural language processing tasks focused on qualifying content. The proposed method as well as the generated data can be found on a GitHub repository. It is also possible to generate new data by running a provided script using Wikipedia's API. The research includes an in-depth analysis of its findings as well as suggestions for potential improvements. One such improvement involves integrating the model with existing neural qualifying models to create a highly efficient and effective classifier. The overall goal of the study is to contribute to the ongoing efforts of Wikipedia editors to enhance article quality by providing a reliable, automated system for qualifying content based on editing habits. The research also presents several open questions and challenges, including the potential for using qualifying patterns to model and predict human behavior. It also examines the relationship between qualifying edits and the distribution of assessments across various articles. The research provides insights into how Wikipedia editors are geographically dispersed and how their assessments correlate with existing leadership structures. As knowledge acquisition techniques continue to evolve, decision-based black-box AI grows in prominence, driven by its straightforward implementation and robust performance. Despite its advantages, this method's reliance on black-box modeling complicates the process of tracking its decision-making process, making it challenging to apply knowledge transfer techniques. To address this limitation, a new framework has been developed to execute in-depth analysis of black-box models and harness their findings to create interpretable decision-making systems, even in scenarios where little to no training data is available. To accomplish this, a novel black-box algorithm, referred to as COTER, has been designed to identify and create a set of relevant black-box models, thus enabling high-accuracy decisions on unfamiliar text categorization tasks with zero-shot knowledge transfer. Furthermore, a black-box clustering model has been devised to enhance the new framework's efficiency by implementing in-place evaluation and training using unlabeled data to establish a system for real-time decision-making. To validate the efficacy of this new framework, a comprehensive evaluation has been conducted using 20 diverse datasets across four domains, yielding a remarkable 93.3% overall accuracy and outperforming existing black-box and white-box systems in various scenarios. Moreover, a practical application has been demonstrated in a real-world context of single-word categorization using a touchscreen interface to facilitate interaction with non-interpretive decision-making systems. To further confirm the dependability of this new approach, a cross-domain evaluation has been carried out, revealing a 91.5% overall accuracy and surpassing black-box and white-box methods across multiple domains. To showcase the potential of this new framework, a series of videos have been made available online. A study of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decays is conducted based on sample data collected by the LHCb experiment, corresponding to approximately 20 pb^-1 of integrated luminosity. The investigation focuses on the $\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ resonance and non-resonant modes within the $B^0_s$ decay spectrum. The analysis yields branching fraction estimates for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ with respect to $B^0_s\to K^+\bar{K}^-$, revealing branching fractions for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ of $4.3^{+1.8+-1.2}$ (stat.) ± 1.2 (syst.) × 10^-5 and $3.7^{+2.1+-1.2}$ (stat.) ± 1.2 (syst.) × 10^-5 for the $\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ and $\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ resonant and non-resonant combinations respectively. Evidence for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ with local significance of 3.5 standard deviations, corresponding to 3.9 standard deviations considering the entire $B^0_s$ mass spectrum, is also presented. In addition, upper limits on branching fractions for numerous $B^0_s$ decays are provided, including $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{(*0)}\pi^-$, $\bar{D}^{(*0)}\eta^-$, $\bar{D}^{(*0)}\omega$, $\bar{D}^{0} K^-\pi^+$, and $\bar{D}^{0} \rho^0 K^-$ decays with limits ranging approximately from 10^-5 to 10^-9 in general. These results are the first to report upper limits for half of the mentioned decays and provide novel insights into rare $B^0_s$ transition phenomena. Furthermore, these findings contribute to a deeper comprehension of the Standard Model and facilitate the search for pathways to its potential alternatives by the investigation of uncommon $B^0_s$ decays discovered through the LHCb experiment. This study focuses on developing novel methods for indistinguishable observers to learn from unmarked data generated by multiple entities. Introducing the concept of co-observation, it highlights interactions between observers that involve mutual influence, even without requiring expertise demonstrations. Two key co-observation types - interleaved and parallel - are recognized, with the former analyzed through the creation of a dynamic system model. Building upon this model, a method is devised to derive a unified policy from concurrent trials. Testing this approach using simulated observatories and three co-observation types, it is compared with established learning techniques and found to outperform them in unspecified environments. Additionally, applying this framework to the realm of self-driving cars, it facilitates learning to coexist with various types of vehicles, including those with lead vehicles and those without, using only unmarked data. Promising results indicate that indistinguishable observers can successfully learn from unmarked data in various scenarios. Code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/grasp-lyra/co-obs-learning.erland.ghc/Language/index.html.

Research on programmable approximate computing in hardware has shown promising results, with a class of codes called PAC codes providing a strong foundation. Recent studies found that PAC codes can efficiently support arithmetic operations like addition, but failed to do so for other operations such as subtraction. To overcome this limitation, this paper proposes two solutions to adapt PAC codes for supporting general arithmetic operations. The first solution involves modifying existing PAC code generators to be compatible with multiple operations, while the second involves creating new, more versatile PAC code generators. The paper also explores how to best utilize modern FPGAs to implement PAC code-based circuits and presents a measurement tool to evaluate the performance of PAC code-based designs. The results show significant reductions in area usage and energy consumption while maintaining high levels of accuracy. The experiments also reveal that current FPGAs can support designs with up to 40 million nodes. The paper further delves into underlying challenges and opens doors for future research to address the mentioned issues. The authors also released a publicly-accessible VHDL library containing implemented PAC code-based circuits. The library can be accessed at https://github.com/ashishk112/PAC-Codes. The authors also released a Python tool for evaluating PAC code performance at https://github.com/ashishk112/PAC-Codes-Analysis. The library contains a wide range of designs, including ones that support addition, subtraction, and other operations with varying levels of precision. The tool allows users to generate and evaluate PAC code-based circuits for specific applications and report their performance in a readable format. The authors also released a flow for mapping applications into PAC code-based circuits at https://github.com/ashishk112/PAC-Codes-Flow. The flow automates the process of selecting suitable PAC codes and generating the corresponding circuit, allowing users to easily prototype and accelerate approximate computing applications using FPGAs. The authors also released a set of PAC code-based circuits for popular ML models at https://github.com/ashishk112/PAC-Codes-ML. The codes allow for efficient prototyping and acceleration of the models using PAC code-based circuits, achieving up to 5x area reduction and 2x energy reduction while maintaining high accuracy.
