We introduce HandRebuild, an engagement monitoring and rebuilding system that uses a kinematic model of the hand to interpret point cloud data from various sources. By tracking the hand's structure, HandRebuild generates a detailed description of objects and their interactions, even in scenarios with ambiguous or incomplete point cloud data. During object manipulation, the system synthesizes temporal point cloud series to reconstruct 3D models of the object and the hand in the wild. As a result, the reconstructed models can be used for various purposes, such as enhancing low-quality scans, resolving view limitations, and constructing 3D models from a single time-series scan. HandRebuild's effectiveness is demonstrated through a new benchmark dataset containing 82 complex engagement sequences with the Freespace robot arm and 14 everyday objects. The system's reconstruction accuracy is confirmed by comparing its results with ground truth data, showing a 12% improvement over similar methods. The project, including the dataset and evaluation code, is open-source and available at https://github.com/SD-RL/HandRebuild. A video showcasing the system's performance is available at https://youtu.be/j6U8o8bH5Gk. The benchmark dataset can also be accessed via https://sdl.mit.edu/HandRebuild. The system has won several awards at the Robot Learning from Datasets Challenge 2022, where it was evaluated by the dataset creators. Moreover, the system has been invited to the IEEE Robotics & Automation Society's Conference in 2023 to be showcased as a notable robot application. As a result of its success, the system has been incorporated into the Open Robotics Foundation's global repository of robot skills, where it will be used to improve the next generation of robotic models and engagement interactions. The incorporation into the robot skills repository has been confirmed by a robot hardware expert from Microsoft's Robot Foundation. To study the impact of treatment disruption, we've developed a novel framework, building on the concept of mutual information introduced by Zhang et al. in 2020. Under the k-nearest neighbors (k-NN) interference model, our method identifies situations where treatment disruption results in differing outcomes. Utilizing this framework, we analyze data from a premature intervention program aimed at reducing opioid overdose deaths in Philadelphia, demonstrating the disruption's effect on reduced mortality rates. Furthermore, we've incorporated treatment disruption into a mutual information metric that estimates treatment efficacy, particularly in cases with unknown treatment assignments. By using this approach on the same Philadelphia dataset, we derive an elevated lower bound for treatment efficacy. Both analyses were performed using the DataSceNario platform. As a complementary method, we also investigated treatment disruption within a propensity-score matched dataset, revealing significant differences in overdose death counts between continuous and disrupted interventions. Lastly, we've explored the relationship between treatment disruption and data coverage, employing synthetic data to illustrate the impact, followed by an application to the Philadelphia dataset. Together, these analyses highlight the importance of addressing treatment disruption in intervention studies to enhance data interpretation. All associated code and data necessary to replicate our results can be accessed via the attached zip file containing a text file detailing the steps to recreate our findings, as well as a pointer to the DataSceNario platform containing the associated code and data. Also included is a separate section containing relevant theoretical definitions. Finally, the associated data can be found at https://github.com/jbuckness/DataSceNaria/tree/main-TreatmentDisruption. In current information technologies, security and privacy are enhanced through the utilization of encryption. A fundamental building block in these encryption systems is a truly random number generator, which typically employs entropic sources like physical randomness seeds. While advanced implementations exist that combine cryptographic techniques with physical entropy, they often lack compatibility with existing system designs or incur excessive power consumption. This paper introduces a novel method, TuRaN, utilizing voltage underscaling to generate high-entropy digits at reduced energy costs. TuRaN leverages the inherent weaknesses in transistors at reduced supply voltages to create randomized addresses within a SRAM array. These addresses serve as a source of randomness for digital circuits. TuRaN's efficiency was evaluated through various metrics such as SRAM yield, area, and energy consumption. Compared to traditional SRAM, TuRaN demonstrates improved energy-to-throughput ratios and approximately 30 times reduced active energy consumption. Furthermore, TuRaN generates randomness at speeds compatible with cutting-edge digital systems. This paper also delves into the implementation and testing of TuRaN within SRAMs, outlining the steps for integrating the method and demonstrating its efficacy through experimental yields under scaled commercial process technologies. Notably, TuRaN's performance surpasses benchmarks for genuine random number generators, producing over 99% of the entropy expected from physical sources at a fraction of the typical random number generator's energy expenditure. This research opens doors for the widespread integration of TuRaN in randomized applications, notably in the realm of cryptography. This work is expected to pave the way for a broad range of randomized applications, significantly enhancing energy efficiency while adhering to established security standards. A crucial factor that receives relatively limited attention in existing research is the impact of the training dataset on the success of in-context learning. In our research, we the exploring the influence of the pretraining dataset on the performance of in-context learning by using Wikipedia as a variable factor. A significant finding from our study is that models trained on Wikipedia exhibit a notable improvement in one-shot learning capabilities when compared to models trained on general web data, a positive trend that is observed across multiple tasks. A suitable pretraining dataset can thus be seen as a practical means of enhancing the models' ability to perform in-context learning without any further fine-tuning. We also identified potential areas for future research by analyzing the discrepancies between Wikipedia and web data, and the potential for using Wikipedia as a means of automatically generating informative demonstrations. A further investigation into these research questions could lead to the development of more innovative and effective methods of in-context learning. Furthermore, our study introduces a new benchmark suite based on the Wiktionary dataset, referred to as WikiHack, consisting of tasks such as generating the definition, synonym, and etymology of a word from its title as input. This benchmark provides a unique set of challenges across three distinct groups of tasks and offers a useful resource for researchers wishing to perform cross-domain adaptation, homogenization, and transfer learning. This work introduces a cutting-edge motion control strategy centered around low peaking variations (LPV) to enhance performance in high-precision motion control systems. By incorporating an LPV sequential loop closing (SLC) approach that uses online system identification, the proposed control method effectively addresses changes within a system by incorporating an adaptive algorithm that incorporates past data to calculate parameters. To validate the proposed control approach, simulations were conducted using a digital servo motor motion system, with the results demonstrating the capability of LPV SLC to achieve superior performance compared to traditional methods, such as robust model predictive control (R MPC) and model free adaptive control (MFAC), under varying loads and conditions. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the feasibility of the LPV SLC method using a low-cost, microcontroller-based hardware implementation. Experimental results from a prototype motion control system also confirm the capability of the LPV SLC approach to achieve performance comparable to sophisticated digital signal processing hardware. Specifically, the motion control system was successful in achieving average positioning errors of less than 0.0006 degrees when using an LPV SLC controller. Due to its ability to effectively handle nonlinear and uncertain systems in real-time, the proposed LPV SLC control approach presents a viable option for a range of motion control applications, as well as other control systems with changing parameters. To facilitate online calculation of the LPV SLC controller, the study also introduces a novel and efficient algorithm utilizing a recursive least square (RLS) method to estimate parameters. The proposed algorithm merges the capabilities of adaptive algorithms and moving window techniques to calculate parameters, effectively mitigating the influence of outdated data and maintaining effective performance. The study showcases the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm by comparing its results to the performance of state-of-the-art deep learning-based identification methods, with the RLS approach outperforming DL-based methods by significantly reducing computation time while maintaining comparable accuracy. The proposed LPV SLC control approach, along with the supporting identification algorithm, has been published as patent applications under files PCT/CZ2021/000012 and PCT/CZ2021/000013, respectively. The related software code for the motion control system and identification algorithm have been publicly shared on the GitHub platform at repositories https://github.com/hadalk/LPV-SLC-FC and https://github.com/hadalk/RLS-FC, respectively. Neural networks trained on point cloud data often produce irregular outputs due to the inherent discrete nature of these representations. To address this issue, a new smoothing technique called TPC is proposed, which relies on the transformation matrices of the coordinate system to smooth the point cloud. By doing so, TPC preserves the geometric properties of the original point cloud. Unlike existing methods, TPC supports a wide range of operators and can be applied within both local and global contexts. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of TPC in preserving the original point cloud's features and improving model performance. Additionally, TPC's code has been made available on GitHub for further exploration. With parameters ranging from a few thousand to several million, TPC efficiently handles models of varying complexity. Notably, a significant enhancement in accuracy can be achieved with a minimal increase in model size. Specifically, a modest rise of 0.4 million parameters enables the attainment of superior output smoothness at the expense of a slight deterioration in semantic segmentation accuracy. This finding offers valuable insights for building optimized models using point cloud representations. Finally, the performance of TPC is exemplified through its use in a self-supervised framework at scale, specifically in processing large datasets of LiDAR roadmaps to yield accurate semantic point cloud predictions. To validate its efficacy, this approach was tested on the mini-semantic-kitti dataset, which comprises 21 scenes derived from the semantic-kitti dataset. With a focus on evaluating the influence of LiDAR spacing on output smoothness, this test revealed that TPC successfully generated high-quality point clouds across a wide spacing range (0.1 to 0.4 meters). At a spacing of 0.4 meters, the trained model produced output with a comparable level of smoothness to its input, with geometric distortion and semantic segmentation error rates comparable to those achieved with narrower spacings. Notably, this result was accompanied by a substantial reduction (6-fold on average) in model parameters required to achieve this level of smoothness, underscoring the efficacy of the proposed TPC technique. This study proposes two medium access techniques, ALOHA (slotted) and CSMA, for use in frequency-modulated continuous wave (FMCW) radar networks. A new analytical model is developed to evaluate uplink and downlink interference in slotted ALOHA systems, leading to a derivation of the average bit error rate. Utilizing this model, design approaches for slotted ALOHA systems are outlined, alongside an analysis of uplink interference in CSMA systems and a method for adjusting transmission time according to signal strength. Notably, both techniques exhibit exponential back-off properties, corroborated by simulation results. With regard to network implementation, an example showing the slotted ALOHA back-off process and a schematic of the proposed receiver architecture for radar signals are presented. Note that the ALOHA technique presents a more attractive option due to its simple implementation and efficient use of spectrum. Additionally, two sub-optimal variants of slotted ALOHA, one with fixed and the other with variable transmission time, are proposed to balance data transmission rate and interference minimization. Finally, a comparative evaluation of slotted ALOHA and CSMA technologies highlights their respective advantages and disadvantages, ultimately suggesting the former as a preferred choice for its ease of implementation and efficient spectrum usage. However, the latter may be more suitable when a guaranteed transmission success rate is critical. This work lays the foundation for future development of slotted ALOHA systems with adaptive back-off, primarily targeting radar applications but also applicable to non-radar scenarios, across various domains, including 5G radio access, LTE-LAA, and IEEE 802.15.1. Furthermore, the presented studies set the stage for exploring performance enhancement opportunities, such as diversity, MIMO, and multi-user techniques, in radar networks. Potential avenues for this include utilizing the same frequency to transmit and receive data, selecting the most optimal transmission time, and integrating slotted ALOHA with existing cellular networks. Such endeavors are anticipated to yield improved system performance, specifically through the utilization of multi-channel and multi-antenna techniques in IEEE 802.15.1 systems. Notably, the utilization of adaptive back-off in slotted ALOHA systems could also lead to further additions in IEEE 802.15.1. This paper explores how background noise affects speech enhancement models by introducing controlled noise into an audio stream captured through a smartphone microphone. Utilizing a dataset of speech recorded under varying conditions of signal strength and background noise, we applied a data-driven approach to create a metric measuring the impact of noise on recorded signals. By utilizing this noise metric, we selected a subset of recordings with uniformly high background noise levels and conducted an experiment to create a test set ideal for evaluating the performance of speech enhancement models in noisy environments. Additionally, we analyzed the difference in speech enhancement outcomes between models trained using a synthetic noise and those trained using actual background noise obtained from smartphone microphones. A comparison of several speech enhancement methods was conducted to create a baseline for evaluating the effectiveness of future methods in handling noisy environments encountered in real-world scenarios. The proposed approach and results are available online for public access. Evaluations showed that models trained using actual background noise outperformed those trained using synthetic noise in reducing background noise while preserving signal quality. However, a significant limitation discovered during this study is the substantial gain in background noise present in recordings captured using smartphone microphones, which poses a challenge for speech enhancement models and calls for more effective denoising methods to enhance the quality of speech. We define and study the characteristics of groups that exhibit rigidity in their algebraic structures when modified slightly, which we refer to as "charmvability." Initially, we establish that charmability is a non-trivial, hereditary property among linear groups, and we identify specific examples of groups that possess this characteristic. Notably, we find that both arithmetic groups with a commutator subgroup contained within a commutative subgroup and groups with a torsion-free abstractly simple commutator subgroup lack charmability. Additionally, we determine the conditions under which groups with these characteristics have rigid algebraic structures, which solves a non-answered query posed by Sahi. Meanwhile, we demonstrate that groups within these two categories can in fact exhibit charmability under certain conditions. Lastly, we investigate relationships between charmability, algebraic structure changes, and torsion elements within groups, and we prove a theorem regarding arithmetic groups with specific torsion elements. This theorem resolves an unanswered question posed by Neuwirth. Moreover, our work has implications for understanding certain properties of groups, and we leverage this understanding to derive new results about torsion elements within arithmetic groups. Finally, we establish a link between charmability and rigid algebraic structures, and we prove a generalization of a theorem initially demonstrated by Hahn. Specifically, we find that groups within a particular family lack both charmability and rigid algebraic structures, whereas groups within a different family possess both characteristics. Additionally, we derive new results regarding arithmetic groups with disabled torsion elements, and we prove a theorem regarding arithmetic groups with disabled torsion elements and rigid algebraic structures. Lastly, we establish relationships between certain properties of groups and their equivalent forms, and we prove several theorems regarding these relationships. One such theorem regards the characteristic of groups with disabled torsion elements and rigid algebraic structures, and another regards the characteristic of groups with enabled torsion elements and rigid algebraic structures. A system's timely behavior can be described in several ways, such as through timing properties like regularity and timing differences. Research has found that certain timing properties are incompatible when specified as regular conditions, leading to the concept of incompatible specifications. We build upon previous studies by broadening the scope to non-regular properties, specifically those defined by Büchi or Parity conditions. Initially, we identify the practical limitations of integrating these conditions into the existing framework for analyzing a system's temporal characteristics. Despite these practical limitations, we show that specifying a system with incompatible non-regular properties is feasible when using Büchi or Parity conditions. Our framework is flexible enough to be applied to other types of topological systems as well. Finally, we explore the computational complexity associated with specifying a system with incompatible non-regular properties, revealing a dichotomy - while it is generally NP-hard for Büchi conditions, it becomes P-time when the properties are restricted to a specific topology. On the other hand, specifying a system with incompatible Parity conditions is generally at least NP-hard. However, we identify a specific topology where specifying such a system is actually P-time. Interestingly, there is a particular class of topologies where specifying a system with incompatible Parity conditions becomes P-time as well. Overall, our study contributes positively to the existing body of research focused on understanding a system's timely behavior. aiming to understand its size and complexity. In an attempt to solve this issue, we
develop an algorithm that generates a public estimate under malicious influence.
Specifically, we assume a scenario in which an untrusted entity controls a subset of
network nodes, manipulating their behavior while attempting to mislead the system.
Despite this manipulation, our approach successfully produces an accurate public
scale estimation for the entire network. Notably, we demonstrate the reliability of
our solution through mathematical analysis and experiments, highlighting its robustness
in the face of malicious interference. Additionally, we reflect on the relationship
between scale estimation and other graph parameters, such as the diameter and average
degree. In an ideal scenario without malicious influence, we devise an alternative
algorithm for estimating these parameters, including the diameter and average degree. 
Experimental evaluation of our algorithms shows that they function efficiently in
various scale ranges. Furthermore, we examine how our algorithms respond to
adversarial interference, emphasizing their capacity to operate effectively even in
the presence of malicious activity. Finally, we assess the resilience of our algorithms
to specific types of manipulation, highlighting their ability to produce reliable
estimates even under such circumstances. Last but not least, we discuss key
considerations for testing these algorithms in real-world settings, emphasizing the
importance of controlling variables like the proportion of affected nodes and the
degree of control exerted over them. Ultimately, we conclude that our algorithms
successfully facilitate reliable public scale estimation in large networks despite
various forms of malicious interference. Also, we discuss the potential uses of
these algorithms in broader distributed computing systems. In particular, we hypothesize
analogous applications in environments involving mobile ad-hoc networks and self-

Given the limited options for propagating perturbations in spacetime, existing methods face significant hurdles in the form of data restrictions. This paper introduces a new approach, Coleham-Batch-Thomas-Klein-Gordon model, incorporating higher-order degrees of freedom within the metric tensor. Utilizing the Hamiltonian constraint to govern the dynamics of these extra degrees of freedom, we demonstrate their seamless integration into the standard numerical relativity framework. This breakthrough addresses the longstanding issue of data restrictions, enabling the exploration of previously unaccessible spacetimes. This abstract summarizes our key findings, showcasing the efficacy of our method in the context of Coleham-Batch-Thomas-Klein-Gordon model. Our innovations have broad applications, encompassing the analysis of gravitational waves, black-hole collapse, and binary mergers. This approach will significantly expand our capacity for numerical analysis in relativity research. This work marks the first public testing of the CTTK model, employing one sophisticated numerical technique and adhering to conservative assumptions. Our results reveal promising outcomes, paving the way for a fresh perspective on numerical relativity. This new CTTK approach will undoubtedly facilitate groundbreaking research in the field. The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves identifying the neutrino mass ordering by utilizing a large, 20-kt liquid-scintillator detector equipped with photomultiplier tubes. For optimal results, over 20,000 individual PMTs must be used, requiring a thorough evaluation of each unit to ensure high quality. A comprehensive examination and verification process of the 20-inch PMTs chosen for JUNO involved testing over 1000 units under precise, scintillator-like conditions to assess their performance. A customized setup was used with excimer-lantern light-sources to simulate neutrino interactions and accurately assess the PMTs' main aspects, including their overall photometric output, response to different illumination angles, and residual non-linearity. This rigorous testing process allowed for the efficient and reliable PMTs to be selected for deployment in the experiment at a rate of nearly 10 units per working day. This thorough testing process has also established a reliable method for testing large-scale scintillator detectors, as well as providing a systematic approach for assessing the PMTs themselves. Furthermore, the outcomes of these tests have also contributed to the development of the PMTs' quality assessment criteria, adding to existing knowledge in this field. This paper details the developed testing procedures, the PMTs' performance characteristics, and the ordered statistics of their quality assessment. In on-sky observations, the blemishes seen in images and data are often attributed to turbulence-induced scattering by the atmosphere, a notion that needs to be verified through detailed modeling of the atmosphere. To do this, we use data from the VLT's MUSE instrument and various atmospheric models, including the Karhunen-Loeve function series expansion, a model that takes into account molecular scintillation, and another that includes contributions from uncorrelated and partially correlated phases. By applying these models to data from different nights and objects, we evaluate their effectiveness at describing the scintillation patterns observed, and assess the feasibility of using them to verify the role of scattering in the data and to estimate the effect of turbulence on the data. A version of this model that includes the phase correlations is particularly effective at describing the observed scintillation patterns, and can be used to verify the role of scattering in the data and to estimate the effect of turbulence on the data. However, we also find that while these models are effective at describing the scintillation patterns observed, they do not fully capture the complexity of the atmosphere, and that further development of the model, incorporating the effects of anisoplanatism and adaptive optics, as well as time-dependent effects, are needed to fully understand the scintillation patterns observed. Furthermore, while we find that the effect of turbulence on the data can be estimated from the scintillation patterns observed, the accuracy of this estimate depends on a number of factors, and in particular on the specific object observed and the atmosphere, and must be verified against other measures of the atmosphere to confirm its accuracy. A confirmation of this estimate is also demonstrated using data from the VLT's MUSE instrument. By combining on-sky data with these detailed atmospheric models, we are better able to verify the role of scattering in the data and to estimate the effect of turbulence on the data, and can use this to inform other estimates of the atmosphere, such as those made through image deconvolution. A comparison with the information on the atmosphere obtained through image deconvolution is also shown. To evaluate the knowledge level of individual online instructors or assess the accuracy of labeled data, we introduce a comprehensive research approach centered on the multi-instructor setting. Building upon recent achievements in distillation-based methods, we develop Pairwise Iterative Logits Coalition (PILE), a novel technique to enhance supervision quality through incremental improvements. Leveraging pairs of experienced instructors and relevant annotations, PILE continuously refines a weak-labeled model by creating multiple stages of stronger supervisors. Each stage is designed to effectively utilize available annotations with theoretical justification, allowing for consistent performance improvements. Notably, PILE surpasses existing methods in data labeling efficiency while also exhibiting adaptable capabilities across various backbones, datasets, and inference tasks, including improving pre-trained models with labeled data and creating custom datasets with annotated fine-grained information. Moreover, our method shows notable adaptability when applied to tasks outside online education, such as computer vision, and can serve as a general approach for building robust models with strong multi-instructor supervision. This study explores the uniform sparsity constraint $|\hat{x}| \leq c$ in the Basis Pursuit optimization problem under continuous and countable dictionary circumstances. It demonstrates that a solution with minimal norm exists and is unique when the constraint includes a boundedness condition, but otherwise the problem has multiple solutions. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between the parameter $c$, the data, and the dictionary $\mathcal{D} = \{d_i\}_{i\in I\subset\mathbb{Z}\cup\mathbb{R}\cup\mathbb{Q}}$ and derive a condition under which the solution is both minimal and unique. When the dictionary dictionary $\mathcal{D}$ satisfies a Finkelstein condition, we find that a solution with minimal norm is both unique and minimizes the $l_1$-norm. Finally, we discuss how our results generalize to various iterative algorithms. To prove these conclusions, we establish a continuous version of a crucial tool known as the Altman-Katz Lemma. This tool, the Discrete Altman-Katz Lemma, asserts that for a countable dictionary $\mathcal{D}$ and a signed measure $\mu$ with finite total variation, the function $f: \mathbb{N} \to [0,\infty)$ defined by $f(n) = \sup_{x\in\mathbb{C},|Rx| \leq c} \re\langle x,\delta\rangle \mu$ has a unique minimum point $m_\mu$. We show that this result leads to a proof of uniqueness for various problems, including the Basis Pursuit optimization problem under a uniform sparsity constraint. Ultimately, the proof hinges on a novel application of Poincaré's Extension Theorem. This study is a product of collaborative work with Y. Peres, M. Shaked-Monderer, A. Sipal, O. Strufolino, and A. This article introduces PComp, an open-source compiler framework that translates high-level flow tables into programmable switch hardware. The compilation process in PComp involves multiple stages to ensure robustness and fault tolerance. By allowing programmers to specify match and action operations at a logical level, the compiler can automatically generate customized switch programs adapted to specific forwarding requirements. The compiler's modular architecture facilitates the integration of new switch models, forward models, and quality-of-service algorithms, making it possible to develop custom compilers for various use cases with adjusted switch models. We evaluated the compiler's efficiency by converting a standard switch program into a customized software program, demonstrating the versatility of PComp and showing compilation times of under 10 milliseconds, with a direct match rate of up to 94%. Furthermore, PComp's flexible design enables extended functionalities, such as automatic bug detection and switch fault tolerance, making it suitable for research in programmable switches and related algorithms. The full source code of PComp is publicly available on GitHub. We are collaborating with other researchers to further develop the compiler and explore new applications, inviting others to join the effort. The code can be found at: https://github.com/openPComp/PComp. The documentation can be found at: https://pcomp.readthedocs.io/en/us.html. Samira Chaouchi contributed to this research. Researchers have developed a method to identify the stimulated $B_c^+$ state by analyzing data collected from proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, which operates at a maximum energy of 13 TeV. To create the $B_c^+$ state, teams analyzed a specific type of event where a $J/\psi$ particle is produced, along with other particles such as a jet and a muon, as a result of a $b$-quark and a $d$-quark or $\bar{b}$-quark and $\bar{d}$-quark interaction. Utilizing advanced software and expertise, teams searched through a large dataset, specifically 3.0 fb$^{-1}$, collected by the LHCb detector to develop this analysis. By comparing observed $B_c^+$ production rates to those predicted by the Standard Model, teams found evidence for $B_c^+$ state stimulation, consistent with expected rates, while setting an upper limit on the ratio of stimulated to produced $B_c^+$ states. This groundbreaking finding marks the first detection of $B_c^+$ state stimulation, providing support for the $b$ quark being a composite particle, made up of lighter quarks, while also serving as a test of the Standard Model's predictions for quark interactions. Additionally, teams discovered an upper limit on the ratio of stimulated to produced $B_c^+$ states, specifically less than 178, with a 95% confidence level, providing constraints on the theoretical model of quark interactions. This research was accomplished in collaboration by teams from the LHCb, CMS, and ATLAS experiments, operating at respective detectors, while attached to the Large Hadron Collider. After conducting a thorough evaluation, teams found no significant differences between observed $B_c^+$ production rates and those predicted by the Standard Model, specifically within selected $B_c^+$ decay modes, while finding $B_c^+$ state stimulation in one decay mode, specifically when composed of an $J/\psi$ particle and a muon, along with other particles such as a jet. To further study $B_c^+$ production and its interactions, teams found an upper limit on the ratio of stimulated to produced $B_c^+$ states, specifically when considering only $B_c^+$ decay modes involving an $J/\psi$ particle and a muon, while providing constraints on the theoretical model of quark interactions, specifically up to 145, with a 95% confidence level. A fundamental theoretical framework, known as the continuous-phase approach, serves as the basis for developing novel, highly efficient algorithms to track frequency and amplitude fluctuations within nonlinear systems. Building upon this framework, a new family of continuous-time predictors is proposed, which is then incorporated into traditional Runge-Kutta integrators to enhance dynamic estimation. Notably, the proposed predictors demonstrate exceptional resilience to common challenges such as missing data and intense noise. In particular, this approach offers a continuous-time solution to the issue of data sampling gaps, providing exact interpolation results. Furthermore, the predicted values exhibit a continuous first derivative that converges rapidly to the true solution. As such, the continuous-phase Runge-Kutta predictors maintain the high level of precision afforded by higher-order integrators while significantly reducing sensitivity to noisy data. Consequently, these predictors emerge as a highly effective solution to the general problem of estimating dynamic trajectories from noisy data, an ubiquitous challenge encountered in numerous scientific and engineering applications. While this work focuses on a theoretical framework, the resulting algorithms are immediately applicable to a wide range of practical problems involving signal processing and control. Specifically, the proposed algorithms are illustrated in practical context through examples of frequency estimation in a single cell and parameter inference in a Stuart-Landau oscillator. Source code for the implemented algorithms is available at https://github.com/NickSAR/CPRK. This paper introduces a novel evaluation technique for parallel training of deep neural networks. Unlike existing assessment methods, which synchronize the main computation flow with evaluation processes, our approach allows for asynchronous evaluation and training. This synchrony requirement can hinder the full potential of model-parallel learning, particularly for complex neural networks, by limiting the size of the model that can be distributed across multiple GPUs. To address this constraint, we have developed an asynchronous evaluation method that can be easily incorporated into any existing training code. This technique involves creating multiple regional evaluators that process data with reduced resolution to accelerate assessment, as switching between training and evaluation stages within these regions incurs overhead due to GPU switching. To minimize data augmentation overheads in the evaluators' processing queues, we compress the original data into lower-resolution representations, preserving its core features. This technique is fully explained in our paper and demonstrated to be effective in practical scenarios. Experimental results show that using regional evaluators, complex neural networks can be successfully model-parallel trained on multiple GPUs without any synchronization issues. This allows for significant performance improvements, as our example shows a speed-up of 4x for training a ResNet-50 model. The code for this technique has been made publicly available on GitHub. This discussion focuses on the role of neutron scattering within the framework of the BOSsum project, whose main objective is to create a comprehensive inventory of short-lived, heavy neutron-rich isotopes through collision experiments involving high-energy projectiles with stable targets.  Neutron scattering serves two essential purposes within the project: firstly, it enables the identification of isotopes through the measurement of specific scattering cross-sections at various energies, and secondly, it facilitates the study of nuclear structure by examining how the nuclei of these isotopes interact with non-pion bosons.  To accomplish this, we are conducting both theoretical and experimental investigations involving the analysis of neutron scattering data off of stable and radioactive targets using the APEX detector system at the Spallation Neutron Source.  Our initial investigation involves the measurement of coherent neutron scattering on lead-204, an isotone of the boson summit.  Our analysis reveals an anomalous fluctuation in the count rate, exceeding typical expectations.  This unusual phenomenon is attributed to a rare event in which multiple neutrons simultaneously interact with the target.  By mapping the scattered neutrons over time, we are able to identify this phenomenon, known as a "snake" event.  Our theoretical calculations using the Monte Carlo method confirm the experimental results, and demonstrate that the probability of a snake event is directly proportional to the square of the number of neutrons present.  Third-generation neutron spectrometers will have the capability of detecting these rare events, occurring at rates of approximately one per million billion.  These events will offer a novel perspective on the dynamics of extremely dense matter, boasting an argument that the production of such matter through the collision of heavy ions may be inferior to that achieved through the collision of high-energy projectiles with lighter targets.  A comprehensive examination of the theoretical aspects of such matter has yet to be performed. Recent studies of Galactic spiral arms utilize millimeter-wavelength CO emissions, 
which can accurately trace the distribution of molecular gas. A newly discovered 
CO peak, CO-MPM 2, has been identified at a distance of 20.2 kpc from the Galactic 
center. This CO peak is part of a massive (~1.2 x 10^8 solar mass) molecular cloud 
aligned almost perfectly in a radial direction (~3 kpc away from the Galactic center). 
Due to non-uniform velocity distribution along the line of sight, the velocity 
distribution of this cloud appears to increase along the radius, resembling a 
temperature gradient often observed in Galactic spiral arms. This unique cloud 
displays all characteristics of a spiral arm limb, specifically located at the distance 
of the 3-kpc arm, which suggests the 3-kpc arm consists of spiral arms present at 
different distances. These spiral arms appear to be young (~10 Myr), hot gas clouds 
regulated by the magnetic force, which causes them to dissipate rapidly (~10 Myr). 
As a result, the arms disappear at distances where the galactic potential is too 
low to sustain their stability. These clouds are eventually absorbed by the spiral 
arms' gas reservoir due to cloud-cloud collisions, which generate the well-known 
r^1/ket{2} density pattern observed in the Galactic spiral arms. Finally, the mass 
per unit wavelength (dM/dr) of these spiral arms is calculated to explain the 
existence and features of the 3-kpc arm using the cloud's unique properties. This 
mass per unit wavelength is characterized by an initial sharp peak at the spiral arm 
radius (~4 kpc), which explains the abundance of young (~10 Myr) gas at this 
distance, which in turn generates the prominent features of the Galactic spiral arm 
pattern. This research also reveals the role of gravitation in regulating the spiral 
arm feature, which is particularly evident in the distance where the 3-kpc arm 
disappears. This research also points out the potential contamination of CO 
emissions by non-circular velocity components along the line of sight, which might 
affect the velocity distribution and the distance where the 3-kpc arm disappears. 
Finally, a model has been developed to explain the abundance of young gas at 
different distances using the spiral arm's morphology, which is expected to be 
experimentally verified in the coming years due to the arrival of the Square 
Kilometre Array

Given these conclusions, we can break down their collective preferences into easily computable units, leading to an efficient and straightforward method for resolving the housemate dilemma. Interestingly, separating their preferences into distinct units also makes the arrangement maximising overall pay-off soluble through a simple, efficient algorithm. Our study examines photon-muon correlations in 200 GeV Au+Au and d+Au collisions to explore the properties of jet-medium interactions. The photon-muon pairs are identified through the detection of a direct photon and muons produced from the decay of a muon particle. The photon-muon pairs are analyzed based on the momentum of the photon and the momentum and rapidity of the muon. The photon-muon correlations in Au+Au collisions show an excess of muons with low momentum and high rapidity, compared to d+Au collisions. This excess is observed at all photon momentum bins and is reminiscent of jets that undergo medium interactions. However, this excess is stronger than what is expected from calculations considering only medium interactions in central Au+Au collisions. This indicates the presence of additional sources, such as photons produced in the collision itself, that need to be accounted for in the analysis. Utilizing an algorithm that tracks charged particles, and using calculations that take into consideration photon production and jet-medium interactions, our results show good agreement with data for both Au+Au and d+Au collisions. This agreement is particularly notable for Au+Au collisions, and highlights our ability to quantify jet-medium interactions using photon-muon correlations. By extrapolating our findings, our study estimates a photon yield equivalent to approximately 118 charged pions, representing about 6% of the final photon yield, which originates from jets that undergo medium interactions in Au+Au collisions. This photon yield is subject to variations based on the assumptions of photon production and jet-medium interactions. Our study also notes that photon-muon correlations are sensitive to cold nuclear effects, which can mimic photon production resulting from jet-medium interactions in d+Au collisions. Therefore, our estimate of photon production resulting from jets that undergo medium interactions in Au+Au collisions should be adjusted accordingly. Our study quantifies photon production resulting from jets that undergo medium interactions, which represents about 6% of the final photon yield, and lays the groundwork for similar studies at lower energies and with larger collision systems. Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and low power consumption. However, these sensors require deep depletion layers to ensure adequate tracking capability at low temperatures. Achieving this depletion depth is challenging with thick active layer CMOS technology. To establish a solid foundation for the CLICTD R&D project, this study evaluated CMOS sensor potential using the THM CMOS processor, which has a high-quality collection electrode design. Leveraging the test beam facility at CERN, researchers analyzed sensors built on 200mm wafer substrates utilizing 200mm SOI epi, 300mm FPGA-compatible Cz-Si, and 300mm Cz-Si with a thick FOWTRAN layer. The 500um thick Cz-Si wafer demonstrated the deepest depletion layer at 50V. Although these results show promise for CLICTD R&D, the substrate materials investigated are not suitable for final detector construction due to the presence of oxygen in the active region, which deteriorates charge collection quality by introducing damaged zones around the collection electrodes at the bevels of the wafers. This issue can be overcome by utilizing silicon material with extremely low oxygen content, known as 'finesilicon'. When conducting a meta-analysis with the goal of estimating population mean correlations, the quality of individual studies can vary significantly.  In this paper, we explore two primary issues:  first, we establish a method to assess the reliability of estimated correlation coefficients when sample means are incomplete;  second, we create reliable estimators of population mean correlations by combining data from high-quality studies.  Through simulation, we evaluate the accuracy of these estimators when population mean correlations are non-zero, and demonstrate their applicability in a real-world context using data from 106 studies measuring the correlation between resting-blood-pressure and body-mass-index.  Furthermore, we outline a method to determine a minimum required sample size for a study to be included in the analysis, based on the variance of its correlation estimate and the desired precision of the estimate itself.  This method is also illustrated using data from 106 studies measuring the correlation between resting-blood-pressure and low-density-lipoprotein.  In addition, we propose a reliable estimator of population mean correlations that incorporates within-study variability in both its numerator and denominator.  This proposal is supported through simulation, and provides a useful alternative to the traditional method of estimating population correlation when sample means are incomplete.  Finally, the software necessary to reproduce all results mentioned in the paper has been made available on the repository https://github.com/mkloes/MetaCorr.  In this repository, the user can also find a package implementing the proposed methods described in the paper.  This package is named metaCorr and has been installed as a package of the R language for statistical computation.  Details on how to install the package are provided in the package documentation available at https://mkloes.github.io/meteCorr/.  The package includes a variety of additional helpful functions not mentioned in the paper.  These functions include ones that estimate population mean correlations for specific subgroups within an analysis and ones that provide a reliability assessment of estimated correlations at the study-level. It is also suggested that the authors engage with relevant research in planetary navigation, as well as stochastic techniques and probabilistic modeling, to strengthen the theoretical foundation of this methodon. This study proposes an innovative approach, focusing on medication interaction analysis and leveraging graph neural networks to embed pair-wise relationships. Our framework consists of two primary networks: (i) a graph attention-based embedding network and (ii) a composite graph convolutional neural network. The pursuit of finding the least number of transactions necessary to generate a given set of association rules has sparked considerable interest. A transaction set is considered adequate for generating these rules if it can produce all the rules through implication, and the smallest collection of transactions that can do this is known as a Deductive Basis (DB) for the rules. Existing studies have proposed different methods for finding a DB, but these approaches often yield results that are not as minimal as possible. In this research, we introduce Inference Schemes (IS) that can generate association rules from transactions, and demonstrate that a DB for the rules can be found by first finding a DB for the transactions themselves, specifically those that can infer new rules. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of Redundancy Inferring Inference Bases (RIIB) to showcase that an IS with optimal redundancy-inferring properties can assist in identifying a DB that is also redundancy-inferring, resulting in the generation of association rules with minimal transactional overhead. Using the RIIB concept, we propose two new algorithms: the Deductive Transactions Generator (DTG) algorithm, which finds a DB efficiently by first eliminating irrelevant transactions, and the dual-purpose Generative vs. Deductive Regions (GDR) algorithm, which can choose between generating a DB or a generator for the association rules based on an analytical condition. Using benchmark datasets, we evaluate the effectiveness of our work, and showcase that the DTG and GDR algorithms can successfully identify a DB and an optimal generator for the rules with superior efficiency and performance compared to existing methods. Moreover, we introduce the notion of overlapping databases, and demonstrate that a DB can be efficiently identified using the DTG algorithm, even at large scales, by treating the inference relations among transactions as a graph. Specifically, we show that a DB can be found by first identifying the inference relations in the graph, and then selecting the transactions that can infer new rules, resulting in the generation of association rules with minimal transactional overhead. Using the overlapping database notion, we evaluate the effectiveness of our work, and showcase that the DTG and GDR algorithms can successfully assist in identifying a DB and an optimal generator for the rules with superior efficiency and performance compared to existing methods, by treating the inference relations among transactions as a graph. Arrested offenders are subjected to a court-ordered psychotherapy program as part of their sentence, which also requires them to attend treatment sessions while incarcerated and after release, with the aim of reducing their likelihood of reoffending by improving their psychological well-being. We investigate whether this program truly enhances the psychological well-being of incarcerated individuals as claimed by the government. To do this, we evaluated administrative data containing information about the program's enrollment and the treatment received by its participants, as well as their incarceration history. We developed a control function that models the program's unobserved impacts while utilizing the treatment variations produced by the program's diverse enrollment criteria as instrumental variables. We discovered that, in the short term, enrolled offenders experienced lower levels of property crimes but no change in their psychological well-being. After releasing from prison, we found no evidence that the program decreased their likelihood of committing crimes or improved their psychological well-being in the long term. Despite the program's high adherence rates, our study indicates that its claimed benefits to the psychological well-being of incarcerated individuals are not supported by the data. On the other hand, the program does appear to have a lasting effect in reducing the commission of property crimes. We suggest that the program's perceived failures to improve psychological well-being may be attributed to its focus on reducing reoffending without providing treatment tailored to the particular needs of its clients. In addition, the program's goals may be hindered by the program's constraints, such as high client turnover and the transient nature of the treatment team, as well as the program's brief duration while its clients are incarcerated. As a result, the program's efforts to improve psychological well-being are likely to be hampered by these structural issues. To address these structural issues, we suggest exploring alternative models for the program, such as providing ongoing therapy to a single counselor, that can help to increase its effectiveness in reducing reoffending and improving psychological well-being. Finally, we suggest modeling the program's unobserved impacts at the counselor level rather than the program level, as a means of gaining a more nuanced understanding of its effects and to help to increase its benefits. This paper sets out to establish a method to identify irregularities in data by assessing how well hidden Markov models fit the data, using a novel gauge probability metric. Unlike traditional approaches that focus on model likelihood or error rates. Our method involves training hidden Markov models on sequences of equal length, then using these models to estimate the probability distribution of gauge probabilities across the sequence space. Regions with high gauge probability indicate the models' most preferred sequence arrangements. By comparing actual data sequences to these probability distributions, we can gauge how well the models account for variations in the data. This metric allows us to assess hidden Markov models as data compressors and use them to predict the information content of the data. Based on the information content, we identify abnormal sequences. The proposed method, using this gauge probability metric, performs well in differentiating normal and abnormal activity, as demonstrated by experiments using synthetic and real-world data. Specifically, the method effectively identifies irregular sleep patterns in human activity data. Details of our method can be found on the University of Washington's Machine Learning Repository under the title "Abnormality Identification with HMM Gauge Probability Examination". In addition, the corresponding data can be found on Figshare, referred to as hg. Furthermore, the generated figures are stored on Figshare under the reference fug. Based on our research, the gauge probability metric offers an invaluable advantage in understanding hidden Markov models' behavior and has a distinct application in identifying irregular sequences. A widespread issue in analytics involves interpreting blended sample data, where the composition and variables measured are represented as random combinations of known distributions. This can be viewed as a non-identifiable estimation problem when prior knowledge is incorporated through probability distributions assigned to unknown parameters. One specific scenario is determining the average component content of a blended industrial material analyzed for its bulk density. Prior distributions are often narrow with significant mass concentrated near the true values, reflecting researchers' confidence in their accuracy. In such cases, a simplified Bayesian approach is usually sufficient. It is analogous to maximizing a standard likelihood function and is used to approximate posterior distributions by iterating an expectation-maximization algorithm. This paper examines the convergence of this algorithm in a general context and illustrates its convergence with concrete examples, including the assignment of average densities to industrial materials and the determination of oil blends based on analyzed petroleum samples. The transformation of fashion images involves multiple operations such as resizing and transforming to match product views, which can be incorrectly applied by commercial websites to conceal image duplications and fake product listings. By utilizing fashion-specific keypoint annotations, we have developed Visual Inconsistency Detection, an algorithm to identify visually incompatible images. With support from keypoint-based correspondence detection and matching loss functions, our model has achieved exceptional performance on the evaluation dataset, achieving true positive rates of 93.75% and accuracy of 88.95%. Notably, our results have surpassed the performance of k-nearest-neighbor-based methods on the evaluation dataset, which included features such as resizing to align image dimensions and transforming to match egg-like characteristics. Moreover, to enhance our model's ability to detect incompatible images, we have introduced a contrastive pre-training approach, which trains the model using pairs of images with different transformations applied, resulting in improved performance on the evaluation dataset, increasing true positive rates to 97.5% and accuracy to 89.75%. Our work has enabled the successful application of the model on real-world commercial websites, utilizing features such as feature embedding matching and bounding box detection to filter out image duplicates and fake listings. With support from fashion-oriented keypoint annotations, our model has achieved exceptional results, performing better than k-nearest-neighbor-based methods and surpassing a top-performing transformer model by 11.5% in terms of accuracy. Furthermore, to further improve our model's ability to detect incompatible images, we have introduced a contrastive pre-training approach, which trains the model using pairs of images with different transformations applied, resulting in a 3.8% improvement in accuracy and 4.1% improvement in true positive rates. A common challenge in Federated Learning is ensuring model convergence with non-convergent client updates. This paper tackles this issue by allowing unconstrained gradient communication from clients to the server. The main text is self-contained, but the reader is referred to supplementary materials for additional proofs. This survey is an expanded version of the introductory chapters to the instructor-led winter school on non-parametric estimation held at University of Geneva in February 2021.

This paper builds on previous research regarding the applicability of hyperbolicity in understanding the convergence rate of Monte Carlo methods, specifically Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). In our analysis, we employ a technique called covering, which involves analyzing a set through the use of a family of subsets with specified sizes. By utilizing this approach, we derive new, high-dimensional expansions for various Monte Carlo methods, including those involving unbiased estimators and maximum likelihood estimation. Our findings demonstrate the association of these expansions with local minimax semidefinite programming principles. We aimed to evaluate various selection tasks using pre-trained models in a zero-shot setting. Our assessment involved examining how well naturally occurring prompts, derived from written texts and used to convey written language, perform in a range of tasks. We discovered through our experiments that native speaker prompts are highly effective in a zero-shot environment, yielding significant improvements over models trained on written text alone. However, non-native prompts failed to demonstrate the same level of effectiveness. Our findings also revealed that models utilizing written prompts struggle to perform well, even when provided with extensive training data. Notably, models trained on a combination of written and spoken data exhibited a tendency to diverge from the prompts, leading to underwhelming performance in tasks requiring comprehension of spoken language. Our analysis suggests that current pre-trained models are better suited to process and make inferences from written input, rather than oral cues. Additionally, models trained on a broad range of data may become less responsive to prompt-based instructions. We hope these observations contribute to the development of more effective models capable of adapting to diverse input types, including speech. We also hope our study influences the creation of prompts that better reflect the variety of human language, rather than just written forms. UGC 8839 is an isolated, ancient spiral galaxy located approximately 250 million light-years away, belonging to the UMa group of galaxies. Due to its lack of close galaxy interactions, the galaxy retains an extremely durable disk, preserving youthful characteristics. Our study aimed to examine the stability and structural composition of UGC 8839's disk through a high-resolution N-body simulation. Utilizing the Constance N-body code with a $2 \times 2$ degree initial grid and a $1$ kpc spacing, our researchers simulated the galaxy's evolution over an extremely long period of time - nearly 1.7 billion years. To account for potential uncertainties in the model, various parameter sets were tested, including different values for the dark matter halo's concentration, the bulge radius, and the disk orientation. By adjusting these parameters, our team identified and evaluated multiple scenarios that could lead to significant changes in the galaxy's life span, its overall mass, and its residual angular momentum. However, all tested scenarios resulted in a highly stable galaxy with minimal changes over time, mirroring the extremely slow changes in the galaxy's morphological features observed in data from the SDSS, including its grand design spiral arms. Notably, our model failed to capture the full extent of the galaxy's dark matter halo as observed in data from the SDSS, indicating the presence of a significant indeterminate mass outside of the visible galaxy. Our study concludes that UGC 8839's exceptionally durable disk is a direct consequence of its extremely unstressed evolutionary history, with its extremely slow changes supporting the validity of $CDM$ cosmological model in galactic scales. Moreover, our study highlights the extremely long time frame over which galaxies maintain their quasi-stable quasi-equilibrium state before their significant dissolution into stellar spheroids. This prolonged period of stability challenges our current understanding of galaxy formation theories that typically predict a much shorter time frame for galaxy formation based on the merger-by-merger hypothesis. Moreover, our study raises questions about the significance of galaxy formation simulations that typically stop after an average galaxy's initial formation is complete. These simulations often terminate too prematurely as they fail to account for the extremely long time frames required for a galaxy's complete evolution. Finally, our study emphasizes the need for lengthy high-resolution N-body simulations that can capture the extremely long time frames required for a galaxy's complete evolution, extending far beyond an average galaxy's initial formation. Recent advancements in audio generation through neural networks have made it possible to create synthetic sounds that are difficult to distinguish from real ones. While typically relying on text-based prompts, we investigate the use of visual inputs to govern audio production. By combining a conditional generator network and a reference audio dataset, we generate audio samples aligned with the temporal structure of the provided visual cue. For example, an image of a walking human triggers a walking sound effect. Our system can be trained to adapt to various visual stimuli by using a pool of related audio samples. We demonstrate its effectiveness on three tests: creating sounds linked to visual descriptions, crafting sounds associated with visual representations, and replicating sounds tied to specific scenes. Our results show that this method produces visuomotionally grounded audio samples superior to those generated through text-based prompts alone. These findings open the door for the development of more immersive, visually responsive audio content. A live demo is available online. Model (MTKDDM), comprising a predictive model and an association rule discovery
algorithm. We choose recurrent models carefully to address the limitations of
traditional methods such as data representation, evaluation metrics, and
temporal knowledge extraction. Experimental outcomes with real-world data from
retail and air traffic control phenomena demonstrate the effectiveness of our
model. Additionally, we compare the performance of various recurrent models and
highlight their advantages over traditional methods. Our study showcases how
recurrent neural networks can be leveraged for temporal knowledge discovery. We
expect our findings to guide practitioners working with time series data. Our code
is available for reproduction of the experiments at https://github.com/
ammarov-mdf/Recurrent Neural Networks for Temporal Knowledge Discovery. Our model
can be accessed via an R package at https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=
RecurrentTemporalKnowledgeDiscovery. Our study has a companion article at
https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10139206. Shorter versions of the study have
been presented at IEEE International Conference on Big Data and Intelligent
Combinations (BIC) and International Conference on Data Science, Computing
and Optimization Technology (DCOT). Our study has been funded by the Natural
 Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC) under grant

valuable feedback. We wish to extend our gratitude to I. A. Almula Naim for her
assistance. This study has been conducted in an effort to acquire temporal
knowledge in an unbiased and automatic manner, eliminating the need for domain
expertise. Our work is centered on the application of neural networks in the
comprehensive analysis of time series data, aiming to discover temporal
associations of any length. This approach differs from existing methods, which
usually require domain expertise to select suitable time periods and evaluation
metrics. We propose an automatic and unbiased method for temporal knowledge
acquisition using recurrent neural networks, addressing their limitations and
showcasing their effectiveness in real-world data. We compare the performance of
different models and highlight their capabilities for temporal knowledge

A underlying concept, central to our discussion, is that of Chow classes, which serve as statistical models, enabling the translation of geometric queries into algebraic problems solvable by computer. Building on this foundation, we investigate how Chow classes' information content varies as data is compressed, applying concepts like entropy and mutual information from information theory. Envelopes, used to capture extremal quantity relationships, also play a crucial role, leading to the derivation of distributional limits, akin to topological invariants, which in turn provide new perspectives on already established results. A key method employed is GIT schemes, with computations exemplified through low-dimension examples, including green-blue boundary analysis. As a consequence of this work, a statistical transfer is demonstrated, transferring knowledge from enumerative algebraic geometry to combinatorial and topological realms. Furthermore, researchers discovered a correlation between the Thurston norm of an integer and the number of unique tight contact frameworks it can support. A previously unknown aspect of the norm's behavior has been revealed as a result of these findings. Additionally, researchers developed algorithms to determine all integers supported by the Thurston norm as well as the exact number of unique tight contact frameworks each integer can support. Moreover, researchers employed the program to explore further properties of the Thurston norm, such as its distribution functions, and to establish relationships between the norm and other combinatorial properties. A newly discovered class of hyperbolic 2-bridge links provides further insight into the existing knowledge about the Thurston norm. The research presented here delves into both the mathematical theory behind tight contact frameworks and their computational analysis. A comprehensive list of 156 unique tight contact frameworks supported by the Thurston norm up to 280 has also been provided. It is hypothesized that the frameworks with the fewest cross-links have the highest number of unique tight contact frameworks. Our analysis delves into the cost characteristics of cryptocurrencies, investigating whether their value dynamics adhere to the cost consistency theory. Cost consistency theory posits that a currency's underlying value is influenced by the costs incurred in producing and maintaining it, leading to a positive correlation between these costs and the currency's price. We tested this hypothesis by applying cost consistency theory to both Bitcoin and Ethereum, selecting transaction fees as a direct representation of costs. Our results indicate a positive correlation between transaction fees and cryptocurrency prices, validating the cost consistency theory. Furthermore, we discovered significant lag effects, where changes in costs predicted corresponding changes in prices. We explored the practical utility of cost consistency, demonstrating its ability to forecast future price increases. Our research offers a novel framework for understanding cryptocurrency price behavior, providing investors and policymakers with an innovative perspective. Our statistical models, rooted in long-term analysis (greater than five years), demonstrate robustness and are relatively immune to short-term fluctuations. Our sample included 14 significant cryptocurrencies, revealing that Ethereum and Bitcoin exhibit the strongest associations with cost consistency. Our findings underscore the importance of fundamental analysis in forecasting, emphasizing the interplay between costs, risks, and returns in shaping the investment environment. In SASE FEL schemes, a natural exponential gain mode inevitably leads to a significant first-order coherence, causing the broadband pulse to reach its maximum power earlier than its center, thus shortening the pulse duration. However, this increased spatial coherence comes at a cost: it causes the emerging pulse to decay prematurely via the tapering process. To optimize attosecond metrology applications using the FEL, we investigate modified SASE patterns that mitigate this disparity between spectral and temporal properties. By introducing a gain-profile-modulation technique, we demonstrate the production of high-energy attosecond bursts in XUV and soft X-ray FEL facilities, thereby achieving increased pulse duration and a enhanced degree of spatial coherence. Consequently, this modified approach yields enhanced peak power, a optimized pulse duration, and enhanced spectral tunability, thereby optimizing attosecond pulse generation. Notably, this technique can be implemented without compromising the typical compression ratio aimed for by the tapering process. Moreover, we demonstrate that this modified SASE pattern can be generated using a relatively low average power if the tapering process commences at a earlier stage than usual, thereby achieving optimized performance with a reduced risk of damage to downstream beamlines. Shear flows in the near-bed layer of a particle-laden channel flow can be divided into
two parts: a particle-free upper section and a solid-phase lower section that experiences
shear. The movement of the particle-rich layer is solely due to the movement of the interface
separating the two regions, as it adheres to Newtonian optics due to its low viscosity.
 Consequently, the shear rate within this layer is equivalent to the rate at which the interface
moves perpendicular to itself, which is why it behaves like a viscous fluid. Researchers have
identified five methods for calculating the shear viscosity of this layer: (i) direct measurement
from experimental data, (ii) an indirect calculation based on local force coupling between
particles and walls, (iii) an estimation technique that takes into account the forces acting on
particles far away from walls, (iv) an estimation method that uses forces acting on particles
close to walls, and (v) an approximation method that requires minimal computational expense.
Some of these methods can estimate the shear viscosity with precision, while others can do
so at a lower computational cost. We compare the accuracy and efficiency of these methods.

calculated using an advanced sampling technique. Computer simulation methods, such

different voting habits distributions affect the fairness score. Utilizing the

eliminate the inherent unfairness introduced by an intentionally biased district

A key component of this research compares the influence of exponents from different sector types on the comparisons of harmonic functions. With this setup, SHiP will be able to detect the desired signals in multiple decay channels with high probabilities. If the proposed particle detection system is implemented, SHiP will be able to detect the desired signals at a significance of five standard deviations for an exposure of 1.5 fb^-1 of integrated luminosity. However, many popular CNN structures overlook the benefits of oblique filters, ultimately limiting their potential in image recognition tasks. In this study, a new architecture was introduced that harnesses the advantages of oblique filters within a oriented Convolutional Neural Networks (OCNNs) framework. By incorporating oriented filters and an extended rotation symmetry, the proposed OCNNs increase the representational power of traditional CNNs. The study demonstrated the effectiveness of OCNNs over standard CNNs through comprehensive experiments across multiple datasets, including the DAWBA dataset, the extended N-Woodson dataset, and the CBCL dataset. Additionally, the researchers explored the benefits of incorporating oriented filters within recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and recurrent convolutional neural networks (RCNNs). Notably, the OCNNs architecture exhibited a substantial improvement in identification accuracy when applied to oriented images, outperforming baseline CNNs and RNNs/RCNNs models. The study also highlighted the challenges and pitfalls of relying on oriented filters for image recognition tasks. Specifically, the authors addressed queries about the feasibility of reducing oriented filters to perpendicular filters and the potential implications on feature representation. Finally, the researchers explored the difficulties of optimizing oblique filters and proposed future research directions in the focused area. Notably, this method excels even when the malice is concealed within large datasets, particularly when focused on specific, critical functions. Measuring ambiguity in text is a crucial task for modern computational research. This study compares different methods for calculating ambiguity in text by using a unified framework. One such method uses a confusion matrix to quantify ambiguity, allowing for a standardized evaluation across various texts and languages. Empirical analysis of eight distinct techniques for calculating ambiguity reveals that four of these methods are incompatible with the proposed confusion matrix approach. An experiment involving 40 scientists across eight domains showed that seven experts agree on the recommended technique for calculating ambiguity. An open-source evaluation platform is provided to compare different techniques and establish common standards for future studies on ambiguity calculation. Furthermore, our findings suggest specific techniques for calculating ambiguity in particular fields, such as text classification, part-of-speech tagging, parsing, and text classification. These recommendations are based on an evaluation across ten distinct datasets from diverse domains. Additionally, we propose new metrics for assessing ambiguity that surpass recall and precision in several application areas. Lastly, we demonstrate the feasibility of using the proposed confusion matrix approach for interpreting the performance of text classification models and highlighting potential improvements. This study contributes to fundamental research in natural language processing and machine learning, shedding light on the underlying assumptions of different techniques for calculating ambiguity and highlighting their implications and limitations. This work may also inform applications in medical diagnosis and decision-making processes. To foster a community effort, we invite fellow researchers to contribute to our research by commenting, critiquing, evaluating, and building upon our findings and the proposed evaluation platform. Our source code, data, and evaluation platform are publicly available for reproduction and further development. Solving large-scale Markov decision processes often poses a significant challenge
due to the limitation on available memory and computational resources, making it
impossible to store or process the entire policy or value function. To overcome
this issue, we present an iterative algorithm within the GMRES framework that
enables policy search in Markov decision processes. Each iteration represents a
distinct approximation of the policy or value function with progressively higher
accuracy, with each component having a corresponding confidence interval. This
method offers two advantages: it only temporarily stores information, and it
only temporarily loads data into memory during each iteration. Notably, our
approach excels at solving large-scale reward-free optimization problems, and we
also extend its applicability to model-based reinforcement learning by incorporating
the iterative GMRES strategy as a pre-processing step. We demonstrate the
efficacy of this method using both synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing
its ability to successfully solve large-scale reward-free optimization problems
wherein the state-space extends beyond the memory limit. Moreover, we highlight
its memory and computational efficiency compared to alternative methods. While
it inherits the convergence rate of GMRES, we present reasons to believe that
its iterative nature may allow it to converge at a faster rate than policy
gradient descent in certain scenarios. We validate this hypothesis using
model-based reinforcement learning by analyzing the convergence rate of both
approaches on a synthetic task. Finally, we propose incorporating memory bounds
into the study of reinforcement learning to better reflect real-world limitations,
and we believe that our method provides a meaningful addition to this area of
research. It also represents a novel application of iterative algorithms within
the GMRES framework to Markov decision processes, and it can be freely accessed
via the GitHub repository. We also present a GYMROM module for automatic vectorization
using PyTorch, as well as a pprocess tool for transient state pre-processing.
