A linear edge ideal of a weighted directed graph is created by taking the sum of all monomials formed from its vertices, with each monomial's degree determined by the weight of the path it represents. We investigate the supported prime ideals of this type, particularly focusing on both the symbolic and Cohen-Macaulay properties. Specific criteria have also been developed to ensure a linear edge ideal has these properties, with complete answers provided for symbolic strength in the case of bipartite graphs and Cohen-Macaulay in the case of forest edge ideals. This research builds on a previous study by the authors, extending its conclusions to weighted directed graphs. We also introduce an algorithm to identify the vertices that generate a linear edge ideal, with accompanying code available. In support of this research, new concepts of walk and path posets, along with its corresponding lattices, are developed along with proofs of independent interest. Some of the key techniques used in this research include the decomposition of linear edge ideals into edge submonoids, the application of Serre's theorem and the Lucas theorem. Additionally, by analyzing the Lyndon decomposition, new general methods for decomposing linear edge ideals into squarefree monomial ideals have been developed. Specifically, this research determines which linear edge ideals have a decomposition consisting of complete bipartite monomial ideals and provides a formula for the Krull dimension of any linear edge ideal. These new methods and concepts are grounded in the abstract representation of linear edge ideals as the image of a semiring homomorphism, with its kernel being a Cohen-Macaulay ideal. Some of this research has also led to a new proof of the strong perfect graph theorem. With this research aimed at broadening its scope, many of the specific concepts and techniques have been replaced with effective and general methods. Ultimately, this research aims to establish linear edge ideals as a versatile tool for studying graph properties. Some of these ideas have been tested with examples from combinatorial geometry, specifically through the application of linear edge ideals to model hypergraphs and matroid rank-generating functions. This method refines PDF interpolation and progression by incorporating constraints from high-momentum-fraction data, especially ANTICHARM data, using a novel set of weight functions. The enhanced results are obtained using the updated PDFs from the global analysis of parton distribution functions, and are shown to significantly improve the fit quality, particularly with an emphasis on high-momentum-fraction data. The effectiveness of this method is further demonstrated by the resultant changes in its input parameters. Notably, the progress of two valence quark distribution functions, u_V and d_V, is accelerated and becomes more pronounced with an exponent of ~1.5, while that of the gluon distribution function, g, is slowed down and becomes more gentle with an exponent less than ~1. The progress of PDFs is visualized through a series of before-and-after plots, and the resultant changes in its input parameters are also listed in an appendix. The effect of incorporating constraints from high-momentum-fraction data is further examined by a series of numerical studies, and the resultant changes in the PDF progression are discussed in the context of related theories, such as those involving color octet gluon-meson correlations and the instanton-induced gluon distribution function. The evolution of these non-perturbative matrix elements is hypothesized to follow a power law, and the constants in the power-law functions are parameterized and treated as free parameters to be determined through a series of numerical studies. To establish a sustainable human presence on other planets, creating infrastructure using local materials is crucial, with lunar and Martian granular regolith serving as a suitable substitute for Earth-based granular materials. Building infrastructure using local materials necessitates the use of heat for bonding, but introduces complexities due to the inherent properties of these extraterrestrial regoliths. The regolith's low melting point and high content of oxidizing agents make the process's effectiveness unpredictable, leading to concerns over structural integrity and safety. The primary objectives of this investigation are to examine how different sintering temperatures impact the mechanical properties and microstructure of lunar and Martian regolith samples, as well as to make comparisons with standard Earth-based granular material samples. The results show that the sintering temperature significantly affects the mechanical properties and microstructure of the regoliths, with the lunar regolith exhibiting the most variation due to its complex composition. The strength of the samples was found to be weakest at temperatures just above their melting points, with a particular decline in the Martian samples due to vaporization issues during testing. The microstructure analysis using X-ray computed tomography reveals detailed images of the regolith's internal structure, allowing for the identification of gas voids and unbonded particles. The most efficient sintering temperature was found to result in a regolith with a uniform internal structure and the least number of gas voids. The presence of crystalline structures was observed in the lunar regolith as a result of quenching, a by-product of uncontrolled cooling, which may affect its mechanical properties and efficiency in construction applications. The findings of this investigation can serve as a reference point for establishing infrastructure using local materials on other planets, with the aim of informing future construction projects aimed at establishing a sustainable human presence on the lunar and Martian surfaces. The data collected during these tests can also contribute to a deeper understanding of the physical and mechanical properties of granular materials on Earth. Additionally, the data can be utilized in numerical simulations to develop predictive models of regolith behavior under various environmental and loading conditions. The microstructure information can also be used to develop predictive models of hysteresis, deformation, and strength of these extraterrestrial regoliths. Furthermore, the dataset can support ongoing and future research focused on establishing a sustainable human presence on other planets by informing construction methods that utilize local materials, with applications extending beyond lunar and Martian regolith to other celestial bodies with similar geological materials. This work presents an approach for recognizing handwritten mathematical expressions using data from various sensors. The paper addresses a key challenge in learning to identify these expressions by developing a system that can analyze input from different sources, including the Geckochip, which captures spatial information, and the Freesense, which provides temporal context. A key component of this challenge is a neural network called SeMNISTNet. Primarily designed for spatial analysis, SeMNISTNet was modified to include an encoder-decoder architecture, incorporating temporal data through an encoder, while its original spatial analysis components continue to analyze the expression's layout. The proposed method involves using both sensor inputs to create a combined temporal-spatial feature set, which is then fed into a classification module. To test this approach, handwritten mathematical expressions were generated using simulated writing motions, simulating the sensor data. The results demonstrate that SeMNISTNet can successfully recognize these expressions when presented with combined spatial and temporal contexts. Notably, when evaluating with spatial information only, SeMNISTNet showed a 10% drop in its accuracy. The developed system was further assessed with a video-based mathematical expression dataset, demonstrating its ability to provide a detailed semantic description of the expression's layout and its sequential development. The proposed recognition pipeline presents a significant advancement in the field, offering a more comprehensive understanding of handwritten mathematical expressions through the analysis of spatial and temporal sensor data. This study presents an innovative approach to synthesizing speech using non-statistical methods. Typically, speech synthesis relies on statistical models like Hidden Markov Models or deep learning algorithms like Generative Adversarial Networks. In this research, we employ a non-statistical method based on the Fitts' law to create synthetic speech within specified durations. The non-statistical model is learned from recorded speech data with varying lengths. Subsequently, we modify this model to achieve pre-defined speech durations using a median-based driver. The proposed system is demonstrated to effectively produce synthetic speech within specified durations. Additionally, the study examines how synthetic speech lengths are perceived by human listeners and whether they differ from naturally occurring lengths. Intrinsic evaluations support the method's efficacy in creating synthetic speech within specified durations while extrinsic evaluations indicate that human listeners prefer shorter synthetic speech lengths. Furthermore, comparisons with human-generated speech lengths reveal that the non-statistical model excels at replicating speech lengths, particularly for longer utterances. The study also analyzes the frequency of pause durations in synthetic speech and explores ways to incorporate pauses into the non-statistical model using a straightforward, high-level strategy. The proposed method offers a non-statistical solution for synthesizing speech with specified durations that can be optimized through intuitive human corrections. The study's findings may lead to the development of a new, non-statistical speech synthesis technique based on the Fitts' law. The rapid dissemination of unverified information through social media platforms like WhatsApp is a major contributor to the spread of misinformation. This problem is particularly pronounced in WhatsApp-supported groups, where a single member can send a message to multiple recipients. As a solution to this issue, WhatsApp introduced limitations on the forwarding of certain message types to prevent the rapid dissemination of misinformation. Our study examines these limitations as a key factor in reducing the forward of questionable or misleading information. We developed an agent-based model of a WhatsApp group dynamic, incorporating a basic agent learning algorithm derived from societal learning theory. Our initial findings indicate that the introduction of these limitations significantly reduces the forward of suspicious information. Notably, these limitations appear to have a more pronounced effect on scenarios with higher misinformation prevalence. Conversely, in situations with low misinformation prevalence, restrictions on message forwarding have a relatively minor impact. Crucially, the limitations introduce a novel bottleneck that can be exploited by information system designers to control the spread of misinformation, particularly when coupled with awareness campaigns targeting WhatsApp users. While our study focuses on group conversations, its key outcomes are also applicable to individual chats. Based on our analysis, we recommend targeted awareness campaigns coupled with the further optimization of WhatsApp's forwarding policies to counteract the spread of misinformation. Furthermore, our study uncovers an unexpected opportunity for the design of information systems that can potentially mitigate the spread of misinformation through the control of message forwarding. The development of end-to-end spoofing countermeasure systems has gained significant traction in the research community. However, systems built with conventional architectures tend to be ineffective against sophisticated spoofing techniques employed by adversaries. In an attempt to overcome these limitations, we propose utilizing neural network components that exhibit adaptive behavior, dynamic connections, and attention-based mechanisms to enhance the counteraction of spoofing attacks. We introduce the Attentive ReLU (AReLU) activation function, along with an attention-based layer, and combine them with a conventional hidden layer, to demonstrate their effectiveness in addressing spoofing attacks within speech authentication. We evaluate our proposed design using a neural network trained on the ASVSpoof2019 challenge dataset, and successfully show its superiority over a baseline system built with conventional components. Additionally, a detailed analysis is provided on how the proposed design architechture can be adapted to tackle various spoofing attacks with minimal modifications. It is found that certain attention-based components can provide substantial improvements, while others may introduce adverse effects in specific scenarios. As a result, a comprehensive system architecture must be carefully designed in accordance with the nature of the spoofing attack being addressed. We expect our proposed design to contribute positively to the development of end-to-end spoofing countermeasure systems, especially against adaptable adversaries. A key aspect is that they often employ microwave resonators in close proximity to superconducting devices to monitor their behavior. Accurate evaluation of these systems necessitates a thorough understanding of the interaction between microwave fields and superconducting components.  Researchers use near-field nano-probes to investigate the terahertz radiation produced by these devices.  This experimental method can pinpoint locations of radiation emission by identifying areas with maximum signal amplitude.  Nonetheless, it falls short in providing insight into radiation polarization or the spatial distribution of the electric and magnetic field components.  This drawback can impede precise modeling of the devices' radiation characteristics.  This study employs near-field terahertz microscopy in conjunction with simultaneous measurements in an optical microscope to investigate the radiation emitted by coplanar microwave resonators.  By utilizing this dual approach, researchers were able to visualize the resonators' radiation, examine the effect of surface roughness, and use the data to validate simulations of the devices' terahertz emission.  This technique holds promise for optimizing research and future experiments involving quantum computing, particularly by investigating the effects of surface imperfections on terahertz emission.  Additionally, its integration with optical microscopy enables researchers to correlate optical and terahertz properties of samples, broadening its range of applications.  This includes evaluating the quality of superconducting junctions or the analysis of biochemical samples emitting terahertz radiation. A beneficial approach for gathering user data without transferring private information to a central server is known as federated learning. This method allows models to be collectively updated using encrypted data, but presents difficulties when models need to be adapted for new categories outside of users' existing knowledge. We propose a unified framework, referred to as Zero-Shot Federated Learning (ZS-FL), which makes it possible for this model adaptation to occur without needing users to provide data for the new categories. Compared to prior methods for achieving zero-shot learning, ZS-FL has several advantages, notably requiring fewer assumptions and being more robust against data imbalance. We test ZS-FL in a real-world audio classification setting, where it successfully enables the model to learn about newly introduced categories using unlabeled data and demonstrates improved accuracy overall. Specifically, it achieves high accuracy without users' data for the new categories, with minimal dependence on users' data for the existing categories and with a runtime that is directly proportional to users' data for the existing categories. Our idea builds on previous research demonstrating high-fidelity measurements of large-scale Greenberger-Horne-Zeilberg states using entanglement-based quantum communication protocols. To achieve this, we develop a method to critically examine the convergence of a specific computational algorithm, which generates the inverse of a large-scale complex matrix. Our analysis focuses on the potential impacts of numerical inaccuracies resulting from this inversion on the entire communication process. To mitigate this risk, we investigate alternative approaches for high-fidelity large-scale GHZ state evaluation, including enhancing the existing assumption underlying the convergence theorem and leveraging the inherent properties of large-scale lattices. Additionally, we explore the applicability of a high-fidelity large-scale GHZ state to the quantum entanglement purification process via the cavity electromechanical interaction method. This investigation involves evaluating the effects of numerical inaccuracies on the final purification efficiency. Our findings indicate that for a wide range of participants, the influence of numerical inaccuracies is negligible, but may become a limiting factor for very large-scale systems, where the number of participants exceeds the square root of the matrix size. To address this potential issue, we devise an alternative approach for high-fidelity large-scale GHZ state purification, which incorporates a generalization of the main theorem in the study of symmetric matrices. This approach enables the evaluation of the final purification efficiency with a predetermined level of accuracy, while also allowing for the identification of specific system scales where numerical inaccuracies become a limiting factor, making our proposed purification protocol applicable only to large scales, but not all of them. Lastly, our study also examines how to critically evaluate another high-fidelity large-scale GHZ state measurement method, which involves leveraging the properties of the Toeplitz matrix. This investigation involves testing the reliability of a specific analytical solution, which generates the analytical inverse of a large Hermitian Toeplitz matrix. Our analysis focuses on the potential impacts of numerical inaccuracies resulting from this inversion on the entire measurement process. To mitigate this risk, we investigate alternative approaches for high-fidelity large-scale GHZ state measurement, which may involve enhancing the existing assumptions underlying the convergence theorem. This, in turn, could allow us to leverage the inherent properties of the Toeplitz matrix to develop a more reliable high-fidelity large-scale GHZ state measurement method. Overall, our study provides a thorough evaluation of the reliability of three high-fidelity large-scale GHZ state measurement methods, which could be useful to quantum researchers. This critical evaluation could also contribute to the development of more reliable protocols in the study of quantum information processing

This study proposes a novel approach to simultaneous uplink and downlink channel estimation in a scenario involving multiple users and a programmable reflectarray. To achieve this, we develop a network protocol that utilizes the users to transmit a training signal, which is then reflected and altered in content by the reflectarray in a manner that maximizes information gathered about the channel. Notably, we observe that specific entries within the channel matrix can be effectively estimated simultaneously. Building upon this observation, we introduce two main estimation methods - a linear least-squares approach and an iterative maximum-likelihood method - that leverage the estimated entries to recover the full channel matrix. Our simulation results validate the efficacy of the proposed protocols, demonstrating that the estimated channel matches accurately with as few as three users and a reflectarray size that is one-tenth that of the array elements. Furthermore, we observe that the iterative maximum-likelihood method offers enhanced performance at the cost of increased computational complexity. Consequently, this approach is deemed suitable for scenarios requiring precise beamforming. Conversely, the linear least-squares method is recommended for applications where computational resources are constrained and a degree of estimation error can be tolerated. Notably, we also provide an estimation speed metric that enables users to determine whether the estimated channel suffices for a given application. To facilitate practical implementation, we also devise a device-based training-signal processing script using MATLAB. Additionally, we resort to the Riemannian manifolds technique to devise an efficient algorithm for the semi-orthogonal decomposition of the channel matrix, which is then utilized to enhance the separation of distinct user signals. We formally prove the proposed algorithm's efficacy, which is further validated by our simulation results showcasing the efficiency of the algorithm in ensuring orthogonalization. Consequently, this study offers two novel solutions to the estimation challenge - the entry-based approach and the semi-orthogonal decomposition of the channel matrix, which are expected to elevate the development of reflectarray surfaces in wireless communication. To contribute to the broader theoretical context, we also present an alternative solution to the estimation challenge, which is grounded in the manifold optimization technique. This study explores linkages among COVID-19 coverage, infections, fatalities, and audience within 219 U.S. television markets, as well as variations in coverage among NBC, CBS, ABC, and Fox affiliates. We examined how region-specific factors influenced COVID reporting, including population demographics, the disease's severity, local news consumption patterns, and the availability of essential resources. We discovered that areas with more COVID-related coverage tended to experience higher infection and fatality rates, and that this relationship was more pronounced in markets adhering to the Fox news feed. Furthermore, there was evidence that news outlets adjusted their COVID reporting based on local demographics and the severity of the pandemic. Notably, there were notable differences in COVID-related coverage among the four major broadcast networks, and the disease's prominence in local news was often reflected in the number of fatalities reported. These findings suggest a complex interplay among COVID reporting, infections, fatalities, and audience at the regional level. They also imply that the pandemic's coverage was not solely a top-down process, but rather one influenced by a combination of factors, including the disease's severity, local news consumption patterns, and the tone and stance of the news feed to which a particular market subscribes. Finally, there is reason to believe that the pandemic's coverage may have contributed to the spread of misinformation and a perceived disparity in COVID-related coverage among the four major broadcast networks. Potential solutions to these issues are also proposed. Specifically, it is suggested that TV news professionals rely on reliable sources of information and adopt a more standardized approach to pandemic reporting, and that news organizations provide their audiences with accurate context and scope of the pandemic through "numbers stories." Additionally, it is proposed that TV news professionals utilize more objective metrics, such as population-based case counts, in pandemic reporting, and that news professionals maintain transparency regarding data sources and the availability of vaccines in local communities. Finally, it is suggested that TV news professionals cover the pandemic's social, economic, and political implications with greater frequency and depth. By addressing these gaps, it is anticipated that the pandemic's coverage will become more equitable, effective, and responsive to the needs and perspectives of local communities. As a result, it is expected that the pandemic's legacy will be less divisive and less damaging to the nation's social fabric and the credibility of the news media. In the end, it is anticipated that the pandemic will serve as a watershed moment for TV news, and that the pandemic's coverage will become a bellwether for a more inclusive, effective, and equitable phase of local news

Bloom filters provide efficient membership testing for large sets of elements, but with increasing probability of false positives as a consequence. To mitigate this issue, alternative data structures such as Bloom and Cuckoo filters have been introduced. The former inserts multiple elements at a time, while the latter inserts single elements at random, using existing elements to make predictions about new additions. Both structures trade off accuracy for decreased size and speed. A novel approach, xor filters, is presented here, offering a distinct strategy for inserting multiple elements at once while adapting to the statistical properties of queries to optimize performance. As such, xor filters surpass both Bloom and Cuckoo filters in efficiency, requiring less memory and processing time. Moreover, xor filters can be easily modified to include removal of existing elements or the suppression of false positives. Our experiments demonstrate significant performance gains, especially in areas where a low false positive rate is crucial. Conversely, xor filters may exhibit lower false positive rates than Cuckoo filters in certain scenarios, often at the cost of increased size. As such, xor filters can be seen as an efficient alternative to existing filters, but with distinct use cases. A related structure, xor sketches, can also be used for statistical estimation, including calculating the size of sets. Our experiments indicate a substantial improvement in accuracy over existing methods, particularly in estimating small set sizes. A new approach is proposed to derive trend analysis insights from order book data captured in the form of sequences of executions. Each execution within these sequences represents a minute's trading activity, with the order book's dynamic nature meaning that current executions are influenced by future events, making it crucial to consider their temporal connection. The sequence of executions, encapsulated in the form of a Markov process, serves as the foundation of a proposed hidden Markov model that aims to identify these temporal connections and understand how future events impact present trading activities. Utilizing this model's capabilities, two key indicators of trend analysis insights can be identified: the magnitude of events and the interdependence of sequences, both of which can be accurately forecasted with the ability to decipher temporal connections within sequences of executions. The model's predictive capabilities are put to the test in a simulation involving four diverse financial time series, with the results demonstrating that the magnitude and interdependence of sequences can be accurately forecasted six minutes in advance, even when the system is operated by a relatively simple algorithm. With the ability to accurately forecast these values within this timeframe, the system offers a valuable tool for analysts to make more informed decisions when operating in environments with limited access to information, as evidenced by the significant differences in accuracy observed when comparing the forecasted values obtained from this model and those obtained from a baseline method. As a solution, we introduce a new framework that uses image gradient information to assign tasks and build environments in a way that translates well from simulation to reality. Our method is fully autonomous and doesn't require any prior knowledge about the scenario, resulting in a consistent and effective outcome. In our experiments, our gradient-based approach excelled at a variety of tasks, including both those that required navigating around obstacles and those involving real-time state adjustments. Additionally, our autonomous pipeline saved a considerable amount of time by automating what would typically be a laborious process. Overall, our gradient-based method enables seamless task assignment and environment building, eliminating the need for goal definitions and resulting in a consistent and effective outcome. Significant progress in deep learning technology has enabled the creation of more convincing deepfakes, which are synthetic media that mask human faces with fabricated ones. However, deepfake creation still presents significant challenges, particularly when producing high-quality videos without revealing manipulation, especially in complex backgrounds. Our research addresses this limitation by developing a new deepfake creation technique that produces more realistic results overall. Specifically, our approach utilizes a background plate to guide the generation of a synthetic video, thereby improving the overall quality. In addition, we introduced and collected the first large-scale dataset, named Unrestricted Deepfakes, consisting of over 108,000 synthetic videos created using our proposed method. To further contribute to the field, we also developed and evaluated a novel video identification technique, which effectively detects deepfakes produced by our creation method using various feature extraction techniques, achieving an accuracy rate of 94.8% on the Unrestricted Deepfakes dataset. Our research provides notable advancements in deepfake creation and identification, opening up new avenues for further exploration. The created dataset is available at https://unideepfake.github.io. The discovery of numerous exoplanets in recent years has led to the potential for a significant breakthrough in the search for life beyond Earth, with many of these planets falling within the temperate zone and having similar sizes to that of Neptune. Soluble compounds like MgCl$_2$ and NaCl are thought to be present in abundance on these planets due to their extremely low pressures and high temperatures, and are therefore considered key factors in predicting the presence of liquid water. However, the abundance of these compounds is highly dependent on thermal vs. chemical equilibria, which could reveal signs of a surrounding ocean or a rocky core. This leads to the possibility of distinguishing between the two equilibria and the two phases (liquid and solid) of these compounds, which could provide crucial evidence of an accretion model based on solid objects. We have found that the soluble compound equilibria can be distinguished from the gas dynamical phase equilibria through measurable differences in transit signatures, which could serve as a primary indicator of an antiphase shift from solid to liquid. This leads to the possibility of distinguishing between solid and liquid phases, as well as the presence of an ocean or core, which could be confirmed through photometry over extended periods of time rather than spectroscopy. This research paves the way for a ground-breaking new approach in the search for extraterrestrial life, and implies a significant shift in the way we understand the composition of temperate sub-Neptunes. Furthermore, the vast majority of these planets are expected to have liquid-water soluble compounds in their atmospheres, which could lead to a massive discovery of ocean-planets. Finally, we could be on the cusp of uncovering evidence of cores with sizes and temperatures similar to that of Earth, which could provide a pivotal clue in our search for life beyond our planet. Moreover, the GRAVITY instrument on the Very Large Telescope (VLT) has the potential to detect clear-infrared signatures from an ocean or core, which could serve as a landmark finding and confirm our new approach. A novel spiking neural network, termed the Leap Frog neuron, is introduced, featuring dynamic membrane periods and adaptive synaptic connections that facilitate learning of input patterns in line with biological neural behavior. In contrast to traditional learning methods, our approach adapts the membrane period based on synapse strength, eliminating the need for tuning. Furthermore, it learns pattern associations through the incorporation of heterosynaptic plasticity, eliminating the need for separate teaching signals. Our analysis explores the learning dynamics of the Leap Frog neuron in response to varying membrane periods and synapse strength. When subjected to a sequence of patterns featuring changing frequencies, our model exhibits expected and biologically plausible responses in the form of phase-locked discharge sequences at the sequence rate, with inter-spike intervals corresponding to the synapse strength ratio between successive patterns. This novel architecture holds significant potential for the development of next-generation, biology-inspired artificial neural networks. Our findings stem from simulations conducted over extended periods of simulated biological time scales, with a particular emphasis on the underlying mechanisms and symmetry breaking in competitive learning scenarios. In-line with our objective of mimicking biological learning, our results reveal a marked disparity in learning speed when employed in a competitive versus cooperative learning environment. Our analysis and model outcomes indicate that robust pattern learning in spiking neural networks is feasible, providing a solid foundation for the creation of more realistic artificial neural networks. Our findings also raise intriguing questions about generalization to larger neural networks and the synthesis of these results with existing deep learning methods. In-line with our focus on biological plausibility, our model does not employ binary spiking, instead using a refined model that incorporates distinct membrane periods and adaptive synapses. Our analysis delves into the learning dynamics of this Leap Frog neuron in response to input sequences, exhibiting expected and biologically plausible responses. This novel architecture holds significant potential for the development of next-generation, biology-inspired artificial neural networks, with our findings indicating a marked disparity in learning speed when employed in competitive versus cooperative learning environments. Our model also exhibits distinct learning behaviors when subjected to input sequences featuring changing frequencies, discharging at the sequence rate in a phase-locked manner with inter-spike intervals corresponding to the synapse strength ratio between successive patterns. Our results suggest the feasibility of robust pattern learning in spiking neural networks, providing a solid foundation for the creation of more realistic artificial neural networks and our model can be applied to deepen the understanding of synaptic computation in biological neural networks. Additionally, it may provide a feasible solution for developing next-generation, biology-inspired neural networks capable of learning and generalizing patterns.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of this error measure in approximations derived from stochastic Galerkin projections, and also showcase its ability to improve the accuracy of approximations derived from stochastic collocation. Notably, our error measure can be computed using existing computational resources, thus allowing us to refine the approximations without incurring additional computational costs. We primarily use stochastic heat equations as our primary study object, although we also touch upon other types of equations with uncertain factors. Our solution employs two methods tailored to accommodate both unexpected fluctuations and anticipated modifications. The first method, with settings and confidence intervals, leverages empirical estimates similar to the Bernstein inequality to track alterations at specific times. It enables us to pinpoint the duration and timing of disruptions and efficiently isolate them without prior knowledge of data distribution or parameters. We also propose a method to efficiently update estimates and confidence intervals during changes. Furthermore, we describe two scenarios where alterations occur due to system changes with known and unknown probabilities, and provide an algorithm to accurately detect such alterations in both cases. Our approach allows real-time adaptation to changes and efficiently accumulates statistics during disruptions, providing accurate estimates and confidence intervals after the isolation of disruptions. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach through comparative analyses of its performance on synthetic and real-world datasets, specifically considering datasets with known and unknown probabilities, and datasets involving finite ranges of values. The efficacy of our detection and isolation methods is assessed through metrics such as accuracy, precision, false alarm rate, processing time, and memory usage, and our results show that our detectors excel relative to other alternatives. Notably, our solution outperforms other methods by as much as 25.66% in terms of processing time and up to 40.13% in terms of memory usage, and we make our implemented code available for reproduction of results and future use. With an average detection accuracy of and confidence intervals that accurately represent the alteration periods, our solution outperforms other approaches in efficiency and memory usage while providing a precise representation of data changes over time. This detailed analysis sheds light on the performance of adaptive algorithms in real-time data alteration detection, and we make the code used in our evaluation available for others to build upon. The development of our detection and isolation methods, along with our analysis and evaluation, contribute to the foundational knowledge of adaptive algorithms in real-time data alteration detection. Our solution has potential applications in areas such as public health, where modeling and adjusting for unexpected fluctuations in disease cases can inform policy-making and resource allocation. We've developed a new research approach focused on examining dwarf galaxies using their galaxy evolution history and chemical composition. This unique method utilizes data from the Miguel O. Werner (MOW) index, a spectral analysis metric, to uncover the contributions of Type II supernovae and stellar winds during the galaxy's early star-forming period. By combining MOW index measurements with a hydrodynamic simulation, we've gained insight into how this index changes throughout a galaxy's evolution. Furthermore, we've identified a direct relationship between the MOW index and outflows produced by star formation, enabling us to investigate a galaxy's history of mass loss and star formation using its chemical composition. This insight allows us to compare simulated galaxy evolution to actual galaxies, including dwarf galaxies like Leo A, Leo T, and Reticulum II, by back-calculating their historical star formation rates and mass losses. This approach includes a novel formula for calculating mass losses using a galaxy's metallicity. This method presents an innovative way to analyze a galaxy's star formation history and mass losses detectable by current observational technologies, even with a limited range of 0.1-100 kpc. It's an efficient tool for examining a galaxy's history using its chemical composition, allowing us to verify fundamental galaxy formation theories and make precise predictions for a galaxy's future evolution. This method could be expanded to various types of galaxies and is also applicable when a galaxy's accretion rate exceeds its mass loss rate. This research can serve as a benchmark for future high-resolution simulations of galaxy formation. Finally, we have found that galaxies with higher outflows have lower accretion rates, indicating a regression trend, and also discovered a correlation between gas expulsion and low-metallicity. This research is a fundamental extension of our earlier work on this subject, and we have made available synthetic spectra for well-studied galaxies, including Leo A, Leo T, Reticulum II, and SECCOS J0159-0948, as well as a Python script for quick analysis of their chemical compositions. This research has a wide range of applications and we have estimated the potential outcomes for an unspecified number of galaxies. Additionally, we have made available derived indices related to the MOW index, including four new ones, for the purposes of simplifying and streamlining galaxy analysis. A major hurdle in teaching AI to extract meaningful information from visually complex documents like identity cards, invoices, and receipts is the expense associated with labeling these images. Given that visually rich documents are ubiquitous in daily life and crucial from an operational and social standpoint, an automated document analysis technique known as OCR (Optical Character Recognition) is highly desirable. Even with an automated OCR process, labeling the extracted information for further use proves costly. To overcome this challenge, we've formulated a new approach called LabelGuide, which uses an automated process to generate detailed labels for visually complex documents at a reduced cost of $0.10 per image. Compared to manual labeling, LabelGuide reduces costs by a factor of 13. Additionally, LabelGuide's accuracy outperforms manual labeling at an equivalent cost, making it a cost-effective and accurate solution for labeling visually complex documents. The source code for LabelGuide is available on GitHub at the repository address labeled-guides.github.io. We welcome contributions and feedback. We show that DCLCM possesses intuitive modal interpretations, and these interpretations have strong connections to the calculus. Specifically, we find that DCLCM's modal formulas can be effectively translated into modal terms and that the calculus's modal axioms have logical counterparts. Furthermore, we identify cut-elimination procedures for DCLCM that are linked to a modified version of the Freytag-Bacci procedure. We also explore how to derive the soundness and completeness theorems for DCLCM's sequent calculus using a modified version of the Muroya-Yoneda procedure. Notably, our research reveals that DCLCM's modal logic is a more substantial extension of the underlying Lambek calculus than was previously observed in the case of modal Lambek calculi without distribution. Finally, we provide a computational analysis of the decidability properties for DCLCM and its associated modal logic. Specifically, we show that while DCLCM as a whole is decidable, its modal extension is inherently undecidable. High-performance computing on GPUs heavily relies on efficient memory allocation to achieve optimal performance. However, traditional sequential memory allocation is ineffective on these parallel processors, resulting in severe performance degradation. To address this issue, a high-speed memory allocator called DynaSOAr has been developed for object-based programming on GPUs, utilizing an optimized memory access strategy through area-concurrent memory requests. By dynamically adjusting memory allocation based on the GPU's memory usage, DynaSOAr ensures both efficient memory management and optimized memory access, overcoming GPU allocation limitations and enabling developers to focus on program development without worrying about memory allocation pitfalls. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's advanced features, including double-free detection, out-of-memory handling, and inter-object reference tracking, have been implemented to enhance overall program reliability and performance. Moreover, it offers a range of useful tools for programmers to leverage these features and easily customize DynaSOAr to suit their specific needs. Our experimental results demonstrate that DynaSOAr significantly boosts the overall performance of the MemAlloc benchmark by up to 60.41% and safely runs on GPUs without any memory-related errors. To cater to diverse user needs, the developed DynaSOAr allocator comes in eight different versions, each designed to address a particular area of concern in memory allocation for object-based programming on GPUs. To streamline the process of switching between these versions, a special memory allocator called MetaSOAr has been created, allowing users to easily change versions by simply recompiling the MetaSOAr code. The MetaSOAr implementation is an innovative adaptation of the MetaII concept, providing an intuitive and flexible interface for selecting the MetaSOAr version that best fits their specific requirements. By offering this level of flexibility and program reliability, DynaSOAr MetaSOAr makes it an extremely reliable and versatile solution for object-based programming on GPUs, further enhancing the overall performance and memory management capabilities of these programs. To showcase the performance benefits of DynaSOAr, a range of object-based program examples have been created, which highlight the advantages of using the allocator in specific scenarios. These demos, along with the DynaSOAr implementation, have been made publicly available on GitHub, enabling users to easily download and integrate the allocator into their programs. In various fields, there's a growing need for making confident predictions when faced with uncertain knowledge. Probabilistic model approximation through inference in Bayesian networks can help with this, but ensuring the accuracy of their probabilistic assumptions is a significant challenge. We've developed a new approach, called Sturdiness Assurance Certificate (SAC), that confirms the reliability of Bayesian networks by guaranteeing a certain level of precision in their probabilistic approximations when dealing with limited knowledge. Our method is based on analyzing the errors in probabilistic approximations over a circuit's parameterization, representing its probabilistic assumptions with a probabilistic circuit, and then ensuring these errors remain within specified bounds by relaxing constraints within this representation. Our technique allows for inferring the range of possible error margins in probabilistic predictions without previously expensive statistical analyses, thus providing a theoretical guarantee for the reliability of these predictions. Our experimental results, carried out in the field of medical diagnostics, have shown the practical applicability of our approach, and our current research is focused on broadening its adaptability to more complex circuits using discrete variables. Its potential applications extend beyond our tested domain to a wide array of fields including decision-making, diagnostic systems, and advice-giving systems. The source code for our approach is available at https://github.com/peski/sturdiness. Our formal description of the SAC method is detailed in arXiv:2205.01646. We propose a distorted resolvent method to obtain Nash equilibria in differential games. This technique involves distorting the resolvent of the Nash equilibrium equation, which can be modeled as a maximal monotone graph, using an extension of Bregman's variance. By studying the properties of this distortion, we show it maintains key mathematical integrity. This approach yields two critical benefits: it enables computation of Nash equilibria through the distorted resolvent's inverse, and it provides a metric for assessing the impact of perturbations in the game's parameters. Notably, the distorsion's effect diminishes as the game's discretized steps converge, ultimately resulting in the original Nash equilibrium as the discretization vanishes. To illustrate the method's utility, we apply it to a second-order differential game. Furthermore, the distorted resolvent operator gives rise to novel, improved regularity results for the Nash equilibrium equation. Specifically, we demonstrate improved regularity in both time and space, surpassing existing results in regularity theory. Lastly, the distorted resolvent operator also facilitates an analysis of the Nash equilibrium's sensitivity to the game's parameters, providing a metric for quantitative stability and convergence in both time and space. Specifically, we establish an estimate for how sensitive the equilibrium is to changes in the game's parameters, and show this sensitivity can be made arbitrarily small through adjustments to the game's parameters. These estimates are found to be sharp in various scenarios. Ultimately, the distorted resolvent method presents an efficient and versatile tool for studying Nash equilibria in differential games. To enhance the paper's readability, two additional sections have been incorporated, detailing key mathematical concepts: the properties of Bregman's variance and the properties of maximal monotone graphs. Additionally, two supplementary sections have been included, exploring novel implications of the distorted resolvent method: the first examines the method's connections to viscosity solutions in partial differential equations, and the second analyzes the method's connections to variational dynamics. Both of these avenues offer promising avenues for further research in the future. Lastly, the paper concludes by highlighting the numerous open directions for further study that it presents. Specifically, the distorted resolvent method presents a range of open research questions in multiple domains, including regularity theory, analysis of nonlinear operators, and the study of Nash equilibria in differential games under perturbations. Additionally, the method offers a range of open research questions in discrete-time settings, encompassing graph-related maximal monotone theory and Nash equilibria in game theory

This research focuses on using a one-stage CNN-based model to identify skin lesions and learn their associated diseases. The study utilizes the public HSII dataset containing 1,095 images to train a deep learning network to distinguish between three skin lesion types: seborrhoeic keratosis, melanoma, and nevus. To enhance performance and handle outlying data, a novel approach incorporating a SK-MVN layer into the CNN model is introduced. The SK-MVN layer identifies anomalous samples by calculating the standard deviation of class-specific probabilities in the cross-entropy loss function. This allows the model to adjust its training by eliminating outlier samples and optimizing its decision boundary. Compared to traditional loss functions, the proposed method yields improved accuracy on outlying samples and ultimately achieves higher overall accuracy across all classes. Furthermore, experiments demonstrating the model's ability to correctly identify outlying samples and its performance under data scarcity have also been conducted. The proposed method demonstrates effective handling of outlying samples and can improve skin lesion identification accuracy. The study's findings and data can provide valuable insights for researchers and clinicians working on skin lesion analysis. A recent study aimed to understand the limitations of these predictive models by exploring under what conditions they can accurately predict the behavior of a dropped object. Utilizing high-speed cameras, researchers collected a large dataset of human-generated minimal movements for a total of 88 objects with known properties. Using specialized software, the resulting data was analyzed to create maps outlining the predicted area where the models can accurately forecast the object's path. These maps showed that the predicted area only partially overlaps the region where the object lands closest to the point where it is dropped. Additionally, the maps varied depending on the type of movement used to generate the predictions and the estimated uncertainty associated with them. Crucially, the study found that even under best-case scenarios, the predictive models never achieve a perfect score in forecasting the object's path. These findings have significant implications for future research on dynamic identification, particularly when it comes to accurately determining an object's mass. It may no longer be sufficient to aim for high precision in such predictions and instead consider exploring other metrics to evaluate their effectiveness. Furthermore, researchers may need to no longer view perfect predictions as the ultimate goal and instead no longer consider static postures as the gold standard for observation. Finally, the study indicates that large datasets like the one collected can provide a more accurate understanding of how prediction models work, even without modifications to their underlying equations. It also identifies new research avenues that focus on quantifying the limitations of these models and developing techniques to validate their performance in practical, real-world scenarios. It further proposes dropping the term "dynamic identification" in favor of a more broad-based term, such as "dynamic estimation," to better capture the complexities and limitations involved. Lastly, the study suggests that large datasets like the one collected can serve as a valuable resource for other researchers working on object tracking. Leveraging this information could enable new advancements in evaluating how well predictive models match up with actual object behavior. It could also enable new breakthroughs in utilizing human minimal movements as a basis for developing simpler models that can predict the behavior of a dropped object. It could finally enable new insights into how the human body moves in a controlled environment. These potential research avenues are outlined in a provided list. It also distinguishes the approach used in this study from others and highlights how its integration of high-speed cameras and large datasets can provide a more comprehensive understanding of the dynamics involved.

Climate forecasting holds significant value for multiple applications such as agriculture, ecology, and economy. The linear regression model and various machine learning algorithms have been successful in climate forecasting, but their limitations become apparent when dealing with complex and intricate patterns. In contrast, artificial neural networks have been shown to adapt complex relationships, making them a promising choice for this task. Despite their potential, most neural networks struggle to capture climate data's dual characteristics of spatial and temporal dependencies. In response, researchers have explored encoder-decoder structures, incorporating self-attention mechanisms to model relationships across different scales and positions. Notably, transformer networks excelled in this task by utilizing multi-scale self-attention to capture spatial, temporal, and cross-scale interactions. Nonetheless, they failed to consider the unique requirements of climate forecasting, notably the dispersion of features along with the temporal dimension. To address this, we propose the Shifted Window Cross-Focus (SWCF) module, an innovative Swin-Transformer adaptation that incorporates a variable-sized window and multiple positional offsets to capture and aggregate dispersed features. When applied to the encoder of a decoder-encoder architecture, the SWCF module outperformed conventional multi-scale Swin-Transformer and adapter-free approaches, achieving notable improvements in accuracy and efficiency. Notably, our proposed method achieved unparalleled success when evaluated using real-world climate datasets, notably reaching 10% better RMSE and 8% better MAE compared to adapter-free models, and marking a significant increase in computational efficiency relative to decoder-encoder methods. The streamlined architecture of this model further boasts up to 50% less parameters compared to encoder-decoder models, thereby displaying superior performance, both in terms of performance and efficiency, across a range of real-world climate forecasting datasets. To facilitate further research, we have released the implementation of this model along with real-world climate data on an open-platform repository, thereby contributing to the field of climate forecasting and making our code publicly available at the specified URL. Furthermore, we have released the open-platform repository containing the model's implementation and climate data for other researchers to access. In brain tissue, the balance of nutrients and waste products depends heavily on a smooth blood-brain barrier, which can become impaired in diseases such as multiple sclerosis. This study aimed to investigate how white blood cells cause damage to this barrier, leading to neurological disorders. To simulate how these cells affect the brain's ability to regulate its chemical environment, we developed an optimization model incorporating partial differential equations (PDEs). Specifically, we focused on a simplified scenario involving a single neuron, sodium, calcium, potassium, and a specific type of white blood cell called a T-cell. Assuming the brain's tissue is homogeneous and not affected by the T-cell's presence, we derived equations that describe how these substances move through the tissue and are consumed or produced at specific rates. As these cells interact with the brain's tissue, they cause micro-scattered lesions, which can lead to the broad brain damage patterns seen in actual MS scans. We applied numerical methods to solve these PDEs and used an optimization approach to determine the best way these cells should move through the tissue to cause the most damage. We tested our model's ability to simulate real-world scenarios, including the effects of certain substances that can worsen or mimic MS-like damage. Overall, this study provides a foundation for further research into how specific cells might contribute to the development of neurological disorders by causing damage to the blood-brain barrier, ultimately leading to changes in the brain's tissue that can be seen in scans. Furthermore, this model can be used to investigate potential treatments by finding the most effective way to prevent this damage, which could lead to improved outcomes. The human brain's operational intelligence can be attributed to distinct regions working together in a coordinated manner, similar to superposition of quantum states. Research in quantum-inspired optimization has shown promising results in solving real-world problems, however most of this work revolves around quantum circuits and their associated hardware implementations. What if we told you that you don't need a quantum computer to harness the power of quantum-inspired optimizations? Can neural networks trained to embody quantum principles outperform their classical counterparts in various baselines? In this study, we demonstrate the capabilities of neural networks modeled after quantum systems in multiple tasks and find that their robustness and efficiency surpasses that of conventional neural networks. Furthermore, the quantum-inspired neural networks' success can be attributed to their training on data that is generated using a special type of graph structure. Building on these findings, we propose a new approach based on the concept of network motifs that enables the discovery of hidden patterns within interconnected datasets without prior knowledge of the underlying graph structure. This methodology maintains high levels of accuracy even in low data regimes and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both graph-based and quantum-inspired neural network approaches. Additionally, the quantum-inspired neural networks and our proposed discovery method exhibit exceptional robustness against various adversarial attacks, making them suitable for high-stakes applications such as financial analysis. The techniques proposed here can be applied to tackle a wide array of challenges across different domains and provide a significant advancement in resolving real-world problems using quantum-inspired optimizations without actually employing quantum computers. This is a significant breakthrough as the developed models and algorithms are purely software-based, thus enabling deployment across a multitude of platforms including GPUs, TensorsFlow, TFX, TFM and JAX. Three-body $\tau$-decays offer a window into the mass spectra of heavy hadrons, allowing the calculation of branching ratios related to the weak interaction. This process involves three-body hadronic decay rates, including terms representing the movement of hadrons and shifts in their motion-related energy. To overcome technical hurdles in computing these rates, researchers developed approximate methods such as the flat shape factor technique. This article challenges this approximation by directly computing hadronic currents and shape factors for certain types of decays, providing a more accurate representation of the movement of hadrons and its associated energy. Consequently, this correction impacts the calculation of absolute branching ratios for $\tau$-decays involving $D$-mesons, leading to a revised ratio of branching ratios between two decay channels. This article also explores how to apply these findings to further understand the quark and gluon structure of hadronic particles, although the precise implications of these findings require further investigation. Finally, this article specifies the necessary mathematical expressions to compute hadronic currents and shape factors for other types of $\tau$-decays. Additionally, this article examines how to express these currents in terms of flat shape factors and explains why certain approximations may not be sufficient in describing the interaction between leptons and hadrons. Finally, this article provides a computation of the shape factors for specific types of $\tau$-decays, including formulas involving gauge-invariant expressions. These shape factors can be used to improve the understanding of the mass spectra of certain hadronic particles, such as the $D_1(2430)$ and $D_1(2400)$ resonances. The study further extends to non-parametrized Tversky metrics, with analysis of their properties and relationships among them. Deep dependency parsers trained with extensive contexts have demonstrated superior performance in NLP tasks. However, models built on rich context struggle to achieve success when data is scarce, particularly in languages lacking thorough syntactic analysis. This study introduces a novel self-learning framework, combining contextualized dependencies with resource-limited constituent tagging. The framework comprises three key components: Contextualized Dependency Self-learning (CDSL), boosted sampling, and adaptive learning rates. CDSL utilizes contextualized dependency trees to generate synthetic training data and a dependency parser, both optimized through resource-rich languages. This approach is independent of specific dependency parsing models and can be applied with or without background data. Experimental results on multiple languages show significant performance gains with the proposed framework, particularly in cases with limited resource. Specifically, accuracy on NLP tasks increased by 6.67% overall, with gains as high as 11.42% in cases of extreme data scarcity. This methodology is available on GitHub under the address https://github.com/pcyin/CDLS. A detailed report on experiments is available through arXiv, https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.14233. The HUMBI dataset is designed to facilitate the development of robust 3D human pose estimation algorithms, particularly in scenarios where multiple viewpoints are involved. To enhance the effectiveness of proposed methods, a benchmark challenge will be launched, utilizing the HUMBI dataset to evaluate a variety of tasks, including 3D human pose estimation from a single or composite image, as well as other related tasks. Participants will be encouraged to submit their work for evaluation, with both traditional and learning-based approaches welcomed. The HUMBI collection and associated challenge can be accessed via the website http://humbi.inria.fr for your reference. The collection was initially made available on May 2nd, 2022. The challenge deadline for submissions is October 15th, 2022. The collection and associated challenge will be maintained in the future to support ongoing evaluation and benchmarking efforts. The code to reproduce the benchmark challenge can be accessed via the repository https://github.com/Cheng-Chen2021/HUMBI. The collection code is based on OpenMPC, an independent repository maintained by Guan, et al. The repository address is https://guan-ci.github.io/OpenMPC/index.html for your reference. The collection was initially made available on June 2nd, 2021. The collection code is designed to be modular, allowing users to access and utilize the HUMBI collection through the OpenMPC repository via standard APIs, such as GetHUMBI, which can be found at https://guan-ci.github.io/OpenMPC/api/HUMBI.html. The collection was initially made available on June 2nd, 2021. The baseline codes for the benchmark challenge will be maintained in the repository https://guan-ci.github/io/OpenMPC/baseline.html. The baseline codes were initially added on November 15th, 2021. The collection and associated challenge were presented for the first time at the Conference of Computer and Robot Vision, held on October 17-20, 2021, in Kelowna, Canada. A short paper detailing the HUMBI collection has been published in the Proceedings of the 2021 Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, which can be found at the link https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPRW42653

To facilitate cross-lingual transfer in NLP without language-specific model preparation, researchers typically rely on costly and time-consuming techniques, such as NLP data translation. We introduce a model-independent approach that enables seamless, language-specific training to testing shifts by leveraging neural machine translation models and a task representation technique, called task depictions. This innovative method eliminates the need for NLP data translation and offers two key advantages: it's both highly efficient and highly effective. We conduct comprehensive experiments across six diverse NLP tasks and find that our approach consistently achieves improvements over direct translation methods. We also provide insight into the effectiveness of neural machine translation models in facilitating cross-lingual transfer. Further details are available on our website at https://ntd-clt.github.io/ntd-clt/. The source code can be accessed on GitHub at https://github.com/ntd-clt/ntd-clt. We anticipate that our task depictions will serve as a valuable model-independent resource for undertaking NLP tasks across languages. Moreover, we envisions that our work will pave the way for novel applications in data-efficient NLP training. With continuous advancements in neural machine translation models and task depictions, we expect that language barriers will gradually erode, enabling seamless and efficient NLP tasks across all languages. It is noteworthy that our work echoes the sentiments of early AI researchers who envisioned a future where NLP tasks could be easily performed across languages. We hope that our research will contribute to the realization of this vision. We demonstrate the efficacy of our model-independent approach by achieving positive cross-lingual transfer results for a range of tasks, including sentiment analysis, semantic role labeling, and question answering. We observe that improvements average 2.5 F1 points and task depictions also enable task selection, enabling researchers to determine which tasks can be successfully accomplished across languages. We anticipate that our models-independent approach will pave the way for efficient NLP training and provide valuable insights into neural machine translation models. A prominent video super-resolution model, BasicVSR, was introduced in 2021 and has since become a standard benchmark in the field. This model successfully combined a custom propagation module with a state-of-the-art image SR model to achieve superior performance. However, its use was limited to specific propagation intervals. This paper proposes an improved model, BasicVSR++, which achieves more flexible and efficient video SR with propagation modules of varying lengths. The model's accuracy is further enhanced by incorporating a novel frame alignment module. Experimental results confirm the superiority of BasicVSR++, which demonstrates a range of $2-10$ times improvement over the original BasicVSR and other prominent models in the field. Details about the model's architecture, code implementation, and datasets used for training can be found in the paper. BasicVSR++ has been successfully applied in a real-world SR video processing pipeline and has shown significant performance gains. This paper employs a temporal and spatial analysis to investigate the connection between severe weather events, electricity consumption, and generation output. A detailed examination of hourly electricity data reveals significant decreases in demand and notable shifts in energy output patterns during hurricanes in the US. Notably, outside hurricane-affected areas, a distinct evening peak in electricity consumption is replaced with a morning peak following the events. Furthermore, a notable drop in energy production from nuclear and coal sources is observed in regions impacted by hurricanes. Additionally, increases in electricity consumption and certain types of energy production are associated with mid-latitudinal tempests in Brazil, primarily influenced by storms bringing warm, humid air from the equator, resulting in elevated electricity demand due to increased air conditioning usage. Our analysis explores how severe weather events influence energy markets and demand for immediate knowledge in this field. Existing literature typically analyzes severe weather events from a singular perspective, such as demand or energy output, rather than exploring their comprehensive impact on energy consumption and generation output. This study fills this knowledge gap by examining the widespread effects of such events in a unified context. Our findings can guide the development of predictive models, informing decision-makers about the far-reaching impacts of severe weather events on energy consumption and generation output worldwide. With the increasing frequency and severity of such events, caused by climate change, understanding their multifaceted effects on energy systems is of utmost importance. As demonstrated by our analysis, these events can result in distinct patterns of electricity consumption, rendering existing models and simulations obsolete. Our work explicitly acknowledges the potential for other mechanisms driving demand patterns during severe weather events, while highlighting the inherent differences in energy consumption between mild and extreme weather conditions. Moreover, our investigation into the impact of severe weather events on energy production sheds light on their far-reaching effects, extending beyond electricity consumption to influence energy output and production. Our analysis provides a quantitative understanding of these effects, revealing reductions of up to 10% in energy output following hurricanes and increases of up to 5% in electricity consumption due to tempests. Meanwhile, the nuclear and coal sectors collectively recorded a decline of up to 20% in energy output following hurricanes. Conversely, our investigation into the effects of tempests revealed a corresponding 2% increase in electricity consumption. Clifford analysis employs the Clifford algebra and monogenic functions to extend classical complex analysis to higher dimensions. The Dirac operator, derived from the Clifford product of vectors and differential operators, plays a crucial role in Clifford analysis, and its eigenvalues/eigenfunctions are pivotal in space decomposition and integral representation formulas. This study involves deriving the latter using eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator as basis functions, and it demonstrates a 'three-sphere' theorem analogous to the complex case. Following this, the article develops expressions for singular values and singular functions of the Dirac operator according to spectral theory principles. The article concludes by establishing an integral representation of square-integrable monogenic functions via singular functions of the Dirac operator. The key findings presented here were initially reported at the 8th, 9th, and 10th International Conferences on Clifford Algebra in 2012, 2014, and 2016. This article offers an expanded version of those presentations, featuring updated content and revised expressions following the initial publications. Firstly, we explore the inherent disorder of 1D systems with rules that vary unpredictably, and secondly, we examine how this inherent disorder interacts with unforeseen events. During both situations, the inherent disorder leads to an unpredictable sequence, and we reveal a universal structure underlying both scenarios, which gives rise to an extensive family of highly organized patterns. We discover that this extensive family is immune to disruptions and always exists in a system capable of producing unpredictable outcomes, and furthermore, we demonstrate a direct relationship between this extensive family and a well-studied sequence related to parsing logic. In this study, we explore a scalar sector consisting of two fields with weights larger than one, both coupled to fermions and gauge bosons in a manner similar to the Higgs mechanism. We propose an extended scalar standard model (ESSM) that naturally incorporates alignment of scalar fields and yields a stable vacuum characterized by heavy, non-degenerate scalars. We demonstrate that heavy scalar masses of 3-6 TeV are feasible given current constraints from LHC runs 1 and 2, although they conflict with standard alignment models. We examine the potential for the SSM and ESSM to be detected through the production and decay of scalar pairs at future colliders like HL-LHC, CLIC, and a possible 100 TeV proton-proton collider. Additionally, the study considers the potential for single-scalar production and decays in these contexts. Based on our findings, the ESSM appears more likely to be detected at future colliders than the SSM. Specifically, detecting the SSM and ESSM may be feasible at 20-50% the rate of standard model observations at HL-LHC, CLIC, and a 100 TeV proton-proton collider if the scalar masses do not exceed 300 GeV, 500 GeV, and 700 GeV, respectively. The proposed research also lays a foundation for a strategic plan to explore the potential for discovering SM-like scenarios with future colliders. The study further highlights the significance of examining the potential for detecting scalar fields with weight larger than one in experiments with the HL-LHC, CLIC, and a 100 TeV proton-proton collider. The research also examines the potential for determining model parameters through the production and decay of scalar pairs at future colliders. The ESSM appears more likely to be detected at future colliders if the model includes light scalar fields at 200 GeV, 300 GeV, and 1 TeV weight, respectively. The proposed research also considers the potential for single-scalar production and decays in these contexts. Based on our findings, the SSM and ESSM appear most detectable through the production and decay of scalar pairs at future colliders if they feature a heavy, light scalar pair at 300 GeV, 200 GeV, and 1 TeV, respectively. The study also examines the potential for discovering the SSM and ESSM through their signature in the goldstone sector at future colliders. This study presents the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet model, an implicit generative framework for raw audio signals. Building on the success of WaveNet in high-quality audio generation, we've refined the approach to better capture long-term correlation patterns essential for generating quasi-periodic signals. Our model integrates pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks into WaveNet, enabling the network to learn pitch-independent features. Experimental evaluations validate the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet's effectiveness in generating quasi-periodic signals of varying fundamental frequencies. Notably, integrating pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks has yielded state-of-the-art results of $0.70 \pm 0.01$ for the SSIM metric, surpassing WaveNet's performance by $0.07$ or incorporating only pitch-sensitive CNNs. Moreover, the model demonstrates resilience to overfitting even when trained using a relatively small number of samples, producing high-quality audio samples even with limited training data. As such, the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet provides a robust foundation for synthesizing quasi-periodic signals, particularly in low-resource scenarios. The effectiveness of collaborative filtering techniques depends on adequately capturing the complex and intricate patterns found in user preference data. Given the challenge of CF's data inherent issues such as data sparsity, noisy data and subjectivity, it is crucial to address these problems in order to improve the algorithms. This research aims to tackle these problems by proposing a novel approach called USCB. It utilizes an unsupervised biclustering method that puts forward a set of key principles: managing preference localization, density, and generalizability within user and item groups separately. This approach aims to uncover and learn these preferences while reducing subjectivity through generalizability. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of USCB compared to state-of-the-art methods in terms of precision, recall, F1-score, F-measure and coverage. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm is also evaluated and shown to be scalable for large datasets including Wikipedia and Delicious. Finally, the efficacy of USCB is validated through sensitivity analysis and its recommendability is confirmed. This study's contributions are threefold. Firstly, it validates the importance of preserving data locality in CF. Secondly, it demonstrates biclustering's generalizability as an effective method for tackling subjectivity in preference data. Lastly, it successfully combines predictability and generalizability simultaneously. The source code for USCB is available at https://github.com/JaychandraUSCB/USCB.
